News.title: Trump live: Zelensky and Netanyahu at White House as Donald set to quiz Putin
News.content:
Donald Trump is holding crucial talks at the White House with Volodymyr Zelensky and Benjamin Netanyahu, who are both in Washington DC for the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham

Donald Trump is set to hold crucial talks with Volodymyr Zelensky and Benjamin Netanyahu at the White House today - just days after Zelensky accused Russia of helping Iran target US troops.

Both the Ukrainian president and Israeli prime minister are in Washington DC to attend the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, who died earlier this month aged 71.

Zelensky has said he plans to discuss strengthening Ukraine's anti-ballistic missile defences with Trump. It comes after the Ukrainian leader said on Saturday that Kyiv has intelligence indicating Russia shared satellite imagery with Tehran, enabling Iran to target US military bases in the Middle East. Trump said that he will "find out if that's true" and "ask Putin about it".

After meeting Zelensky, Trump will hold talks with Netanyahu - marking their first in-person meeting since the US-Israeli war on Iran began on February 28.

News.title: France wildfires live: Thousands of tourists evacuated from coast near Bordeaux
News.content:
Flames are nearing the French Atlantic Coast with raging wildfires now nine miles from Bordeaux as the city's mayor says he's prepared for 'all eventualities'

More than than 4,000 tourists have been evacuated from an area near the French Atlantic Coast as inferno wildfires burn nearby.

Holidaymakers have been forced to leave campsites, tourist homes, holiday villages and leisure parks around Lacanau, which is around 40 miles from Bordeaux. The order comes as firefighters race against time to bring the fires under control before the country's south-west is blasted by a forecast 40C heatwave tomorrow (Wednesday).

Officials say the largest blaze has "stabilised" but have warned it could still burn out of control again as temperatures rise and humidity falls.

French President Emmanuel Macron says the wildfires are the "most difficult situation" his country has dealt with since World War Two, with more than 260,000 people now evacuated from their homes in the south-west.

The mayor of Bordeaux, Thomas Cazenave, says he is preparing for "all eventualities" and that authorities are preparing to "accommodate a large number of people should further evacuations be ordered".

Meanwhile in Spain, 63,000 people have been evacuate from their homes near Madrid, with the country's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez calling it "the most painful expression of the climate emergency".

News.title: Japan earthquake live: 'Many fatalities' as mall explodes during 7.1-mag quake
News.content:
Multiple people have died while more are missing after a shopping centre collapsed following a huge 7.1 magnitude earthquake on the Japanese island of Kyushu

Authorities in Japan say there are 'many fatalities' following the horror collapse of a major shopping centre during today's powerful earthquake.

Up to 30 others remain missing at the Aeon Mall in Kumamoto, while employees are also missing at the nearby Nippon Paper Industries Yatsushiro Plant.

The massive quake measured at the highest possible level seven on Japan's own Shindo "scale of shaking" and has left tens of thousands without power. Kumamoto Airport has been closed indefinitely after the earthquake rocked its runway.

A tsunami warning was issued after the 7.1 magnitude quake rocked multiple towns in Kumamoto province on the southern Japanese island of Kyushu - where roughly 13million people live. The alert was for the province's Ariake bay but has since been lifted.

Kumamoto was hit with a deadly quake in 2016 that left more than 50 people dead, 1,800 injured and tens of thousands of homes damaged or destroyed.

News.title: Love Island final LIVE: Winner Lorenzo responds to doubts about his relationship with Julia
News.content:
Yesterday's final of Love Island crowned Lorenzo and Julia as the 13th season's winners and he has now responded to fans' doubts about their relationship's strength

The Love Island has officially ended with Lorenzo Alessi and Julia Majchrzak announced as winners, beating out stiff competition from Kavan Murphy and Jasmine Muller.

News.title: Seven-year-old boy 'in critical condition' after two die at West Mersea Beach tragedy
News.content:
Seven-year-old boy 'in critical condition' after two die at West Mersea Beach tragedy

Sameeha Rahman, 15, her mother Shelina Rahman, 41, and seven-year-old Musa Ahmed were in the water along with three other family members when they got into difficulty

View 3 Images The Coastguard helping at the scene on the beach at West Mersea (Image: BBC)

A young boy remains in critical condition following an incident at West Mersea Beach which left his teenage cousin and her mum dead, police have said.

‌



Sameeha Rahman, 15, her mother Shelina Rahman, 41, and seven-year-old Musa Ahmed were in the water along with three other family members when they got into difficulty on July 22.

‌



All family members subsequently made “significant efforts to help each other”, Essex Police said on Tuesday.

‌



Sameeha and Shelina Rahman, from the Ilford area in east London, died, while Musa was flown to hospital where he remains in a critical condition.

View 3 Images Samiha Rahman, 15, died in the tragedy

A number of family members were also taken to hospital as a result of the incident and are recovering, the force added.

‌



Detective Chief Inspector Al Pitcher, who leads the investigation, said: “We are continuing to support Shelina and Sameeha’s family through this extremely difficult time.

“They had been enjoying a family day at the beach together when this tragedy happened. We are working to establish the circumstances which led up to this incident and our inquiries are ongoing.

“We have spoken to a number of key witnesses and will continue to do so over the coming days and will work with partners including the fire service, local council, and coastguard.”

‌



Chief Inspector Michelle Sparks, district commander for Colchester, thanked the local community for their response to the incident.

View 3 Images Shelina Rahman died after getting into difficulty in the sea

“There were members of the public who rushed to help the family and I want to thank them for their courage and selflessness,” she said.

‌



“Since this tragic incident we have also seen an outpouring of support and sympathy. At times of tragedy you get to see how strong a community is, and we have a fantastic community on Mersea Island, and across the Colchester district.”

Essex Police previously said officers were called by the ambulance service at 5.35pm on July 22 after reports that several people had got into difficulty in the water near Seaview Avenue.

The East of England Ambulance Service said one patient was transported by air and three taken by road to hospital after the incident at Sea View Holiday Park.

‌



Musa’s father Shahin Ahmed released a statement early on Monday in which he called for “a review of safety measures” at the site.

“I strongly agree with the calls from local residents for a review of safety measures at West Mersea Beach, including the provision of additional life-saving equipment and clear warning signage,” he said.

“While no action now can undo the pain we are suffering, we hope lessons can be learned to help prevent similar tragedies from happening in the future.”

News.title: Inside King Charles’ search for new right-hand man to take Royal Family’s most demanding job
News.content:
Inside King Charles’ search for new right-hand man to take Royal Family’s most demanding job

King Charles’ most senior aide, his principal private secretary is stepping down, with Buckingham Palace now facing the gruelling task of finding a successor

View 6 Images Charles' principal private secretary is stepping down (Image: Getty Images)

Buckingham Palace faces the major task of replacing the King’s right-hand man — and most senior aide — as he is stepping down.

‌



Sir Clive Alderton, who has worked for the Royal Household for 20 years and is currently Charles and Queen Camilla’s principal private secretary, will vacate his role next year to coincide with his 60th birthday in May 2027.

‌



It means the search is on to find someone ready to take on one of the most demanding roles in the Royal Household, overseeing the monarch's official business while acting as a key adviser to the King and Queen.

‌



In a message to staff, Sir Clive had said: “It has been the greatest imaginable honour to serve the King and Queen in my present role through such historic times and with unforgettable humour along the way. That support will continue, in a less formal capacity, for all of my life.”

Disgraced Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor set to lose final honour after failing to respond to request READ MORE :

Meghan Markle’s MasterChef episode ratings soar despite mixed reviews from viewers READ MORE :

6 View 6 Images The King with Sir Clive Alderton at Sandringham earlier this year (Image: Getty Images) 6 View 6 Images Sir Clive has worked for the Royal Household since 2006 (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Royal sources say an open and rigorous recruitment process for his successor will begin, with the aim of identifying the highest calibre external and internal candidates.

And it seems whoever is the King's new principal private secretary must possess a combination of constitutional expertise, diplomatic experience and personal discretion, as they must be across all official work of the monarch, as well as many private matters.

This behind-the-scenes figure takes on responsibility for everything from speeches and correspondence, to official presents and congratulatory messages to members of the public, according to the Royal Family’s website.

‌



The role requires extensive knowledge of the politics, history and culture of not only the United Kingdom but also the 14 other realms where the King is head of state, including Australia, New Zealand and Canada.

View 6 Images Sir Clive will step down from his role in May next year (Image: PA)

A strong understanding of the Church of England is also essential, as is knowledge of military affairs, reflecting the sovereign's role as head of the armed forces.

‌



On a personal level, the position also demands the ability to handle sensitive family matters with discretion, as a source told the Times, this can include offering guidance to the monarch when difficulties arise involving "a brother or perhaps a son."

View 6 Images Sir Clive receives a renumeration package of approximately £300,000 a year

Sir Clive receives a remuneration package of approximately £300,000 per year, although the only guaranteed break in the working week for the principal secretary is a single hour on Sundays while the King and Queen attend church.

‌



The role of the principal private secretary is arguably the most important in the Royal Household, with the individual seen by the King’s side at almost all events. Sir Clive was most notably seen supporting the monarch when he formed part of the walking procession behind the coffin during the state funeral of Elizabeth II in 2022.

Former royal correspondent and author of Courtiers: The Hidden Power Behind the Crown, Valentine Low previously spoke of the demands of the job, giving a fascinating insight into the world of the royals' right-hand staff and why their work is so crucial.

View 6 Images Sir Clive with the King leaving an event at St Paul's Cathedral (Image: Getty Images)

‌



"They're the machinery of the palace," Low said of the key staff members during an appearance on HELLO!'s podcast in 2024. "They organise their public life, engagements, they're their gatekeeper, they determine who gets to see the member of the royal family, they write speeches, they advise, they advise on policy, and they're also a constant companion. They are with them a lot of the time."

Sir Clive has been one of the most influential figures in the British Royal Household for 20 years. Alderton first joined Charles's household in 2006 as Deputy Private Secretary when Charles was Prince of Wales, before he was promoted to Principal Private Secretary to the Prince of Wales and the Duchess of Cornwall in 2015, becoming Charles's most senior aide.

Article continues below

During his time as the King’s principal private secretary, he has led the monarch through his cancer diagnosis and many incoming and outgoing state visits, including his trip to Washington DC to meet US president Donald Trump, where Charles delivered an historic address to Congress. Alderton has also steered the King through more personal matters, helping to manage the fallout of Prince Harry and Meghan quitting their royal roles.

However, Harry is said to have regarded Sir Clive as one of the “men in grey suits” at the Palace and although he did not refer to him by name, appeared to give him the nickname “the Wasp” in his autobiography. He wrote in his controversial memoir Spare: “Without warning, he’d give you such a stab with his outsized stinger that you’d cry out in confusion.”

News.title: Michael Sheen chose folk icons over Duran Duran during 1980s upbringing
News.content:
Good Omens and Frost/Nixon star Michael Sheen says he’d choose folk music over new romantics any day - despite being a teenager in the 1980s. The Welsh actor says: ”Jethro Tull, I was absolutely obsessed by growing up in the 80s. I mean, don’t get me wrong, I like Duran Duran as well, but Jethro Tull had my heart.”

And the Blackpool band, who blend progressive rock with folk and classical music, will feature prominently on Michael’s playlist when he hosts the Radio 2 Folk Show tonight at 9pm.

His next injection of folk came when he made the 2002 comedy drama Heartlands with Celia Imrie.

View 3 Images Duran Duran in 1981. Left to right guitarist Andy Taylor, bassist John Taylor, singer Simon Le Bon, drummer Roger Taylor and keyboard player Nick Rhodes. (Image: Getty Images)

‌



He says: ”The music for that film was done by Kate Rusby [folk singer/songwriter]. She, in fact, appeared in the film as well. She played a few songs live for us which was a real treat.”

Michael, who is a judge for The Daily Mirror’s Pride of Britain Awards with P&O Cruises, has another treasured musical memory, involving English folk group, The Unthanks.

Michael, who lives in Port Talbot, South Wales, with his partner Anna Lundberg and their children Lily Mo, Lyra and Mabli, says he made performers Rachel and Becky Unthank sing for their supper, after seeing them perform at his local arts centre in Pontardawe.

View 3 Images Becky Unthank and Rachel Unthank from The Unthanks perform on stage during the Cambridge Folk Festival 2019 (Image: Getty Images)

‌



He says: “They came over to the house, and we gave them a spag bol and a glass of mulled wine in the lead up to Christmas. It was wonderful to be able to host them at our house there and, in fact, my then 5-year old daughter Lyra, overwhelmed by the fact that there was a real band in our kitchen, forced them to sing for their supper .

“Becky and Rachel Unthank sat in our kitchen harmonising live. It’s something I will always remember.”

*Michael Sheen will present The Folk Show on Wednesday 29 July on Radio 2 from 9-10pm, or listen on BBC Sounds

News.title: Most dangerous places to live in 2026 mapped and ranked - is yours on the list?
News.content:
Most dangerous places to live in 2026 mapped and ranked - is yours on the list?

The latest Home Office crime figures show there has been a rise in some serious offending including stalking and harassment, robbery, drug crime and possession of weapons

View 2 Images Our map highlights the crime rates across England and Wales - the darker hue, the higher the rate

An industrial Yorkshire town has overtaken a popular seaside resort as the most dangerous place to live.

‌



Data obtained by the Mirror shows the crime rate in Middlesbrough in North Yorkshire is worse than any other place in England and Wales, excluding central London and the City of Westminster. Blackpool in Lancashire did have the unenviable tag in 2025, but its rate has improved.

‌



Our map, embedded below, shows the locations of the towns and cities. The latest Home Office recorded crime figures show that there has been a rise in some serious types of offending across England and Wales, including sexual offences (by 4 per cent), stalking and harassment (4 per cent), robbery (10 per cent), drug crime (12 per cent), and possession of weapons (8 per cent).

‌



But the general trend of falling crime over the past decade has continued. In the year ending March 2026, more than five million non-fraud offenses were recorded, a 1 per cent drop on the previous 12 months.

View 2 Images Middlesborough historically had a large shipbuilding industry (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

‌



Abandoned town still has furniture in homes after 20,000 residents left overnight READ MORE :

Driver caught doing 114mph in a 30 near primary school and another did 161mph READ MORE :

The highest volume of offences are committed in the nation’s biggest cities, including Birmingham, Leeds, and Manchester. But crime rates, which take population size into account, are generally considered the fairest way to compare crime across areas of wildly different sizes.

Published quarterly, they reveal the areas where people are most likely to experience crime. As of December 2025, Blackpool had the highest crime rate, according to these figures. But in the most recent update, covering the 12 months up to March 2026, Middlesbrough has overtaken Blackpool as the most crime-ravaged part of England and Wales, excluding central London and the City of Westminster.

Article continues below

That is because crime has fallen by 4 per cent in Blackpool over the past 12 months, while it has increased slightly by 1 per cent in Middlesbrough. In the past 12 months, there have been 23,419 crimes in Middlesbrough, translating to a crime rate of 150 crimes per 1,000 people in the North East town.

Despite the drop in crime, Blackpool has the second-highest crime rate in the country, with 146 offenses per 1,000 residents. Manchester is third, with a rate of 143 crimes per 1,000 residents, followed by Hartlepool (134) and Bristol (131).

Meanwhile, Broadland in Norfolk has retained its title as the safest place to live in mainland England and Wales, with the nation’s lowest crime rate of 35 crimes per 1,000 residents. You can see how it compares where you live using our interactive map.

News.title: Powell says student loan system at top of in-tray
News.content:
Lucy Powell has said she wants to make sure the student loans system is "fair" and that the issue is at the top of her in-tray as the new education secretary.

Labour's deputy leader told the BBC she stood by comments she made in February that the interest rates graduates with Plan 2 loans were paying were "egregious".

She said she was committed to looking at the issue, although acknowledged she "can't make any promises" about changes.

Plan 2 loans were taken out by students in England between September 2012 and July 2023, and are still issued in Wales. Graduates pay back what they earn above the repayment threshold at a rate of 9%.

In November last year, then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves said the repayment threshold for students with Plan 2 loans would be frozen at Â£29,385 between 2027 and 2030, instead of rising with inflation.

The change would result in students starting to repay their loans sooner than they would otherwise have done, and their rising salaries leading to greater repayments.

Campaigners have called for that decision to be reversed.

Reeves later said the government's measures were "fair and proportionate" for getting "the balance right between tax and spending".

In April, the government said interest on some student loans in England - including Plan 2 - would be capped at 6%.

Speaking to Matt Chorley on BBC Radio 5 Live, Powell said she was "very familiar" with the issue as her eldest child has a Plan 2 loan.

She said: "I think it's not just about the threshold of when people start to pay it back, but also the interest rate which is RPI [retail prices index] plus 3%.

"I think I've called it in the past egregious and I'm not going to change my opinion on that just because I'm now the secretary of state.

"The government has committed to a review of that, it's very much at the top of my in-tray as the secretary of state, and I want to make sure we look at this so it's fair for students."

Powell described it as a "real cost-of-living issue" for young people, adding: "They're paying high repayments and never, ever paying off the capital of their student loan."

Pressed on whether it is something she will look at, Powell replied: "Yes. I can't make any promises, but it needs looking at."

MPs on the Treasury Committee this month said comparing student loan repayments to phone contracts or cinema tickets "amounted to mis-selling" by government.

It came after a BBC investigation found the government compared student loan repayments to Â£30-a-month phone contracts in promotional presentations to teenagers a decade ago.

Earlier this year, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she would cut the rate of interest charged on Plan 2 loans, capping it at RPI only. The current RPI rate is 3%.

News.title: Funeral director 'left baby's remains on floor for two years'
News.content:
This story contains details some might find distressing.

The remains of a stillborn baby were left on the floor of a funeral home for almost two years and his grieving parents given the wrong ashes, a court has heard.

Former undertaker Robert Bush admitted 67 offences, including failing to bury and cremate people at Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull.

Jasmine Beverley told Hull Crown Court that learning her baby Sunny-Beverley Conlin was discovered in a brown paper bag on the floor of the Hessle Road parlour in March 2024 "will stay with me for the rest of my life".

Addressing Bush through tears, she told him: "I trusted you with the most precious person in my life."

News.title: Naga Munchetty to leave BBC Breakfast after 17 years
News.content:
Munchetty, 51, is among the best-paid presenters on the BBC's star salaries list, earning about Â£360,000 a year, according to the latest accounts.

She has interviewed major celebrities and politicians on the programme over the years ranging from Hillary Clinton and Michelle Obama to Sir Keir Starmer, Sir David Attenborough and Sir Rod Stewart.

In 2016, she appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing.

She has also been at the centre of some controversies during her time on BBC Breakfast.

In 2019, she was initially found to have breached the BBC's guidelines over comments she made about a social media post from Donald Trump about four female politicians of colour.

However, the BBC's director general then reversed that finding after deciding her words were not "sufficient to merit" upholding part of the complaint.

In 2021, Munchetty and co-presenter Charlie Stayt were "spoken to and reminded of their responsibilities" after complaints about their reaction to a government minister's flag. Munchetty apologised for liking "offensive" tweets about the exchange.

In June 2025, the Sun reported details of two alleged incidents which the paper said caused BBC bosses to speak to Munchetty about her conduct.

That came amid reports of behind-the-scenes tensions on the show, and at the same time as the programme's editor Richard Frediani took extended leave following allegations about his behaviour.

Frediani returned to work two weeks later and remains editor of BBC Breakfast.

At the time, the BBC said it did not comment on individual cases but took all complaints about conduct at work extremely seriously. Munchetty and Frediani did not comment on the reports.

The programme won a Bafta TV Award last year for best news coverage for a special about the Post Office scandal.

News.title: Odyssey translator writes scathing review of Nolan film adaptation
News.content:
Sir Christopher Nolan's latest film, The Odyssey, may have won rave reviews from critics and done storming business at the box office - but one person is definitely not happy.

Emily Wilson, the academic whose 2017 translation of Homer's Odyssey was cited by the director as an influence on his adaptation of the poem, has written a scathing review of the movie.

Published in the London Review of Books, external, Wilson said she "would be ashamed to have written any of this script", describing the film's narrative structure as "gimmicky."

"The writing is abysmal," she said. "None of the characters has convincing motivation for their actions or words. There are no sex scenes, and all the food looks horrible."

News.title: Mother and boyfriend guilty of murder of girl, two
News.content:
Warning: This story contains distressing details

A mother and her new boyfriend have been found guilty of murdering her two-year-old daughter, with the man also convicted of sexually abusing the girl.

Isabelle Welsh suffered multiple injuries in the weeks before she collapsed with a fractured skull at her home in Thornaby in September 2025, Teesside Crown Court had heard.

Alexandra Walker, 25, and her partner Harrison Simpson, 22, were both found guilty of murder and child cruelty, with Simpson also convicted of sexual abuse of a child.

They will be sentenced on Thursday. Isabelle's family said she had her "whole life ahead of her" but it was "taken in the most heartbreaking way".

Prosecutors previously said the couple, who began a relationship in June 2025, were both responsible for a "wicked" campaign of sexual abuse and violence against Isabelle.

Walker and Simpson blamed each other for the girl's injuries and suffering.

News.title: Can Burnham's vision for Manchester's schools really work for the rest of England?
News.content:
Two years ago, I stood at the back of a conference room in Manchester Hall, sipping a coffee and watching Andy Burnham unveil his vision for transforming technical education in Greater Manchester.

He had announced plans for the Manchester Baccalaureate, or MBacc, the year before, and, armed with PowerPoint slides and guest speakers, was running through the ins and outs in front of a room full of education and business leaders.

Now, as prime minister, Burnham has announced plans to make that idea national, and overhaul the technical education system across the whole of England.

The details are still scarce at this stage. We know it will involve giving pupils the option to study more vocational courses and take up work experience from Year 10, but how it will work in practice is still up in the air.

One thing that is certain is that the thinking behind it, and the ambition, is the same as that which underpins the MBacc: a determination to give teenagers a clear, step-by-step route into more practical and technical jobs.

The trouble is, the MBacc itself can be quite a difficult concept to get your head around if you're not familiar with it.

Let's be clear from the start: it's not another type of qualification, like the T-levels and V-levels announced in England in recent years.

Instead, it's a framework that aims to give teenagers a "clear line of sight to good jobs" in vocational and technical areas.

The best way to think about it is a step-by-step route - picture a flow chart - that teenagers can follow from school into any given technical career.

It's set up in parallel to a more clearly defined academic route. During that conference event in July 2024, Burnham and other speakers made clear that those who want to go on to desk jobs can follow a well-trodden path of GCSEs, A-levels, and a university degree.

But for those who want more practical careers, the landscape is much more complicated.

The MBacc is best seen as an effort to simplify that landscape, spelling out for teenagers who want to go into more vocational or technical careers which courses they can study, and ensuring they have the opportunity to study them along with hands-on work experience.

It spells out routes to careers in seven different categories:

Construction and the green economy

Creative, culture and sport

Digital and technology

Education and early years

Financial, business and professional services

Health and social care

Manufacturing and engineering

Its success is difficult to measure, since the MBacc is still in its infancy.

It's not until 2030 that it seeks to achieve its mission of guaranteeing every young person a clear path to good jobs. By 2035, the aim is for every young person to have 45 days of work experience by the time they're 19.

According to the most recent data, the MBacc has been rolled out across 101 secondary schools and colleges in Greater Manchester - about 40% of the total.

The Greater Manchester Combined Authority says 1,405 young people accessed workplace experiences during its second year.

Time will tell, as those teenagers leave school and enter the world of work, how transformative it will be.

News.title: Schools to offer technical subjects to pupils from age 14 in England, Burnham says
News.content:
Secondary school pupils in England will be able to study subjects like manufacturing and AI in addition to core academic learning under reforms outlined by Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

The government said the courses, which would be available from Year 10, would be linked to local industries and designed to give children a clearer pathway into work.

Data published this year showed more than one million young people across the UK were not in education, employment or training, the highest level in more than 12 years.

Few details have been published about how the new vocational courses would work in practice and it is not clear how they would operate in areas with low industrial activity.

The BBC understands that the government expects the new pathways into work to be up and running in some areas by 2028.

Later on Tuesday, the government also announced a new bursary of up to Â£4,500 for some families who would lose out on money if their children wanted to do an apprenticeship, because the child benefit they would lose out on would be worth more than the apprenticeship starter salary.

Speaking at a train manufacturing site in Derby, Burnham said: "We've had a system built for too long around the university route and it sends a message to some young people that they're some kind of second-class citizens, and it's just not right.

"They need an education system that works for them as well, that offers a path to all young people, that's balanced between academic and technical."

The prime minister said he was "on a mission" to reduce the number of young people not in education, employment or training - known as "Neet" - but declined to put a target date on his ambition.

"The trend is rising at the moment, so the first thing I've got to do is to stop that rise," he said.

"It's hard to put a firm date on the moment when you can say there are fewer than now."

However, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said while there was a "broad consensus" on improving vocational education, it was "not a big bold announcement".

She told BBC Breakfast: "What's going on there is a drastic shortage of jobs because Labour's policies over the last couple of years have killed job opportunities for young people. This announcement will not solve that."

News.title: Fourth heatwave grips parts of UK with 35C forecast
News.content:
A fourth heatwave of the year is now under way for parts of the UK, with temperatures expected to climb into the mid-30s Celsius later this week.

This latest spell of heatwave threshold-level temperatures is expected to peak on Wednesday in the south-east and east of England.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has warned the rising temperatures could increase health risks, particularly for vulnerable groups.

It has issued amber heat health alerts, external for much of eastern England that come into force on Wednesday.

News.title: Laughter and tears at Dame Penelope Keith funeral
News.content:
Dame Penelope Keith's funeral has been hailed as "wonderful, beautiful and absolutely amazing" by her friends.

The actress, who starred in The Good Life and To The Manor Born, "died peacefully whilst living with cancer at her home" on 29 June at the age of 86.

Crowds lined the streets to say their goodbyes to the "very special lady" as her coffin travelled through her home town of Milford in Surrey before the service at Guildford Cathedral.

Broadcaster, writer and former politician Gyles Brandreth said the funeral was "filled with a mixture of sadness but laughter and gratitude as well because we were celebrating a great actress".

"It was a wonderful way to remember a remarkable person," he told BBC Radio Surrey.

Posting on X later, he said: "There was laughter and tears at Guildford Cathedral this morning - a truly beautiful and deeply moving funeral service for Dame Penelope Keith - what a lady and what a perfect service.

"It caught her completely. She was very special."

News.title: Unsolved Suzy Lamplugh case 'haunts' detectives
News.content:
Police officers investigating the disappearance of estate agent Suzy Lamplugh in west London say they remain "haunted" by the case, four decades after she went missing.

Lamplugh, 25, vanished after leaving her Fulham office to meet a client on the afternoon of 28 July 1986. She never returned and her body has never been found.

As the Metropolitan Police investigation is due to be mothballed next year, cold case detectives say they are troubled by the continuing mystery.

To mark the 40th anniversary of her disappearance, the Lamplugh family has released previously unseen photographs featuring her siblings Lizzie, Tamsin and Richard and her parents Paul and Diana.

In releasing the intimate family images, her siblings described her as "a truly beautiful person inside and out".

News.title: Man guilty of murdering two men found in woods
News.content:
A man has been found guilty of murdering two men he met in a homeless shelter.

James Desborough had previously admitted preventing the lawful burial in 2025 of 57-year-old Claudio Aquilino and 43-year-old Daniel Coleman.

A jury at Winchester Crown Court heard the 40-year-old, of Old Oak Woods, Lower Sticker, Cornwall, dismembered his victims' bodies, tried to burn their remains and hid them in woodland where he owned a cabin.

He is due to be sentenced on Wednesday. In March, Desborough was found guilty of murdering his cellmate in Exeter Prison while on remand for this trial.

During the trial, the court heard Aquilino was last seen alive on 18 April 2025 and Coleman was last seen on 3 June 2025.

Both men had suffered from serious addictions and were seen in the company of Desborough on pub CCTV in Newquay and Truro respectively.

Prosecutors said both men were likely killed by Desborough soon after they were last seen.

News.title: Hundreds of thousands of women get morning-after pill via free pharmacy service
News.content:
The morning-after pill, known as emergency contraception, external, is medication designed to prevent unwanted pregnancies. It usually has to be taken within three to five days of having unprotected sex. The sooner it is taken, the more effective it is.

It works by delaying or preventing the release of an egg, but will only prevent pregnancy if ovulation has not already happened.

Alternatively, women can visit a doctor or nurse to have a coil or intrauterine device (IUD) fitted to prevent pregnancy at any time during their menstrual cycle. To be effective, it needs to be fitted within 120 hours or five days of unprotected sex.

The government said making the morning-after pill available free from pharmacies would end the "unfair" barriers and postcode lottery some women faced - with access varying dramatically depending on where they live.

Under the scheme, women can visit their local pharmacy and have a confidential consultation with a pharmacist or trained pharmacy technician, before receiving the medication on the same day.

Prior to this, women had to book an appointment with their GP, sexual health clinic or pharmacy to get the morning-after pill. Women could also access it privately, as they still can now.

In 2024/25, there were around 150,000 NHS prescriptions for the morning-after pill - far fewer than under the new service.

Dr Sue Mann, NHS National Clinical Director for Women's Health, said the pharmacy service was a "major step forward for women's health", with "no appointment, no waiting and no judgement".

"This service is already making a real impact, particularly for women living in more deprived communities, by making contraception easier to access closer to home," she added.

Women can check online, external to find their nearest participating pharmacy. All pharmacists and pharmacy technicians delivering the service have received specialist training to provide emergency contraception and wider contraceptive care.

News.title: Richard Hammond fined £999 for  speeding offences
News.content:
Former Top Gear presenter Richard Hammond has been fined Â£999 after being caught speeding twice in three weeks while driving luxury cars.

The 56-year-old was captured driving his Porsche Taycan Cross Turismo at 68mph in a 50mph limit on the A40 in Pencraig, Herefordshire on 2 December.

He was later clocked driving his Bentley Continental GT at 82mph in a 70mph limit on the M50 Rudhall Overbridge, also in Herefordshire, on 22 December.

Hammond pleaded guilty to two speeding charges through his solicitor. Two further charges that he had ignored the police letters and failed to identify himself as the guilty driver were withdrawn by police.

He was also given seven penalty points for his licence at the hearing last week.

Magistrate Ann Minton ordered him to pay a total of Â£1,771, comprising two fines of Â£333 and Â£666, Â£240 in costs and victim surcharges totalling Â£532.

News.title: The 10 most overcrowded commuter trains revealed
News.content:
The most overcrowded train service in England and Wales last autumn was a Thameslink morning rush hour service between Bedford and Three Bridges in West Sussex, according to the Department for Transport (DfT).

Second on the list was a West Midlands service from London Euston to Crewe, Cheshire, departing at 17:46, the government figures reveal.

Overall, they show overcrowding on commuter trains serving major English and Welsh cities fell slightly, for the first time since 2020, due to an increase in capacity.

Only 1.1% of peak-time travellers were on an overcrowded train, the DfT said. More than 1.2 million of the average 1.9 million journeys on a typical autumn day were in London.

The DfT says work is under way to improve capacity where there are pinch points during peak hours.

The Thameslink service which topped the list had a "load factor" â meaning how full the train was â of 176% at London St Pancras shortly after 08:00.

The West Midlands service to Crewe had a load factor of 170%. It was busiest when it departed Euston.

The third most crowded train was a Transport for Wales service from Bridgend to Rhymney, with a load factor of 161%. It was busiest at Llanishen.

Four of the top ten services were operated by South Western, and Thameslink appeared twice more.

A powerful tornado remained on the ground for more than 20 minutes as it tore through northeastern Wisconsin Monday, leveling homes, tossing cars and bringing down power lines.

Officials were going door-to-door assessing the damage Tuesday after the twister devastated the Fox Cities region, which includes Appleton, Menasha, and Neenah, approximately 100 miles northwest of Milwaukee. There have been no reports of deaths or missing persons.

The National Weather Service reported that the tornado, which struck in the early afternoon after residents received warnings to take cover, traveled approximately 12 miles (19 kilometers). At its widest, the storm stretched nearly a mile (1.6 kilometers) across, tearing roofs from homes and businesses, overturning vehicles, stripping tree tops, and felling utility poles.

"The depth of the tornado and its impact is incredible, devastating. We’re really still at the assessment stage," Winnebago County Executive Gordon Hintz said at a Tuesday news conference. He noted that while some injuries occurred, the midday timing was fortunate as many residents were at work rather than at home.

open image in gallery The tornado remained on the ground for about 12 miles ( AP Photo/Kayla Wolf )

Over 15,000 customers in Winnebago and Outagamie counties remained without electricity on Tuesday, according to PowerOutage.us, with restoration potentially taking several days. Shelters have been established for displaced residents, and a boil water advisory was issued for a section of Fox Crossing's water system that lost pressure.

It was a relatively powerful twister

The twister was spun off by a large storm system that moved through the Great Lakes, fueled by a buildup of heat and humidity, the weather service said.

Weather service officials were assessing the damage Tuesday, said Roy Eckberg, an agency meteorologist.

“To get that kind of tornado is pretty rare in northeast Wisconsin, but they do happen from time to time,” he said, adding that it was unusual that the twister moved southward instead of to the east or northeast.

open image in gallery It hollowed out homes, tossed around cars and toppled power lines ( AP Photo/Kayla Wolf )

Preliminary data indicates it was an EF3, meaning it packed winds of 136-165 mph (219-266 kph), the weather service said.

Residents describe terrifying moments as tornado barreled through

Heather Schroeder said she heard cracking and popping all around her as the twister tore apart a laundromat, bakery and tavern along a street corner in Menasha.

Rescue workers pulled someone out of one of the buildings and it wasn't clear if they had survived, said Schroeder, who works nearby. Cars were turned upside-down, and there was a gas leak at the laundromat, she said.

“There’s nothing left,” Schroeder said.

open image in gallery Preliminary data indicated it was an EF3, meaning it packed winds of 136-165 mph (219-266 kph) ( AP Photo/Kayla Wolf )

Aerial video Tuesday showed homes in Menasha without roofs or that had been completely hollowed out.

Greg Van Driest was working in downtown Appleton when the sky got as dark as night.

“The word we all were using was ‘ominous,’” he said. “It’s like, ‘Whoa, look at that.’ ... You looked outside and you thought it was three in the morning, it was that dark.”

Gordon Hintz, Winnebago County’s top elected official, said he received multiple reports of buildings destroyed and vehicles overturned. All storm warnings that could be made ahead of time to get people to safety were activated, he said.

“Obviously when you look at the damage, Mother Nature doesn’t really care,” he said.

The sting of the United States’ abrupt exit from the 2026 World Cup, following a 4-1 defeat to Belgium in the round of 16, continues to resonate deeply with goalkeeper Matt Freese.

He admits the memory is far from fading, and he’s not convinced it ever will.

"Big losses in tough moments are things you never really get over because they stay with you for the rest of your career," Freese told The Associated Press ahead of the Major League Soccer All-Star Game in Charlotte. "They continue to motivate you for the rest of your career."

Freese was at the center of a critical moment in the match, making a costly error when he rushed out of his box to clear a long ball, then hesitated under pressure. Belgium swiftly capitalized on the miscue, converting it into a goal that extended their lead to 3-1 in the 57th minute, effectively sealing the Americans' fate.

The incident has not been forgotten by American soccer fans; in his first MLS match since the World Cup, the New York City FC goalkeeper was reportedly booed by fans every time he touched the ball during a game in Columbus, Ohio.

Despite the public scrutiny, Freese maintains a philosophical outlook.

open image in gallery Freese was at fault for Belgium's third goal ( Getty )

"It’s important to not let bad things define you, but I think it's also important not to let good things define you either," he said. "It's important to be a consistent presence with consistent energy." Freese is one of four U.S. national team players selected for the upcoming MLS All-Star Game.

Veteran defender Tim Ream, another All-Star, openly acknowledges there’s no secret formula for the Americans to reach the World Cup quarterfinals. He points to one undeniable factor for success: relentless hard work.

"You put your head down and do as much as you possibly can," Ream said. "And, at some point you will break through that barrier. It just takes work, more work and more work. ... Before you know it, you're past that." Ream believes better days are ahead for the national team despite the recent disappointment.

Wing-back Max Arfsten shares this optimism, suggesting that the increased fan attention on the World Cup, with the majority of games played in the United States, will inspire more athletes in the country to embrace the sport.

"The next step for us is to keep growing the sport," Arfsten said. "The more people that are playing, the better players there will be. The more competitiveness, the more players playing in the top leagues in Europe is important as well. I feel like all of those combined is going to lead to success."

Ream added that players can hold two truths simultaneously regarding the World Cup: disappointment over their performance and "crashing out" against Belgium, alongside excitement for their earlier accomplishments.

open image in gallery Tim Ream believes hard work will help the US reach the next level ( Getty )

"You can be proud of how much it galvanized the country, the people around it and the sport — and just how much fun it was," Ream reflected. Freese echoed this sentiment, emphasizing the importance of recognizing positive outcomes to inspire future generations to surpass the round of 16, reach the quarterfinals, and ultimately contend for the semifinals and finals.

Meanwhile, Charlotte is set to host the MLS All-Star Game for the first time at Charlotte FC owner Dave Tepper's Bank of America Stadium. However, the league's biggest star, Lionel Messi, will not participate.

Messi, who led Argentina to the World Cup final before their loss to Spain, is taking allotted time off before returning to Inter Miami CF, and has been replaced on the roster. He has recorded 12 goals and eight assists in MLS play this season.

Several players, including Ream, have noted a significant surge in fan interest in MLS games and soccer generally since the World Cup.

"We could see it while we were playing in the World Cup, but now it's like I can't leave my house," Ream remarked, not as a complaint, but as an observation of the sport's growing popularity.

"Being able to inspire more people to play is obviously secondary to what our job is, which is compete and win games, but it's such a rewarding feeling knowing that so many more people are paying attention to our sport," he concluded.

Police in Guyana filed murder charges on Tuesday against the captain and two crew members of a state ferry that capsized, killing more than 70 people, with 30 passengers still missing.

Accused are Captain Kevin Price, 40, chief mate Rondell Dwayne Roberts, 42, and cargo superintendent Delon Granderson, 33. They appeared in court on Tuesday morning but were not required to enter pleas. No attorneys were present for them.

Authorities believe 179 people were aboard the ferry that departed the capital, Georgetown, on July 18 and capsized in Atlantic waters before reaching its destination, the northern town of Port Kaituma near Venezuela. It was the South American nation’s worst maritime disaster on record.

Prime Minister Mark Phillips told Parliament late Monday that while 77 people were rescued, one of those passengers recently died.

During his speech, opposition lawmakers pounded desks and heckled legislators as they called for the resignation of Works Minister Juan Edghill and Junior Minister Indar Persaud, holding them responsible for the disaster.

On Sunday, Guyana’s government announced the creation of a five-person commission made up of international legal and marine experts tasked with investigating the sinking of the 87-year-old MV Barima.

The government has said the ferry was still in operation because work is ongoing to build a pier at Port Kaituma to accommodate a new $12.7 million vessel acquired from India in recent months to replace the MV Barima.

Some survivors told reporters that the ferry was leaking and overcrowded with passengers and cargo. The government has asked the commission to examine those allegations.

Phillips, the prime minister, said it’s likely that the vessel, which now lies 50 feet (15 meters) underwater, will remain there and not be salvaged.

A second hearing is set for Aug. 3 at a court in the western Essequibo region near the sunken wreckage.

A man who fears persecution in Iran has spent 15 years in the UK battling a failed asylum claim, homeless and unable to lead a normal life, after repeated refusals by the Home Office to allow him to stay.

In the more than a decade he has been trapped in the asylum system, Mostafa Rahmani has not been allowed to work and has refused Home Office accommodation for most of his time in the UK – forced to depend on the kindness of friends to get by.

Mr Rahmani, now 41, he arrived in the UK from Iran in 2011 as a 24-year-old student looking to learn English. He came on a student visa, but claimed asylum a few days after arrival when he says Iranian security forces turned up at his family’s home in Tehran looking for him. He said that he had taken part in anti-government protests in 2011.

Since 2012, he has been involved in an Iranian women’s rights campaign group in the UK, called 8mars, relying on its members for support and friendship. He says he is at risk of persecution and death at the hands of Iran’s security forces if he returns due to his anti-government campaigning. But the Home Office disagrees, saying that Mr Rahmani does not hold a sufficient political profile in the UK or Iran to be considered at such risk.

Mr Rahmani, supported by Birchtree Law Chambers law firm, has had his asylum application rejected several times and is now waiting to hear the Home Office’s verdict of his latest challenge.

open image in gallery Mostafa pictured in Iran before he came to the UK on a student visa ( Mostafa Rahmani )

Speaking about his time in limbo in the UK, Mr Rahmani told The Independent: “My programme and dreams for my life, for years and years, are all gone.”

He explained: “I used to sleep in the street, and in an Asda parking area, or on buses. Often big apartment blocks have rubbish rooms, and when it was cold I would sleep there. One supermarket was in Wembley, another was in Acton. Sometimes I would stay in churches and they would give me food.

“I made friends and I could go to different places to shower if I needed, around Enfield and Acton.”

open image in gallery Mostafa Rahmani has been a supporter of an Iranian womens’ rights group since 2012 ( Mostafa Rahmani )

“It is only recently that I have been allowed accommodation from the Home Office, but even now it is sometimes better to live on the road than stay in their accommodation. I have to share a bunk bed with a man who talks all the time to his family back in Afghanistan, which makes it hard to sleep. So when that happens, I go out and look for a bus to sleep.”

Iran has been the most common country of nationality among asylum applicants and small boat arrivals to the UK in recent years. Around 63,000 Iranian citizens applied for asylum in the UK in the decade between 2016 and 2025, according to data analysis by the University of Oxford’s Migration Observatory.

Last year, 58 per cent of Iranians were granted asylum the first time they applied. However, those who are refused are unlikely to be sent back as very few Iranians are deported due to the country’s terrible human rights record, and since March 2026, conflict with the US and Israel has engulfed the country and wider Middle East region. In the first three months of 2026, 42 Iranians were forcibly deported from the UK, and 15 people returned voluntarily, Home Office data shows.

Mr Rahmani described his life before the UK, saying: “Back in Iran I had my own car, I had my father to support me, I had a good life, I had my own room. My situation here, it is not comparable to the standard of living that I had. I thought about going back to Iran so many times, but the Iranian government kill and hang people and I know I cannot.

“Most of all I wish for a visa so that I can go abroad to see my mum, who is 70 years old. I hope that I can one day meet my parents in Turkey, before anything happens to them. My friend got his visa after eight years but his mother died before they could reunite – I am worried this will happen to me.”

open image in gallery Mostafa Rahmani, an Iranian asylum seeker who has been in immigration limbo for 15 years ( The Independent )

His friend Leila Parnian, a member of 8mars has known him for 20 years. Speaking about his time in the UK, she explained: “They did not give him a chance to live like a normal person. He doesn’t have a future, a life, kids or work. He’s stuck here. For 15-16 years, they have played with his life and he doesn’t have anything. Not even one room for himself to do what he wants.

“He doesn’t know what to do with his life, he cannot stay here like this. He cannot go back to his country. Every day the Islamic regime is hanging young people. It’s not fair, to play with somebody’s life for nearly 16 years, without any reason.

“He came as a young person and he is now 41, and he has nothing in his hands.”

Rashad Nawaz, director at Birchtree Law which is supporting his asylum application, said: “Having worked on Mr Rahmani’s case I can say he is genuinely committed to his cause and has over a decade consistently informed the secretary of state about his work campaigning for women’s rights in Iran.

“8mars have very clearly stated that his life would be in danger upon return to Iran because of his political activities in the UK. Mr Rahmani puts on a brave face when facing the world but I have witnessed first-hand his mental health deteriorating.

“It is frankly bizarre for the secretary of state to consistently deny Mr Rahmani permission to stay when she cannot remove him to Iran because she accepts Iran has an awful human rights record. I hope sense will prevail and he is given permission to stay."

The Home Office said it does not comment on individual cases.

Human rights groups have condemned Israel’s plans to build a crocodile-filled moat around a prison holding Palestinian detainees as “vicious” and “nonsensical”.

Far-right national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir is seeking to introduce the reptiles at Ketziot Prison in southern Israel in a move directly inspired by Alligator Alcatraz, the US immigration detention facility which closed in June.

Last week, a source in Ben-Gvir’s office confirmed that digging was already underway at the maximum-security prison after the Israeli government reclassified the Nile crocodile as a “tended wild animal”, allowing them to be kept on the site.

The 170-metre-long moat, which will cost $6.3m, will surround the prison.

Ketziot currently holds an undisclosed number of Palestinian prisoners who are accused of being members of Hamas’ elite Nukhba force, who were involved in the Nova Festival massacre in October 2023.

Ben-Gvir’s project has faced significant domestic and international backlash, despite his claim it will reduce the burden on prison staff.

Moazzam Begg, director of human rights group CAGE International, told The Independent: “Modelling a prison on Alcatraz is nonsensical.

“The fact that we’re even trying to rationalise using crocodiles as a legitimate security apparatus in the 21st century feels outright satirical.”

open image in gallery The plans are being managed by Itamar Ben-Gvir ( Getty )

Former Homeland Security secretary Kristi Noem’s flagship detention centre, Alligator Alcatraz, was scrapped in the face of several lawsuits alleging inhumane and unconstitutional conditions and threats to a sprawling protected nature preserve in June this year.

A report published by Amnesty International found that the conditions in Alcatraz were tantamount to torture, including the routine and prolonged use of shackles and the use of the “box” – a 2x2ft cage-like structure that prisoners were put in as punishment.

Mr Begg expressed concerns that the attempt to emulate Alcatraz could lead to similar human rights violations, saying: “Israel regularly acts with impunity under the pretext of national security.

“Adding crocodiles is just another vicious decision in the consistent mistreatment of Palestinians.”

More than 50 harrowing testimonies of prisoner abuse at Ketziot were published by B’Tselem, an Israeli human rights organisation, following the October 7 attacks.

open image in gallery Trump (centre), Florida Governor Ron DeSantis (right), and secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem (not pictured) tour a migrant detention centre, dubbed ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ ( AFP/Getty )

However, the Israeli government has maintained that the proposed crocodile moat addresses a “real need” for security due to the penitentiary system’s acute overcrowding crisis.

Israel’s environmental protection minister, Idit Silman, said: “Yes, it serves as a deterrent. They have a very great fear of crocodiles. We are speaking in a language our enemies understand.

“Everyone can laugh if they want, but the number of terrorists has increased by thousands, while the number of prison guards has not.”

In a bid to accelerate the project, Ms Silman has signed an administrative order that reclassified the previously “protected” Nile crocodiles, as “managed wild animals.”

open image in gallery Nile crocodiles were previously classed as a ‘protected’ species ( BBC )

The decision means that government bodies – including the Israel Prison Service (IPS) – can hold them under specific security conditions.

Ben-Gvir celebrated the decision on Facebook on Thursday, posting an AI-generated image of himself holding a crocodile on a lead.

“Damn terrorist, thinking of trying to escape? Think again,” the minister wrote.

Silman’s decision has drawn major opposition from the Israel Nature and Parks Authority (INPA) and environmental groups, which argued the move is unlawful and puts both crocodiles and the public at risk.

In a statement to The Times of Israel, the INPA said there was "no sufficient professional basis" to permit crocodiles to be kept at security facilities.

The statement concluded that “security should be achieved through real means, not through animals”.

Ben-Gvir said that the choice to proceed with the plans was part of a “unique mission against terrorists.”

During his tenure, the treatment of Palestinian prisoners has deteriorated dramatically, according to a report authored by the United Nations.

In a now-deleted post on X in July 2024, the national security minister said: “One of the ultimate goals I set for myself [as minister] is worsening the [incarceration] conditions for terrorists in prisons, and to reducing their rights to the minimum required by law.”

News.content:

A Michigan father, who police say killed his family before taking his own life, has been identified as a former American Heart Association executive who lost his job weeks earlier, a family friend revealed.

Kristopher Karolkiewicz, 47, was found dead Friday inside the family’s home in Grand Haven Township alongside his wife, Amanda “Mandy” Karolkiewicz, 39, the Ottawa County Sheriff’s Office confirmed to The Independent. Firefighters first responded to the home Friday morning after reports of smoke but found no fire. They returned hours later after white smoke was spotted and discovered the family members dead inside.

The couple’s six children, including four biological boys ages 15, 12, 11 and 5 and two 11-year-old girls adopted from China as infants, were also found dead inside the home. Mandy and her daughters had returned from a China trip just days before the killings, local outlet 13 On Your Side reported.

Autopsies determined all eight family members died from gunshot wounds, authorities said. The deaths of Amanda and the children were ruled homicides, while Kristopher’s death was ruled a suicide. The fire was intentionally set in multiple areas of the home after the killings, and the family’s pets died from fire and smoke exposure, investigators said.

open image in gallery Kristopher Karolkiewicz a former vice president of sales and marketing at the National American Heart Association, has been identified as the man authorities say killed his wife and their six children Friday in Grand Haven Township, Michigan ( TikTok/@MandyKarol )

Kristopher Karolkiewicz worked remotely as the National American Heart Association’s vice president of sales and marketing beginning in September 2023, the association confirmed to The Independent. The organization said his “employment ended” earlier this month.

The American Heart Association said it does not comment on personnel matters due to company policy. However, a family friend told 13 On Your Side that Karolkiewicz had been fired from his position.

“As an organization with professional staff who are dedicated to helping others, we are devastated by the news out of Grand Haven, and our thoughts are with the loved ones of those who lost their lives in this tragedy,” the American Heart Association told The Independent in a statement.

Family spokesperson Emily Jones recalled Mandy Karolkiewicz as spunk as she spoke after her death.

“She was just somebody that you loved whenever they walked in the room because your day was about to be better,” Emily Jones said, according to WOOD-TV.

open image in gallery The couple’s six children, between the ages of 5 and 15, were found with gunshot wounds inside the home that had been set on fire ( AP )

Mandy Karolkiewicz was remembered as a beloved substitute teacher who worked with students in Grand Haven Area schools.

"Mandy goes above and beyond for students, especially when they’re having a hard day, responding with empathy, patience, and care. She pours her heart into her work, is always willing to help wherever needed, and helps make Peach Plains a better place to learn and work," a Facebook post praising her work earlier this year reads.

If you are based in the USA, and you or someone you know needs mental health assistance right now, call or text 988, or visit 988lifeline.org to access online chat from the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This is a free, confidential crisis hotline that is available to everyone 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

If you are experiencing feelings of distress, or are struggling to cope, you can speak to the Samaritans, in confidence, on 116 123 (UK and ROI) or visit the Samaritans website to find details of your nearest branch.

If you are in another country, you can go to www.befrienders.org to find a helpline near you.

News.title: Uefa issues furious response after Fifa plans to sell stakes in the World Cup
News.content:

Uefa has reacted furiously to reports that Fifa president Gianni Infantino is planning to sell stakes in the men’s World Cup to investors.

Infantino is plotting a scheme whereby Fifa would retain majority control of the World Cup and the rest would be sold, partly to each of Fifa’s 211 national associations, and partly to private investment, according to reports by The Times and Financial Times on Tuesday.

The plan could potentially see Infantino installed as the “commissioner” of the World Cup when his Fifa presidency finally ends in 2031, a position which would prove extremely lucrative.

Uefa, the governing body of European football and a long-term critic of Infantino, said in a statement: “This crosses a line that football’s governing institutions should never cross.

“UEFA takes it extremely seriously. So should every National Football Association. So should every stakeholder: leagues, clubs, players, supporters, governments and everyone who cares about the future of the game. The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade - especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially.

“None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA’s to sell.”

Gianni Infantino has defended Fifa’s handling of the World Cup (Bradley Collyer/PA) ( PA Wire )

The investment would be led by Joshua Kushner, the brother of Jared Kushner who is married to President Donald Trump’s daughter Ivanka, through his Thrive Eternal fund.

Thrive Eternal, a new investment strategy launched by venture capital firm Thrive Capital, is expected to be ⁠a lead investor in the entity, the source said. The strategy is a permanent capital vehicle focused on making a small number of long-term investments in franchises and cultural institutions.

Thrive Eternal took a minority stake in Major League ‌Baseball’s San Francisco Giants this year. The ​vehicle was founded by Joshua Kushner, ‌the brother of Jared ⁠Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law. Former ⁠Walt Disney CEO Bob Iger serves as an adviser.

Fifa has not responded to comment.

Last week, Infantino praised Fifa for “delivering the best show in the world” and spoke of the World Cup bringing “joy and togetherness,” in a 900-word statement published across a 15-page post on his Instagram account and on Fifa website.

“Sorry that you were so consumed by hate and criticism that you missed it all,” the FIFA leader wrote, addressing his comments to “those behind their pens and papers, behind their screens spreading hate and false rumours.”

Fifa and Infantino faced criticism during the World Cup for Iran team officials, a Somali referee and fans being denied entry to the United States; alleged political influence by US President Donald Trump in letting Folarin Balogun avoid a ban for a red card; unprecedented high ticket prices and commercialized breaks in play midway through each half of all 104 games.

“Every city was packed with fans from all around the globe,” Infantino wrote. “While they celebrated, you were busy planting seeds of hate.”

A pair of Airbnb hosts who record themselves inspecting their accommodation after guests depart have gone viral for their strict house rules.

Cassie and Jon, a couple in their early twenties, document themselves doing a post-checkout clean of their property in Glennville, Georgia, remarking on everything from how clean the guests have left the toilet to what snacks have been eaten and whether the furniture is out of place.

TikTok viewers have roasted the couple for their extreme attention to detail, since they have strict house rules and sometimes complain about what state the guests leave the property in after checkout.

One video shows the couple criticizing their checked-out guests for leaving the TV remote out of place, for “disrespecting the house rules” by leaving a box of leftovers in the fridge and for moving the ottoman a few inches closer to the couch.

“It is so simple to put your trash in the trash can,” Cassie said in one video, remarking on pizza boxes left on the counter. “The pillows and the blankets are all out of place,” Jon said in another clip.

“Y’all need to lighten up,” one person commented. “Why do I feel like you’d be mad if they used the blankets?” said another.

“Can [guests] sit on the toilet when they need it?” joked a third. “They USED the SPACE?!”

“I was defending y’all bc I thought it was a skit. Now I have to go apologize to people,” quipped another. “Honestly this is so obnoxious.”

Since Cassie and Jon’s videos have gone viral, other content creators have parodied the couple, skewering their strict house rules and their reactions when the accommodation has been lived in.

The content creator @daadisnacks criticized the couple for complaining about small details when they charge a $50 cleaning fee per stay. “Influencers run an Airbnb with more rules than a maximum security prison,” he captioned the post.

“Oh my god, you guys, the guests who paid $350 to use our home, used our home, and I’m literally shaking,” he said in the skit.

Airbnb hosts have been the subject of parody videos for their strict house rules ( Getty/iStock )

@ambercatherphoto also recreated the videos, telling the camera:

“Hey Y’all, we’re gonna go in and check out and see how bad these renters messed up the Airbnb...

“We already know the renters had a dog or some kids because this stick was out of place in the yard... can’t imagine what they’ve done inside.”

Later in the video, the content creator, in character as Jon, comments on how the ottoman has been moved a few inches.

“They moved the furniture! That’s house rule number 71!” they quipped to the camera. “Look at all the laundry in the laundry basket... they were here for two weeks.. How many showers did they need?”

The Independent has reached out to Airbnb and Cassie and Jon for comment.

News.title: Recovery aids and building muscle: Welsh weightlifter Laura Hughes answers your questions
News.content:
Laura Hughes first discovered weightlifting while training at her local Crossfit gym, making the transition from amateur gym-goer to competitive lifting.

Now a member of the Welsh national weightlifting squad, the 33-year-old holds the Welsh record for both the snatch and the clean and jerk (the two official competitive lifts in weightlifting) and is currently third overall in the women’s Welsh rankings. Hughes won bronze at the 2018 Commonwealth Games in Australia and was selected again for this summer’s Games in Glasgow.

We caught up with her for our Readers Ask series, where industry specialists answer questions from our Telegraph Recommended Reader Panel.

Who inspired you to get into weightlifting?

Olamilekan, South East

Originally, it was lots of different people, particularly general gym goers who were doing weightlifting at my gym. As I’ve grown as an athlete and become more competitive, I’ve had other inspirations.

Most notably, coming into [the Commonwealth Games], it has to be Gareth [Evans], our coach. Looking back at his performance in 2018 when he won his gold medal is so inspiring. [English lifter] Emily Godley was another competitor in 2018. She won the gold medal in my category and I just remember thinking that she was on fire that day.

What are the best exercises for you to build muscle mass?

Norman, Wales

We spend a lot of time doing our main lifts, so snatches, clean and jerks, but we also do lots of pulls and squats. I spend a lot of time doing accessory work to make sure that my body stays healthy, especially being an older athlete. I’ve put on quite a lot of muscle in this last block just from going heavier and pushing my limits with my main lifts.

What advice would you give to people who want to improve their strength?

David, North West

The most important thing is consistency. As long as you’re doing something, do it regularly, even if it’s twice a week. Don’t be afraid of picking up some dumbbells. If you’ve got somebody that can teach you how to lift weights properly, that’s going to be the best option. Do it safely, do it consistently, and don’t be afraid to try new strength exercises.

News.title: Explosive mpox outbreak causes 3,000 cases in Madagascar
News.content:
More than 3,000 cases of mpox have been recorded in Madagascar after the virus spread from a single port city to some of the country’s busiest coastal hubs.

A total of 3,022 cases and 20 deaths have been recorded as of this week, with cases in Toamasina and Taolagnaro accounting for more than half of all diagnoses.

The outbreak has been linked to Clade 1b mpox, a strain that emerged in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2024, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to declare a global public health emergency at the time.

“The main factor driving the continued spread of the disease is human mobility, seeding new outbreaks in areas where the virus has not circulated before,” Professor Carlos Maluquer de Motes of the University of Surrey told The Telegraph.

“Under-reporting is likely, with the real number of cases exceeding what is being reported.”

News.title: Chelsea in 10-goal thriller as ‘Alonso ball’ brings risk and reward
News.content:
Chelsea’s first match under the management of Xabi Alonso was a 10-goal thriller in Australia, as the Premier League side eventually showed their class in a 6-4 win over Western Sydney Wanderers.

Star striker João Pedro, who was controversially left out of Brazil’s World Cup squad, scored a nine-minute hat-trick after coming off the bench with half an hour of the friendly remaining.

Alonso had selected a youthful team for the first hour before bringing nine senior players, including João Pedro, into the side in the second half. According to Transfermarkt, Chelsea’s squad is valued at over £1.3bn while their opponents a more modest £5.86m.

Teenage signing Dastan Satpayev, midfielder Dario Essugo and winger Jamie Gittens also found the net for Chelsea, who were defensively vulnerable for long spells for the game.

Here are five things Telegraph Sport learned from Alonso’s first match.

João Pedro picks up where he left off

João Pedro scored 13 goals in the second half of last season and his impressive performances resulted in the 24-year-old being named Chelsea’s player of the campaign. It was something of a surprise, then, when he was left out of Carlo Ancelotti’s Brazil squad this summer.

The good news for Chelsea is that João Pedro’s absence from the World Cup has given him plenty of time to recover ahead of the new campaign, and he looked thrillingly sharp in his second-half performance against Western Sydney Wanderers. The difference in class between João Pedro and Liam Delap, the man he replaced, was clear for all to see.

Two of the Brazilian’s three goals were classy, composed finishes — and he also created a goal for Gittens after surging past three defenders on the left wing. João Pedro looks like he means business.
