World.title: Mozambique: Nudges Toward Dialogue in Cabo Delgado
World.content:
Two public pushes for peace talks this month, changes in Frelimo and the insurgents, and a more public recognition that the Cabo Delgado war will continue indefinitely may be slowly changing the mood within government toward some sort of talks with Cabo Delgado insurgents.

Today the Institute for Security Studies (ISS) hosted a briefing by Mozambican journalist Borges Nhamirre which pushed harder on the ISS December 2025 Policy Biref "Inclusive dialogue: a priority for resolving the Cabo Delgado insurgency". In today's briefing Nhamirre stressed that dialogue is essential to "identify grievances and conflict drivers, rebuild trust," and create the conditions for formal negotiations. But he warned that today, "no dialogue is happening" and the government does not support informal contacts.

And a publication this month by three Mozambican security experts with extensive knowledge of Cabo Delgado says "it is possible to engage in dialogue and negotiations" with the insurgents. They are Salvador Forquilha, João Pereia and Emílio Zeca, who are part of a newly formed NGO, the Tibverane Foundation, founded with Swiss funding and Mozambique government support.

Both stress the importance of starting with the roots of the insurgency – lack of jobs, political and economic exclusion particularly affecting Muslim communities, abuse by security forces, and control from Maputo instead of locally.



Nhamirre stresses the importance of changes within Frelimo and government. The previous president Filipe Nyusi was from Cabo Delgado and was put into the job by the powerful Frelimo Makonde elite there. It was said he did their bidding, in particular trying to win the war militarily and not negotiate. The current president Daniel Chapo grew up in Beira, Sofala, in the centre of the country, which has a very different elite which often does not follow the line set in Maputo. All three authors of the Tibverane paper are also from Beira. África Monitor Intelligence (13 July) says Pereia is close to Chapo and was chosen by the President to be director of Tibverane. Nhamirre reports that the Makonde have lost substantial power in Frelimo and the government, with few ministers, and Chapo has more space for movement.

The final change has been on the ground. At the start of the war a decade ago, the insurgents showed their power by beheading local villagers. This stopped as the insurgents learned the importance in any guerilla war of 'winning hearts and minds'. Thus there is an accommodation between insurgents and local people across much of Cabo Delgado. Internally displaced people are now returning to their villages, in part because of poor conditions in the camps for the displaced, and in part because they fear the Mozambique security forces more than the insurgents.

The other change is the realisation in the international community that the civil war will continue indefinitely. It has already been agreed that the entire gas liquification process will be inside a fortress on the Afungi peninsula (near Palma) with access only by sea and air, but not by land. The Afungi fortress concept assumes that the war continues outside the walls. And on 10 July TotalEnergies announced an entire new security ring surrounding the Afungi fortress with an electrified fence and 120 cameras . At the same time it delayed the building in South Korea of 17 LNG tankers, already delayed from a planned delivery in 2023. The new delivery date is 2030, and LNG cannot start without boats to take it away. And Japanese ambassador Keiji Hamada announced on 23 July that Japan would stop giving aid for reconstruction because the 'instability' makes it impossible to do infrastructure construction. This harsh judgements comes from one of the oldest and most loyal aid donors, who see no end to the war. Humanitarian aid for those affected by the war will continue, he said.

The involvement of the Swiss is important and there needs to be more coordinated support from donors, There are at least six NGO and INGO attempts to push for negotiations, but all are small and they do not cooperate because they are all fighting for the limited pool of donor money.

Despite the UK's virtual withdrawal from Mozambique, there is one thing it could still do. Tony Blair was in Maputo 20 July and met with Chapo who apparently asked for military support. More useful would be for the UK to provide help from Jonathan Powell, Prime Minister Andy Burnham's National Security Adviser. He was chief British negotiator in the successful peace settlement in Northern Ireland, and has worked in Mozambique. He was also Chief of Staff to Blair when he was Prime Minister, so Powell's assistance might be via the Blair Foundation which is present in Mozambique. Powell wrote the excellent 2014 book Talking to Terrorists: How to End Armed Conflicts which should be read by NGOs, government and donors involved in this war – it is available on Kindle.

Close 

And it should be remembered that at the end of the Proxy War there were peace talks in Rome (July 1990 to October 1992) with Renamo which led to elections and some "terrorists" becoming members of parliament.

+ Borges Nhamirre, 'Dialogue initiatives for peacebuilding in Cabo Delgado, slides, ISS, 27 July 26 https://bit.ly/ISS-Nhamirre-CdG

+ Borges Nhamirre, 'Inclusive dialogue: a priority for resolving the Cabo Delgado insurgency, ISS, 3Dec25 https://bit.ly/ISS-dialogue-Dec25

+ Tibverane, (9 Mb) 'Is it possible dialogue and negotiate with al-Shabaab?' https://university.open.ac.uk/technology/mozambique/sites/www.open.ac.uk.technology.mozambique/files/TIBVERANE_POLICY_PAPER_02_06_2026 Is dialogue possible.pdf

World.title: Kenya: Court Lifts Shisha Ban in Major Blow to Government Crackdown
World.content:
Nairobi — The High Court has lifted the ban on shisha, ruling that continued enforcement of the prohibition is unlawful and unconstitutional after the government failed to regularise the underlying regulations.

In a judgment delivered Tuesday, Justice Bahati Mwamuye held that the Public Health (Control of Shisha Smoking) Rules, 2017 ceased to have legal effect after the government failed to comply with a 2018 court order requiring the regulations to be regularised within nine months.

The judge ruled that state agencies could no longer rely on the lapsed regulations to enforce the ban, declaring unlawful a February 3, 2025 Ministry of Health press statement and an April 14, 2025 directive ordering a nationwide crackdown on shisha outlets.

Justice Mwamuye further found that the continued enforcement of the expired regulations violated the constitutional rights of members of the Novel Tobacco Products Association, and issued orders restraining the government from enforcing the 2017 rules and the subsequent directives against the association.

The ruling effectively removes the legal basis that authorities had relied on to sustain the ban, pending any fresh lawful regulatory action by the government.

World.title: Cote d'Ivoire: Over 400 Liberians Left Homeless After Demolition of Communities Outside Abidjan
World.content:
Abidjan — More than 400 Liberian nationals have been left homeless and stranded after a large-scale demolition exercise carried out by Ivorian authorities destroyed hundreds of homes in the Vridi Canal community on the outskirts of Abidjan, according to leaders of the Liberian diaspora in Côte d'Ivoire.

The demolitions, which took place approximately three weeks ago, formed part of the Ivorian Government's ongoing urban redevelopment and settlement clearance program aimed at addressing unauthorized structures and improving urban planning in rapidly expanding areas surrounding the commercial capital. However, the operation has had devastating consequences for hundreds of Liberian migrants and their families who had lived in the affected communities for decades.

Speaking on the situation, Mr. Robert Varney Zoker, Vice President of the Liberian Community in Côte d'Ivoire, described the humanitarian conditions facing displaced Liberians as dire and worsening by the day.

"The situation is extremely difficult," Mr. Zoker said. "Hundreds of Liberians have lost everything--their homes, personal belongings, businesses, and important documents. Many are now living in temporary shelters under very challenging conditions."



According to the community leader, the demolition exercise swept through several settlements housing migrant populations, including a large number of Liberians who had established roots in the area over many years. The affected population includes women, children, elderly persons, and individuals with special needs, many of whom now lack access to adequate shelter, food, healthcare, and sanitation facilities.

Community representatives say the destruction of homes has left many families vulnerable and uncertain about their future. In addition to housing, residents also lost household items, fishing equipment, small business assets, savings, and official documents, making recovery increasingly difficult.

In an effort to provide immediate relief, members of the Liberian community have mobilized limited resources to assist the displaced. Some families have been temporarily relocated to school buildings and other makeshift facilities, but community leaders warn that these arrangements are unsustainable.

"We took some of them to temporary shelters in schools and other locations," Mr. Zoker explained. "But conditions remain very, very difficult. People are sleeping in crowded spaces, and many families are struggling to find food and necessities."

The humanitarian impact has become particularly alarming for vulnerable groups. According to Mr. Zoker, some displaced women have been forced to give birth under inadequate conditions while taking refuge in temporary shelters.

"Imagine someone delivering a baby in a school building because they have nowhere else to go," he said. "It is heartbreaking and demonstrates the severity of the crisis facing these Liberians."

Many of the affected Liberians were residing in communities along the Vridi Canal area, a strategic zone in Abidjan that serves as a major maritime gateway connecting the Port of Abidjan to the Atlantic Ocean. The area has historically attracted fishing communities and migrant workers due to its access to economic opportunities.

Mr. Zoker noted that a significant number of those affected are fishermen and their families who have lived and worked in Côte d'Ivoire for decades, contributing to local economic activity while maintaining strong ties to Liberia. "These are people who have been living here for more than 60 years," Mr. Zoker said and added, "Most of them are fishermen who built their livelihoods around these communities. Today, they have nowhere to go."

Concerned by the deteriorating conditions, the Liberian community in Abidjan has formally appealed to the Governments of Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire, as well as humanitarian and international organizations, to provide urgent assistance.

The community is requesting emergency support in the form of temporary accommodation, food supplies, medical care, sanitation services, and psychosocial assistance for affected families. Leaders are also seeking transportation support for Liberians who wish to voluntarily return home and rebuild their lives in Liberia.

According to Mr. Zoker, a petition outlining the plight of the displaced Liberians has already been submitted to the Liberian diplomatic mission in Abidjan, urging immediate intervention and engagement with Ivorian authorities.

Community representatives have emphasized that the issue requires swift diplomatic attention to prevent further suffering and ensure that vulnerable families receive the protection and support they urgently need.

The plight of the displaced Liberians has drawn comparisons with recent interventions undertaken by the Government of Ghana. Following the same demolition exercise, Ghanaian authorities reportedly assisted approximately 327 Ghanaian nationals who had been affected by the demolitions. Among them, 228 individuals were repatriated through a special operation coordinated by Ghana's Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Ghanaian officials said the intervention was designed to ensure the safety and welfare of their citizens while facilitating the transport of families and their belongings back to Ghana. The operation has since been cited by members of the Liberian community as a model that could be replicated to support Liberians facing similar circumstances.

Drawing on that example, community leaders are calling on the Government of Liberia, through its Embassy in Abidjan and relevant national agencies, to undertake a comprehensive assessment of the affected population and develop a coordinated response plan.

Recommendations include engaging directly with Ivorian authorities, documenting the number of affected Liberians, facilitating humanitarian assistance, and arranging the voluntary and orderly repatriation of those seeking to return to Liberia.

Community leaders believe that urgent diplomatic engagement and humanitarian intervention will be critical in alleviating the suffering of displaced Liberians and restoring hope to families who have lost nearly everything.

Close 

As efforts continue to determine the full scale of the displacement, many affected Liberians remain in temporary shelters, relying on the goodwill of fellow community members and local support networks. While uncertainty hangs over their future, community leaders remain hopeful that the Liberian Government, in partnership with Ivorian authorities and development partners, will move swiftly to address the crisis and provide relief to citizens affected by the demolitions.

For the hundreds of Liberians now struggling to rebuild their lives, timely assistance and coordinated action could mean the difference between prolonged hardship and a pathway toward recovery and dignity.

According to Ivorian authorities, the demolition campaign formed part of a broader government initiative aimed at eliminating structures deemed unsafe, reducing environmental and public safety risks, and reorganizing urban spaces to support modernization and sustainable city planning. Officials maintain that the exercise is necessary to improve living conditions, enhance infrastructure development, and prevent settlement in high-risk areas vulnerable to flooding and other hazards.

However, the operation has generated significant criticism from affected residents and human rights advocates, many of whom argued that the evictions were carried out with little or insufficient prior notice. Residents claim that families were given limited time to remove their belongings before demolition crews arrived, leaving many unable to salvage personal possessions, business assets, and important documents.

World.title: Kenya: Expert Debunks Kindiki Duty Transfer Claims As DP Dismisses 'Fake News'
World.content:
Nairobi — Deputy President Kithure Kindiki's brief dismissal of viral claims that he had been stripped of key government responsibilities has now received backing from a governance expert, who says the controversy is based on a misunderstanding of Kenya's legal framework rather than an actual transfer of power.

The debate erupted after social media was flooded with reports alleging that President William Ruto had reassigned Kindiki's role in coordinating intergovernmental affairs to Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi.

However, Kindiki brushed aside the reports in a short message posted on X.

"Fake news," Kindiki wrote.



His response came as speculation continued online, although neither State House nor the Office of the Prime Cabinet Secretary has issued an official statement confirming that any such reassignment has taken place.

Governance and devolution expert John Burugu argues that the claims have been exaggerated and fail to consider how Kenya's intergovernmental system is established under the Constitution and various Acts of Parliament.

According to Burugu, if any administrative adjustments have been made, they should not be interpreted as stripping the Deputy President of constitutional or statutory powers.

Instead, he says the issue highlights a long-standing administrative gap created by the absence of a substantive Cabinet Secretary responsible for Devolution.

"The perceived loss, politically, by the Deputy President is misplaced because it is a move to correct a mistake by the same administration aimed at easing operational and administrative hiccups," Burugu said.

He added that assigning certain administrative responsibilities elsewhere would merely address operational challenges rather than diminish the office of the Deputy President.

"Therefore, there is no political fodder as is being hyped over the matter," he stated.

Burugu further noted that one of the Deputy President's most significant intergovernmental responsibilities remains protected by law.

He explained that Section 187(1)(a) of the Public Finance Management Act expressly provides that the Deputy President chairs the Intergovernmental Budget and Economic Council (IBEC), the body responsible for coordinating fiscal relations between the national and county governments.

According to the expert, that position cannot change unless Parliament amends the law.

"It is expected that legal provision under the PFM Act would prevail and allow H.E. Prof. Kithure Kindiki to continue chairing this fiscal intergovernmental structure," Burugu said.

Close 

He added that only an amendment to the Public Finance Management Act could remove the Deputy President as IBEC chair.

Presidential Special Projects Head Dennis Itumbi also rejected the reports, saying the claims were based on a misunderstanding of Kenya's intergovernmental governance structure.

According to Itumbi, intergovernmental relations are shared among several legally established institutions, including the National and County Government Coordinating Summit, IBEC, the Intergovernmental Relations Technical Committee (IGRTC) and the Council of Governors.

He maintained that IBEC remains chaired by the Deputy President as required by law and argued that suggesting one office had taken over another's constitutional mandate was inaccurate.

"The claims are FAKE NEWS," Itumbi said.

"Each institution has a specific mandate. Suggesting that one office has taken over another's constitutional or statutory role is simply inaccurate."

World.title: Africa: Rethink. Rebuild. Rise. - AIDS 2026 Charts the Next Phase of the HIV Response
World.content:
Rio de Janeiro, Brazil — The global fight against HIV has never had more powerful scientific tools or faced greater political uncertainty.

More than 7,000 scientists, activists, policymakers and community leaders gathered in Rio de Janeiro for the opening of the International AIDS Conference. Global leaders warned that decades of progress against the epidemic could be reversed by shrinking international funding, geopolitical tensions and growing attacks on human rights.

The warning comes at a contradictory time in the HIV response.



Science has made breakthroughs that seemed impossible. It has changed HIV from a deadly diagnosis into a manageable condition. Researchers have developed highly effective long-acting prevention medicines and are working on simpler, longer-lasting treatment options. However, many of these gains are out of reach for millions of people because of political choices, funding gaps and rising inequalities. The science exists. The question confronting AIDS 2026 is whether the world can find the political will to deliver it.

In this context, the six-day conference began with the theme "Rethink. Rebuild. Rise." This theme calls not only for celebrating scientific progress but also for reconsidering how it is funded, delivered, and safeguarded in an increasingly uncertain world.

International AIDS Society President and AIDS 2026 International Co-Chair Professor Beatriz Grinsztejn said the meeting comes at a pivotal moment for the global HIV response, with scientific advances colliding with mounting political and financial challenges.

"We are here because the world needs us to be - Rethink. Rebuild. Rise. And by meeting here in Latin America and the Caribbean, we are showcasing the value of investing in the creativity and strength of the Global South," she said.

Grinsztejn said that the choice of Brazil as host reflected the country's long-standing commitment to universal access to HIV care and treatment. The region is one of the few in the world where new HIV infections are still rising, even as case numbers fall elsewhere. Brazil has been a global leader in adopting a science-driven, human rights-based approach to HIV. It has also played a key role in advancing HIV prevention research.

The global HIV response, she said, is being battered by converging crises, geopolitical shifts, sudden funding cuts, and rising hostility toward the communities most affected by the virus. "We gather in the shadow of decisions made by a few and felt by too many in clinics and communities across the planet," she said.

Despite those challenges, Grinsztejn said the HIV response has repeatedly demonstrated what science and political commitment can achieve. This year marks 30 years since the introduction of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), which transformed HIV from a near-certain death sentence into a manageable chronic condition. It is also 15 years since the HPTN 052 trial results, presented in Rome in 2011, established the scientific basis for the principle of Undetectable = Untransmittable.

Since then, she said, treatment has moved from complex multi-pill regimens to single daily tablets and long-acting injections; this week's program will preview a once-weekly oral treatment now in development. Prevention science, she added, has advanced just as far, with long-acting injectable tools that would have been unimaginable at the outset of the epidemic.

"These advances could bend the curve of the pandemic, if we follow the evidence on where and how to implement them, and if we make access the number one political priority," she said.

However, Grinsztejn warned that scientific breakthroughs alone cannot end the epidemic. None of it matters, she said, without access, and access, thirty years on, remains the field's unresolved problem. Nearly nine million people still cannot get life-saving treatment, a gap she attributed not to missing science but to political choices, financing failures, and a persistence of stigma and discrimination that no drug can dismantle on its own.

She also criticised the international response to financing the HIV epidemic.

Many of the countries carrying the heaviest HIV burden are simultaneously being pressured to fund their epidemic responses while servicing colonial debt.

She added that demands rebuilding the way we deliver the HIV response with a sustainable global solution, including debt restructuring and a serious reckoning with historical injustice. And social justice demands the realization of the right to health as a fundamental human right.

We must never forget that upholding democratic values is an integral part of public health.

"But to achieve that, we need political will," said Grinsztejn. "We need far greater political commitment than was demonstrated at last month's United Nations High-Level Meeting on HIV. The fact that some Member States turned their backs on the discussions and the Political Declaration itself shows just how significant the challenges ahead remain."

"AIDS 2026 will be our moment to push back," Grinsztejn said.

Grinsztejn said AIDS 2026 would put the scientific evidence on the record, hear the testimonies of communities most affected by HIV and help drive the political will needed to turn scientific evidence into policy and financing decisions around the world. She urged delegates to remain focused on the people most affected by the epidemic.

"We rise because the evidence is clear, our voices will not be silenced, and people living with and affected by HIV cannot wait," said Grinsztejn.

We are not going back

UNAIDS Executive Director Winnie Byanyima said the world was entering a new phase of the HIV response, shaped by shifting geopolitical realities, funding uncertainty and growing inequality.

She thanked Brazil and the International AIDS Society for convening scientists, communities, policymakers, and activists in one room. She credited Brazil specifically for demonstrating, over decades, that universal access to health care is not an aspiration but a decision that governments can make.

That spirit, she said, is what the moment now demands. The global order has shifted profoundly since the field last met at this conference two years ago, and there is no reversing it.

"We are not going back... We must build something new, an AIDS response for the world that we have today, not the world we wish existed, not the world of yesterday," she said. She pointed to the political declaration on HIV that UN member states adopted just weeks ago, despite deep geopolitical tension, as evidence that a shared global commitment to ending AIDS still holds, and as a roadmap the field now has to act on.

Geography, she argued, must never be what determines who lives and who dies.

She said every breakthrough in the response had come from confronting exclusion through science, human rights and global solidarity. However, she warned that many of those gains were now under threat. On rights, she argued that the AIDS response has always advanced by putting people and human rights at its center, driven by communities demanding dignity and treatment.

That progress, she said, is now under strain for the first time since UNAIDS began tracking rights globally; criminalization is rising rather than falling, with more countries criminalizing same-sex relationships last year alone. She pointed to Senegal, where she said fear has displaced trust and HIV services for the people who need them most are closing as a result. Facing that reversal, she said, will require broader coalitions than the field has built before, uniting the HIV response with women's movements, LGBTQI movements, and democracy movements, since she argued health, gender justice, and democracy will rise or fall together. "History tells us that organized people eventually defeat organized money," she said.

Such policies, she said, were already forcing vulnerable communities away from HIV services.

She praised researchers for transforming laboratory discoveries into life-saving medicines available around the world. But she said access to the latest HIV prevention technologies remained far too slow. Two years ago, at the same conference, trial results identified a twice-yearly injectable as the most effective HIV prevention tool yet developed. Today, she said, the rollout is moving far too slowly. She said the world should already be working towards reaching 20 million people rather than only a fraction of that number. She rejected the idea that the higher target is unrealistic.

"During COVID, 4.5 billion people received vaccines within a year... We can move just as urgently to deliver HIV prevention," said Byanyima.

Byanyima also called on pharmaceutical companies to expand licensing agreements and technology sharing so that low- and middle-income countries, particularly in Latin America and Africa, could gain affordable access to new HIV medicines. Her call to industry was direct: open access, scale production, and share the underlying technology.

"Open the gates. Scale production. Share technology," she urged. "Millions of lives depend on the speed of implementing this."

She also warned that the global HIV response was facing one of its greatest financial challenges in decades. She described the response as one of the largest acts of global solidarity in public health history, built through the Global Fund, PEPFAR, UNITAID, governments, and communities, and now under unprecedented pressure. International HIV financing fell by more than US$1.5 billion last year, she said, while many heavily affected countries were spending more servicing debt than investing in health. She said it cannot substitute for external funding cut abruptly.

"This is not economic inevitability. This is the result of political choices," Byanyima said, calling for debt restructuring, fairer international taxation and sustained international solidarity alongside increased domestic investment.

Despite the challenges, she said there were still reasons for optimism, pointing to renewed commitments by African governments, Brazil's leadership on regional pharmaceutical production and growing international efforts to reform global financing.

"The world has changed," Byanyima said. "But our values have not changed and will not change. We still believe that every person deserves dignity. We still believe that scientific progress must benefit everyone. And we still believe that inequality can be defeated."

She said ending AIDS as a public health threat remained within reach if governments matched scientific innovation with political commitment, equity and global solidarity.

Progress is real, but it's fragile

WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the global HIV response stood at a defining moment. He warned that decades of progress were under threat but could still be protected through renewed commitment to science, communities and stronger health systems.

Tedros praised Brazil's leadership, saying that Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva had demonstrated the power of political commitment to expand treatment access. He cited Brazil's defense of free HIV treatment, its work making medicines more affordable, its support for production partnerships in Africa, and its record on protecting human rights.

"For more than four decades, HIV has tested humanity - not only our science, but our solidarity," he said. "Again and again, when the world predicted failure, communities proved it wrong."

He said that scientists, working alongside affected communities, had transformed HIV from a fatal diagnosis into a manageable condition. Countries have expanded lifesaving treatment to millions of people. But he warned that the global response was now facing its most serious disruption in a generation. "We have not come to Rio to mourn what is at risk," he said. "We have come to defend it. And to build what comes next."

Close 

He said the conference theme, Rethink. Rebuild. Rise, reflected what was needed to keep the world on track to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030.

"We must rethink how we deliver services, making them more integrated, more people-centered, and more resilient. We must rebuild partnerships that put countries and communities at the center of every decision. And we must rise, not by lowering our ambition, but by renegading it," he said. "The goal of ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030 is still within our reach," Tedros said. "But only if we're willing to act differently."

Tedros launched WHO's progress report on its Global Health Strategy on HIV, viral hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infections for 2022–2030, which he said tells two stories at once: evidence that new infections and AIDS-related deaths have fallen sharply where countries have invested in health, science, and communities, alongside proof of how quickly funding cuts, emergencies, and inequality can reverse those gains.

He also announced new WHO guidance on HIV surveillance and updated service delivery recommendations designed to help countries strengthen routine monitoring, improve long-term care, and integrate HIV services into broader primary healthcare systems. He committed WHO to continuing to fold HIV services into primary health care and universal coverage more broadly, and to accelerating access to innovations from long-acting prevention and treatment to diagnostics and digital tools.

He said that a scientific breakthrough only counts once it reaches everyone, not only those who can pay for it. That integration, he said, will extend to tuberculosis, viral hepatitis, sexually transmitted infections, sexual and reproductive health, mental health, and noncommunicable disease services, alongside continued work to eliminate mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B.

"A scientific breakthrough only matters when it becomes a public health breakthrough for everyone, everywhere - and not only for those who can afford it," he said.

None of it, he said, works without communities, whom he described not as optional partners but as the architects of the response. These are the ones who reach people health systems cannot, defend human rights, and hold everyone else accountable. Tedros urged countries to protect HIV financing, strengthen community-led organisations and repeal laws that criminalise key populations. "Progress is real, but it's fragile," he said.

"We have the science. We have the tools," Tedros said. "What we need now is what has always mattered most in this fight - the will to stay united and the determination to finish what we started."

World.title: Kenya: Ruto Vows Every University Student Will Get Full Govt Funding
World.content:
Nairobi — President William Ruto has reaffirmed his pledge that every student joining university will receive full government funding, saying education remains the country's biggest investment despite growing concerns over where the money will come from.

President Ruto said the government is refining its university funding model to ensure every learner has access to higher education regardless of their financial background.

"We have made very good progress with our new student-centered funding model, and I want to tell our Vice-Chancellors we will be engaging them as we now progress to even a better funding model that will make sure that every student has full funding for their education," Ruto said.

He added: "That is the commitment I have made."

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The President acknowledged that many Kenyans are questioning how the government will raise the money needed to finance the ambitious plan.

"I know many people are asking me, 'Where are you going to find the money to fund these universities?' And I want to tell them... if you think education is expensive, try ignorance, and you will know which one is more expensive," he said.

Ruto insisted investing in education is critical if Kenya is to become a developed nation.

"It is the single most important thing that we must do. Because for us to move this country to a first-world status, knowledge, education is central to that journey," he said.

He added that no country can achieve meaningful development without investing in its people.

"I have said no nation can develop beyond its capacity to think. If you cannot imagine the future, you cannot get there."

The President's latest remarks come a week after he announced plans to replace the current needs-based university funding system with a universal model.

If approved by Parliament through the proposed amendments to the Higher Education Loans Board (HELB) Act, every student admitted to a university, college or the Kenya Medical Training College (KMTC) from September 2026 would qualify for 100 percent government funding, regardless of family income.

The proposal follows mounting pressure on the current student-centred funding model, which has faced criticism over affordability, funding gaps and financial challenges facing public universities.

Government figures show higher education institutions continue to face significant funding shortfalls even as student enrolment continues to rise sharply.

While Ruto has maintained that no deserving student should miss higher education because of lack of money, education stakeholders have questioned whether the government has the financial capacity to implement the plan.

Close 

Despite the concerns, Ruto remained optimistic about Kenya's future.

"So, I am very confident about the future of our nation, and I am very confident about the young people who will make sure that that future becomes our reality," he said.

World.title: Miami Secret Service agent charged in near-deadly fraternity hazing, officials say
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A U.S. Secret Service agent has been arrested and charged with five felony counts, including attempted manslaughter with a deadly weapon, after allegedly being involved with hazing "rituals" that left two victims with life-threatening injuries.

Marquez Pinder, a 29-year-old special agent with the Miami Field Office, was ordered to be put on house arrest with a GPS tracking device.

Pinder held the title of "dean of pledges" during four, hours-long hazing sessions for a Miami chapter of the Kappa Alpha Psi fraternity, according to an affidavit filed with the Circuit Court of the 11th Judicial Circuit of Florida. In that role, Pinder was allegedly involved in the hazing of two prospective members of the fraternity.

SECRET SERVICE AGENT ON JD VANCE'S DETAIL INVESTIGATED FOR ALLEGEDLY LEAKING OPERATIONAL SECURITY INFO

According to court records, the two victims were "paddled" and struck with "canes" by Pinder and two other fraternity members. One victim’s concern was "dismissed" by the fraternity when he reported "urinating blood" during the first hazing session, records show.

Days later, the man had to be intubated at a hospital while receiving "critical care to prevent further physical deterioration and death," a law enforcement officer reported in a sworn statement.

The other victim was treated for "blackened" and "necrotic" tissue on his buttocks from the beating, court records show. "Substantial portions of skin and soft tissue" needed to be surgically removed, and he received "extensive skin grafts to cover the areas," according to an affidavit.

AMERICA'S TOP PARTY COLLEGE HIT BY ANOTHER SEX ATTACK WEEKS AFTER BRUTAL CAMPUS RAPE CASE

His "mobility and quality of life have been significantly impacted," a law enforcement officer wrote. And without emergency medical care, "his injuries would have resulted in renal failure leading to death."

The alleged hazing occurred every day April 1-4 at two different residences in Miami-Dade County, court records show.

During the meetings, the two victims were tested with questions about the fraternity and its history, according to the affidavit. Victims told law enforcement officers that when they failed to answer a question correctly, they were placed in what they called a "stress position," the affidavit shows.

RIDESHARE DRIVER ARRESTED IN ALLEGED SCHEME TARGETING IVY LEAGUE STUDENTS FOR SEX: PROSECUTORS

They described the "stress position" as a half-squat with one arm pointed forward. While in that position, the victims said they were "struck on their buttocks with a paddle." One of the victims said that, before the hazing, he was told that "if he ever felt that he was reaching his physical limit," he should tell Pinder, his "dean of pledges," officers reported. He said he was told that indications of reaching that limit might include urinating blood or feeling that he was going to pass out, according to the affidavit.

World.title: One of these eight college football teams will be hoisting the national championship trophy in 2026
World.content:
At the beginning of every college football season, the age-old adage of "hope springs eternal" rings true for every fanbase.

Every team is 0-0 and all their goals for the coming year are in front of them.

Many programs, coaches, and fanbases all believe they have a chance to win a national title, and in a mathematical sense they aren't wrong.

I'm here to tell you, however, that it's rarely that wide open and, during any given year, only a handful of teams can actually win the whole thing.

This year, I've identified eight teams who I believe can hoist a national championship trophy.

MISSOURI'S ELI DRINKWITZ BECOMES LATEST SEC COACH TO MAKE RIDICULOUS COMPLAINTS ABOUT BIG TEN SCHEDULES

Through some combination of returning production, transfer portal talent, and elite coaching, one of these eight teams will more than likely be the last one standing next January.

Ohio State Buckeyes

The Ohio State Buckeyes could probably get penciled into this list every year while Ryan Day is their head coach and their talent acquisition stays at the level it's currently at, but this year in particular feels like a big one in Columbus.

Coach Day has assembled a staff consisting largely of former NFL coaches and coordinators, and the addition of offensive coordinator Arthur Smith feels like a particularly noteworthy one to keep an eye on.

The Buckeyes have been recruiting at a top-five level for the past several cycles, and have supplemented that with a small but elite transfer portal class, including bolstering their defense with the likes of Alabama defensive linemen Qua Russaw and James Smith as well as Florida State safety Earl Little Jr.

On offense, Ohio State returns what may end up being the best quarterback-wide receiver tandem in the country, as Julian Sayin looks to build on a quietly brilliant 2025 while Jeremiah Smith could be argued as the best overall player in college football.

An early test on the road against Texas as well as a rematch of the Big Ten Championship in Bloomington against the Hoosiers will tell us everything we need to know about how real the Buckeyes are in 2026.

Texas Longhorns

Speaking of those Longhorns, Texas will be looking to right the wrongs from a disappointing 2025 heading into this year.

Last season, the Horns were a popular preseason national championship pick, but a less than ideal start had them on the outside looking in by season's end.

Texas will likely be near the top of the preseason polls again this year, but unlike in 2025, they know what they have in signal caller Arch Manning.

Manning's first half of last season was forgettable, but by November, you could argue he blossomed into one of the best quarterbacks in the country.

He has the weapons he needs to be truly elite, with receiver Ryan Wingo returning and wideout Cam Coleman coming over from Auburn, so there won't be any excuses for another sputtering start out of the gate in '26.

Texas' defense will be among the best in the country, and veteran leaders like edge rusher Colin Simmons and linebacker Rasheem Biles (both preseason All-Americans) will bolster a fearsome unit.

There has never been a dearth of talent in Austin, but coach Steve Sarkisian may finally have his most complete team since stepping foot on the 40 Acres, and that alone has people starting to feel like it's 2005 in Central Texas again.

Miami Hurricanes

The Miami Hurricanes were a fourth quarter Carson Beck interception away from winning the national championship in January, but the scary thing is they might be even more dangerous in 2026.

Head coach Mario Cristobal has built a machine in Coral Gables, and the Canes have the most talented roster they've had since the early 2000s.

That's not to say they don't have to replace some absolute studs, particularly along the lines of scrimmage, but Cristobal and co. have recruited well enough in the trenches that this may be a matter of reloading rather than rebuilding.

On the offensive side of the ball, Miami has an embarrassment of riches for offensive coordinator Shannon Dawson to tinker with.

The Canes return wide receiver Malachi Toney and running back Mark Fletcher Jr. from their CFP runner-up squad last season, and they added Duke wide receiver Cooper Barkate, who was one of the most coveted pass catchers in the portal from this past offseason.

The real prize, though, was Duke quarterback Darian Mensah.

Miami will be paying Mensah a pretty penny, but he will be worth every cent of his exorbitant paycheck, as the redshirt junior may end up being the most talented signal caller Cristobal has had while in South Florida.

The schedule is forgivable, even by ACC standards, but a rematch on the road against Notre Dame will separate the Canes as contenders or pretenders.

Indiana Hoosiers

It's crazy that I made it halfway through the list without mentioning the defending national champions, but I think coach Curt Cignetti and crew almost like it that way.

Last year, no one outside of the locker room at Memorial Stadium thought this team had a chance to win the whole thing, but the Hoosiers won't be sneaking up on anyone this year.

Cignetti doesn't have a star-studded roster like Miami, Texas, or Ohio State, but that's never stopped him before (obviously) and the talent in Bloomington is only getting better.

The Hoosiers signed a top-ten portal class, and although it was a relatively small class (17 total players) there were some gems to be found.

Quarterback Josh Hoover comes to Indiana by way of TCU, and will look to be the next big thing in Cignetti and offensive coordinator Mike Shanahan's system.

The last transfer quarterback they took ended up becoming a Heisman winner and number 1 overall NFL Draft pick, so Hoover will hope to continue the tradition.

Former Michigan State wide receiver Nick Marsh will give Hoover an elite target to throw to and will pair nicely with returning wideout Charlie Becker, who had a brilliant 2025 campaign averaging nearly 20 yards per catch.

Indiana likely won't be tested until the midway point of the season in a home game against Ohio State, and by then the team should be firing on all cylinders for the second half of the year.

LSU Tigers

Of all the teams on this list, the LSU Tigers are the wild card and have the widest range of potential outcomes to consider.

It's no secret the Bayou Bengals went out and got Lane Kiffin to be their head coach, who can be a bit of a wildcard in his own right.

But, when Kiffin is on, he's one of the best in the business at scoring points and talking smack in the process.

Paired with Kiffin is a pair of elite coordinators in Charlie Weis Jr. (OC) and Blake Baker (DC) as well as a rumored $40 million roster.

LANE KIFFIN MAKES RIDICULOUS EXCUSES FOR SEC'S POOR RECENT PERFORMANCE IN COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF

LSU also landed the number one transfer portal class and has studs at plenty of key positions, so conventional wisdom says they will be contenders right out of the gate.

The truth of the matter is, it doesn't always work out that way, and if you told me the Tigers won a national championship or went 7-5, I'd find both outcomes equally believable.

They have the firepower and an elite coaching staff, but they also play a pretty loaded schedule, starting with Clemson Week 1 and getting two more Playoff teams from last season (Ole Miss and Texas A&M) before the calendar even flips to October.

I could easily see them stumbling out of the gate and imploding, but I could also see them catching fire early and riding that wave to the promised land.

LSU can win a national championship in 2026. The question is will they?

Oregon Ducks

Things have gone about as well as one would want when it comes to coach Dan Lanning's time in Eugene.

The 40-year-old head coach is entering his fifth season with the Ducks, and his resume looks pretty stacked by any metric.

He's 48-8, captured the Big Ten title in Oregon's first year in the league, and has won 10 games or more every year he's been the coach there.

But he's missing that one thing to make his list of accomplishments feel more complete: a national championship.

While 2026 isn't championship or bust in the Pacific Northwest, some fans are starting to question if Lanning will ever get it done as a head coach, especially after last season's beatdown at the hands of Indiana in the CFP Semifinals.

This would be the year for him to slay that dragon, though, as Oregon will once again have one of the most talented teams in the country.

The Ducks and Lanning have been an absolute Death Star on the recruiting trail, and this season could be the culmination in all that hard work on the talent acquisition front.

Veteran signal caller Dante Moore eschewed the NFL Draft to come back and lead his team to a natty, and he will have two absolute weapons to throw the football to this coming year.

Sophomore Dakorien Moore, a former five-star recruit in his own right, had a very good freshman year but will be looking to take the next step in 2026, while senior Evan Stewart is back and 100% healthy and ready to show anyone who forgot about him why he was one of the most coveted players in the country when he transferred from Texas A&M two years ago.

On defense, the Ducks boast a trio of preseason All-Americans in defensive back Brandon Finney Jr., linebacker Teitum Tuioti, and defensive lineman A'Mauri Washington who will look to continue the trend of elite defensive play in Eugene.

The talent will have to rise to the top, because Lanning will be replacing both coordinators, as DC Tosh Lupoi and OC Will Stein departed for head coaching jobs at Cal and Kentucky, respectively.

Notre Dame Fighting Irish

When Brian Kelly departed South Bend for Baton Rouge nearly five years ago, I thought Notre Dame had seen their peak as a football program in the modern era.

Always the bridesmaid but never the bride, I figured new head coach Marcus Freeman would, at best, keep them in that 10-win/CFP first round exit realm.

Little did I know the former defensive coordinator turned full time head coach would prove me so wrong.

Two years ago, Freeman had the Irish on the doorstep of a national championship, and after a minor setback in 2025, the Golden Domers look to be right back in the thick of things.

This might be Freeman's most talented group of players yet, and it all starts with quarterback CJ Carr.

The offseason buzz around this young man has been Manningesque, and his growth over the second half of last season should be enough proof that those words aren't just hot air.

The Irish have also started recruiting at a championship level, and that should start to bear fruit as early as this season, as Freeman's efforts on the trail have considerably raised both the floor and ceiling of talent on this roster.

Having to replace two first-round draft picks at running back in Jeremiyah Love and Jadarian Price will be a tall ask, but I think the sum will be greater than the parts for Notre Dame in 2026 and, aside from their opener against Wisconsin, the team will be able to ease into their schedule before their ultimate test on Nov. 7 against Miami.

Georgia Bulldogs

No list of national championship contenders is complete without Kirby Smart and the Georgia Bulldogs, but they aren't making this roster of teams on the merits of their logo alone.

Georgia recruits better than almost anyone in the country, and the 2026 edition of this roster will feature a ton of former big-time prospects who waited their turn and were developed the old-fashioned way.

That includes quarterback Gunner Stockton, who has a ton of experience and a very solid 2025 campaign to build off of.

The third-team All-SEC selection will have a familiar face in offensive coordinator Mike Bobo coaching him up and will be able to lean on a fantastic running back in Nate Frazier as well as a trio of all-conference offensive linemen.

The defense will look to return to form as a vintage Kirby Smart unit, led by defensive backs KJ Bolden and Ellis Robinson, both of whom were tabbed as preseason first-team All-SEC selections by the media.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Dawgs have a tricky six-game stretch in the middle of the season, starting at home against Oklahoma and featuring road games against Alabama and Ole Miss along the way.

It remains to be seen just how high the ceiling will be for this Georgia team in 2026, but they have the requisite talent and a coach who has been to the mountaintop twice in recent history, so count the Bulldogs out at your own risk.

World.title: Heart-shaped Las Vegas resort gets green light as critics roast wild design online

Nevada officials unanimously approved plans for a heart-shaped resort hotel and recreational venue on the far south end of the Las Vegas Strip — and the unusual design is already attracting plenty of attention online.

The Clark County Zoning Commission unanimously approved plans for the proposed heart-shaped resort last week, Fox 5 Las Vegas reported.

The development is proposed on about 12 acres east of Las Vegas Boulevard South, between Mandalay Bay Road and Four Seasons Drive near Haven Street.

BARGAIN BUFFET REFUSES TO DIE WHILE LUXURY DINING TAKES OVER VEGAS

Planners trimmed the project's scope to a height of 317 feet and 752 hotel rooms, down from the original proposal of 406 feet and 874 rooms, according to industry publication NVBEX.

Renderings show the project — which doesn't have an official public name yet — centered around a massive, illuminated heart-shaped hotel tower, with a casino, restaurants and retail space spread across the base of the development.

Fox News Digital reached out to Steelman Partners, the project's architectural firm, for comment.

The concept is planned as a "pedestrian entertainment corridor," Fox 5 Las Vegas reported.

During the meeting, officials said the site has changed little since the early 2000s, after a previous proposal to build a Ferris wheel stalled.

LAS VEGAS OFFICIALS WEIGH BANNING CRIMINAL OFFENDERS FROM STRIP TO REVIVE TOURISM

On a Reddit forum dedicated to Las Vegas, reactions to the proposal were mixed, with many users criticizing or mocking the design.

"It honestly looks so ugly," one person wrote.

"We just need a diamond, spade and club hotel," another joked.

Massachusetts lawmakers are taking steps towards prioritizing the hiring of American Muslims for state government positions under a permanent so-called Muslim commission.

The group would help recommend Americans who practice Islam to appointed government positions in the New England state at the same time the Trump administration is moving to dismantle such diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs nationwide — teeing-up a standoff between local leaders and the president.

A proposed bill would create a panel of 11 Muslims appointed by Democratic Gov. Maura Healey and other state officials to represent the Islamic faith on issues such as business, economy, healthcare and other concerns.

DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST ACTRESS CYNTHIA NIXON HANDED POWERFUL ROLE IN HELPING CHOOSE NEW YORK TOP JUDGES

The Muslim commission would influence government recruiting and, "Identify and recommend qualified American Muslims for appointive positions at all levels of government, including boards and commissions, as the commission considers necessary and appropriate," according to language in the bill.

"Massachusetts has always prided itself on being a leader in equality and civil rights, a legacy this bill builds upon," said Democratic State Senator Jamie Eldridge, the bill's primary sponsor.

"American Muslims in my district and across the Commonwealth enrich our communities as students, healthcare workers, educators, small business owners, and civic leaders," Eldridge added in the press release on the proposal. "This commission will help the state better understand and address the challenges they face, while strengthening inclusion and civic participation. "

Senate Bill S.2134 currently sits in the state's Senate Ways and Means Committee after clearing initial committee markups and votes.

Muslims account for an estimated 2% to 3% of Massachusetts' population, according to approximate figures from Pew Research Center and the U.S. Census.

COAST GUARD ENDING RACE-BASED ADMISSIONS FOR OFFICER COMMISSIONING PROGRAM UNDER TRUMP DEI CRACKDOWN

Massachusetts' push comes as President Donald Trump has made it a mission of his administration to cut back on DEI programs in the private sector, as well as in the federal government.

"President Trump was resoundingly elected with a mandate to end divisive, racist policies and restore merit and efficiency," White House spokesperson Allison Shuster told Fox News Digital.

"DEI ran rampant during the Biden Administration, and Americans ultimately paid the price for these destructive policies with a restricted labor pool, higher operational costs, and workforce inefficiencies," Shuster added. "The Trump Administration will always promote equal treatment under the law for every American, regardless of race or ethnicity."

The president's team has terminated federal DEI-related contracts and eliminated DEI federal government programs.

Part of Trump's initiative during his first 100 days with the Elon Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) was to put an end to programs that prioritized hiring and representation in the work place based on applicants' protected classes.

Many Republicans, including the president and Musk, claimed that DEI was "reverse discrimination" that provided unfair preferences against majority groups in the U.S.

Gov. Healey's office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on the legislation.

World.title: Flock surveillance spreads across the South as red-state lawmakers seek to axe '1984'-style tracking tools
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

State lawmakers in West Virginia's Freedom Caucus are seeking to ban AI-powered Flock surveillance cameras statewide, arguing the technology violates citizens' Fourth Amendment right to privacy.

"The West Virginia Freedom Caucus strongly opposes the unchecked expansion of automated surveillance technologies, including Flock Safety camera systems, automated license plate readers (ALPRs), AI-powered facial recognition, multimodal vehicle recognition, and emerging 'gun detection' software that claims to identify armed citizens based on body shape or movement," West Virginia Delegate Chris Anders, the Chairman of West Virginia's Freedom Caucus, said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"These technologies represent a dramatic expansion of government surveillance that is fundamentally at odds with the Fourth Amendment," Anders added.

THE SURVEILLANCE CAMERA ON YOUR STREET CORNER: LAWFUL SPYING OR CONSTITUTIONALLY PROBLEMATIC?

"No state or local government should be mass tracking the daily movements of law-abiding citizens without a warrant. Mass surveillance has no place in a free society," Anders also said in a statement posted to the caucus' X account.

The caucus is calling on all state municipalities to immediately remove automated license plate readers such as the ones run by the security company Flock Safety.

"The Constitution does not disappear because technology advances," Anders added.

The caucus plans on combatting the cameras and surveillance technologies by reintroducing a previously failed legislative measure called the Fourth Amendment Restoration Act.

The bill would prohibit a series of AI-powered surveillance technologies from being used by law enforcement and other agencies in the state. The technologies it would ban include facial recognition software, surveillance drones, license plate readers and more.

"For two consecutive years, the Fourth Amendment Restoration Act has been introduced in the West Virginia Legislature, yet it has failed to reach the Governor's desk. That must change," Anders also said, placing blame for the bill's previous failures at the feet of the state's legislative leadership.

"Despite growing public concern over government surveillance, Speaker Roger Hanshaw and House Judiciary Chairman JB Akers declined to bring the bill forward for consideration. As a result, the House was never given the opportunity to debate or vote on the legislation," Anders wrote in an email to Fox News Digital.

"If House leadership continues to deny the people's elected representatives the opportunity to vote on this fundamental constitutional issue, the Freedom Caucus will use every parliamentary tool available to insist that the Fourth Amendment Restoration Act receive an up-or-down vote in both chambers. Constitutional rights should never be quietly buried in committee," Anders added.

Chairman Akers, in a response to Anders' comments, told Fox News Digital, "We actually passed a bill last session that limits the amount of surveillance law enforcement may engage in on private property. Unfortunately, Chris Anders submits sloppily drafted bills given to him by outside groups. In the 4th Amendment context, his proposals would prevent even normal law enforcement actions that conservatives support."

"Last session, he tried to amend a bill in a way that would have prevented police from entering property even if a dead body were in plain view in the front yard. Bluntly, his idea was dumb," Akers said of Anders' proposal draft. "He left me no choice but to say that. If he’s going to blame others for failing to get his bills through, then he needs to do better work. Frankly, I think he’d rather see his bad bills fail so he can then scream RINO for clicks."

Other Freedom Caucus members also objected to the Flock cameras.

"The Fourth Amendment was written specifically to stop the government from engaging in generalized surveillance and warrantless searches," West Virginia Freedom Caucus Secretary Henry Dillon said in a statement. He argued that "Flock cameras don't just identify criminals — they create a database documenting where law-abiding citizens worship, seek medical care, conduct business, and travel."

"That is fundamentally incompatible with a free society," he said.

JOHNSON FACES GOP REVOLT OVER WARRANTLESS SURVEILLANCE POWERS AHEAD OF KEY VOTE

Another Freedom Caucus member, state Sen. Craig Hart, pointed to a series of alleged police abuses involving Flock cameras in Georgia, including a 2025 incident in which Braselton Police Department Chief Michael Steffman was arrested for allegedly using automated license plate readers to stalk and harass people.

According to the Electronic Frontier Foundation's Atlas of Surveillance, at least five West Virginia municipalities incorporate Flock Safety license plate readers, while other municipalities like Wheeling and the state capital of Charleston operate drones, camera registries and intelligence fusion centers.

The American Civil Liberties Union is suing the West Virginia city of Huntington after its mayor and city council agreed to a $2.1 million deal with Flock for AI-powered surveillance equipment.

"If the Court allows the contract to proceed, Huntington would be blanketed in license plate recognition cameras with vehicle fingerprint technology, live video cameras, gunshot detection audio devices, and even automatically dispatched drones," the ACLU wrote in a statement.

The ACLU said more than 50 citizens attended the city council meeting to voice their disapproval of the agreement.

Meanwhile, Huntington Mayor Patrick Farrell argued that Flock cameras in other states have already helped catch West Virginia suspects.

Recounting a pursuit of a murder suspect who allegedly shot a woman in the head near Huntington, Farrell said "he was going back to Michigan, and luckily for us, some other city had license plate reader cameras that caught the car."

"That gave us the lead that led to his arrest in Michigan. So it helps our law enforcement do its work faster, more efficiently, and that’s the kind of success that I think we need more of," the mayor said.

Despite the safety argument, Anders and his caucus insist the technology violates the Constitution.

"The Founders did not fight a revolution so government could monitor innocent citizens everywhere they travel," Anders told Fox News Digital. "George Orwell's 1984 was intended as a warning, not an instruction manual. We should be striving for more 1776, not more 1984."

"The Fourth Amendment Restoration Act does not prevent police from investigating crime. It simply requires government to do what the Constitution has required for over two centuries: obtain a warrant based upon probable cause before engaging in targeted surveillance of Americans," Anders concluded.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Flock Safety maintained that the company protects personal privacy and claimed to support legislation that sets guardrails for license plate readers.

"Flock strongly supports legislation that creates clear guardrails for how license plate recognition data is used and shared, while preserving the effectiveness of an important public safety tool," a company spokesperson told Fox News Digital in a statement. "These systems play a critical role in helping law enforcement solve crimes, locate missing people, and keep communities safe. Taking away or weakening access to this technology would have real consequences for public safety. We believe the right approach is not to eliminate an effective tool, but to regulate it responsibly. State lawmakers should establish strong safeguards that ensure accountability, oversight, and responsible use, while preserving the ability of law enforcement to use these technologies in ways that communities expect and rely on. We stand ready to be a resource as lawmakers consider these important issues."

"Flock customers retain full ownership and control of their data. Flock does not sell data. Access is limited to authorized users, and agencies determine whether to share data with other law enforcement agencies through opt-in sharing relationships that they can change or revoke at any time. Data is automatically deleted after 30 days by default," the company spokesperson concluded.

World.title: Washington says goodbye to Sen. Lindsey Graham
World.content:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump, congressional colleagues and world leaders Tuesday will say their final goodbyes to Sen. Lindsey Graham, the influential and colorful foreign policy hawk whose sudden death this month at age 71 stunned Washington and reverberated in capitals around the globe.

Two days of ceremonies and funeral services began Tuesday morning when Graham’s American flag-draped casket arrived at the Capitol for a special ceremony in the rotunda — his last visit to a building where he served for more than three decades.

In honor of the senator’s long military career, an armed forces body bearer team slowly carried his casket up the Capitol steps. Graham served as an Air Force judge advocate general, or JAG, officer and retired from the Air Force Reserve in 2015 with the rank of colonel.

The casket of late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham during a ceremony in the rotunda of the U.S. Capitol on July 28. Frank Thorp V / NBC News

Senate colleagues, past and present, Cabinet members and Graham’s family and staffers packed the Rotunda. Among those paying tribute were former Sens. Rob Portman, R-Ohio; Richard Burr, R-N.C.; Jeff Flake, R-Ariz.; Pat Toomey, R-Pa.; and Kelly Ayotte, now New Hampshire’s GOP governor.

Vice President JD Vance, who served with Graham in the Senate, said the late senator was incredibly funny but also had a way of connecting with people, whether it was political leaders or the waitstaff in the Capitol.

“Lindsey Graham loved people from all walks of life. … He was fascinated in the waitstaff in the Senate dining room. He was fascinated in the people who made the food. He was fascinated in the lowest staffer who had been hired three days earlier,” Vance said at the Capitol ceremony. “He was fascinated by, of course, the very leadership of our country, and I think he was fascinated in people because he loved people.”

Others on hand were former South Carolina Rep. Trey Gowdy, a Fox News host; acting Attorney General Todd Blanche; Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, a former senator; and White House budget director Russell Vought.

“It’s difficult to believe that we’re here today to say a final farewell to Lindsey as he leaves the Capitol for the last time. My heart is heavy,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said at the ceremony.

“Lindsey was a towering figure here in the Senate and on the international stage. ... Lindsey will be remembered as a senator and as a statesman,” Thune said. “But for me, most of all, I will remember him as my friend. It’s hard to think that there will be no more Senate dinners with Lindsey.”

Graham’s sister and only sibling, Darline Graham, who was appointed to replace him in the Senate, walked tearfully up to the casket alone, then placed her hand on the casket. She was joined by her family. Then a parade of Trump officials, senators and Senate staffers paid tribute.

From the Capitol, Graham’s casket will depart for the Washington National Cathedral for an invitation-only funeral service at 2 p.m. ET. That also will be livestreamed.

Trump is expected to speak at the funeral. Cabinet officials and congressional and military leaders are expected to be on hand, as are global leaders who viewed Graham as a key American ally on defense and foreign policy matters, including Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Also present will be Graham’s sister and successor, Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., who was sworn in to her late brother’s seat this month and plans to run for a full term in an Aug. 11 primary.

Remembrances will continue at the South Carolina State House on Wednesday morning. Graham’s casket will be carried by a South Carolina State Guard horse-drawn military wagon, known as a caisson, followed by an F-16 flyover to mark his more than three decades in the Air Force and Air Force Reserve.

A funeral service, open to the public, will be held at First Baptist Church of Columbia. A private family burial will take place in Pickens County, where Graham was born and raised.

World.title: Nasdaq 100 slides into correction as global chip and memory stocks sell off
World.content:
Chip stocks around the world sold off sharply on Tuesday, the latest chapter in the months long jitters surrounding artificial intelligence, memory and chip stocks.

The sell off briefly pushed the Nasdaq-100 index into correction territory, which is a drop of 10% or more from its most recent record high. The influential index tracks the top 100 non-financial companies traded on the Nasdaq exchange.

Shares of several chip and memory giants, including Sandisk, Western Digital, Seagate, Micron, and AMD all fell around 10% in early trading.

Dell Technologies, which produces servers that use chips and memory made by those firms, tumbled 13%. Intel shares slid 7%.

The selling kicked off overnight in Asia, with stocks traded on markets in Korea, Japan, and Taiwan.

Both Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, the primary manufacturers of memory used in AI data centers, plunged more than 15%. Kioxia, another computer storage maker, plummeted 18%.

The latest wave of investor unease followed a report on Monday that a Chinese state-backed firm was beginning mass production of domestic chip-making tools.

However, the report did not name the company. NBC News was not able to verify the report.

Still, shares of established firms that make chip manufacturing equipment such as ASML, Canon and Nikon fell sharply on the news.

Tuesday’s moves also come ahead of major earnings reports later in the week from Meta, Amazon, Microsoft and other companies that are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build AI data centers. Those results could prove pivotal to the trajectory of the market.

Last week, Alphabet shares plunged 7% after the company reported its own results and increased its projected capital expenditures to as much as $205 billion. Most of that will go to building and expanding data centers.

Evercore technology analyst Mark Mahaney said last week that Alphabet would likely set the stage for Microsoft and Amazon to do the same when they report this week.

“The Capex increase increases the odds of similar behavior from AWS and Azure,” he wrote in a note on Wednesday, referring to capital expenditures, or money companies spend on building physical infrastructure.

Still, despite investor jitters, “cloud demand appears relentless,” he added.

On Friday, JPMorgan said that artificial intelligence-related spending by companies is set to approach “about $870bn by year-end 2026.” That’s 77% higher than the same spending a year ago.

So-called hyper scalers like Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Alphabet represent “about $750bn of that total,” said JPMorgan head of cross-asset strategy Fabio Bassi.

Apple, which is not spending hundreds of billions of dollars building its own data centers, rallied about 1% Tuesday to a more than $5 trillion market cap for the first time. Apple has also surpassed Nvidia as the world’s largest public company.

Nvidia shares were slightly higher mid-morning.

Beyond the rout in chip stocks, U.S. markets overall continued to power higher.

In mid-day trading, the S&P 500 traded higher, while the Russell 2000 was only slightly lower.

“Nothing seems to shake this market,” wrote HSBC’s Max Kettner in a Monday note.

Part of that has to do with positive earnings results so far this quarter. “Even when excluding the blockbuster numbers from Alphabet, the average earnings surprise is well in excess of the post-COVID-19 pandemic average,” he wrote.

World.title: Search for North Carolina woman Liz Waddell is still a missing person case, Grenada police say
World.content:
Grenadian police said Tuesday that their nearly week-old search for a missing North Carolina woman is still active, with hopes of finding the swimmer alive.

Elizabeth “Liz” Waddell, a 44-year-old Cary resident, was last seen going out for a swim at Grand Anse Beach on Wednesday, the Royal Grenada Police Force said.

“At this time, the matter continues, continues to be treated as a missing person investigation,” acting Commissioner of Police Randy Connaught told reporters on Tuesday. “I repeat, at this time, the matter continues to be treated as a missing person.”

Surveillance cameras captured Waddell walking on a jetty near the water at 11:36 a.m. the morning she went missing, Connaught said.

She went into the water at 11:51 a.m. and more footage captured her swimming under the jetty at 12:04 p.m., the police official said.

Witnesses have told investigators they later saw Waddell in the open water, police said.

Waddell’s traveling partner was captured on surveillance cameras on the beach at 12:46 p.m. and she reported the swimmer missing to police at 5:50 p.m., Connaught added.

“There is nothing questionable about her account of the investigations and we continue to receive cooperation from her,” Connaught said of the traveling companion.

Even though Waddell hasn’t been seen in nearly six days, police said they still seek to rescue her.

“It is our hope that Elizabeth will be found and found alive and well,” Connaught said. “The Royal Grenada Police Force remains equally hopeful that she will be safe and that she is safe.”

Local police had been appealing to fishermen, boat operators and residents along the southern coastline to keep their eyes peeled for medium build woman with short blonde hair.

Waddell and her friend first arrived in Grenada, the island nation in the eastern Caribbean Sea that’s about 100 miles north of Venezuela, on July 11.

The missing woman’s husband has since come to the island to help in the search effort, officials said.

“Any bit of information will do at this time, and we do hope that we can locate Elizabeth very soon,” Connaught said. “Again, we empathize with the family, relatives, and friends, and we are hopeful that Elizabeth will be found alive. Thank you.”
