Frequently Asked Questions

Why does Windhoek need N$15 billion for roads and water?

Windhoek’s road network is valued at N$15.4 billion but has a maintenance backlog of N$2.67 billion due to years of underfunding. The city also needs N$11.72 billion to revamp aging water and sanitation systems. Together, these represent the core infrastructure required to support urban growth and prevent further decay of essential networks.

How does Namibia’s national infrastructure gap affect Windhoek?

Namibia faces a national infrastructure funding shortfall of roughly N$150 billion over five to six years. The Road Fund Administration covers less than half of national maintenance needs. Windhoek competes with other municipalities for limited allocations, receiving only a fraction of what it requests from central agencies.

Which foreign powers are involved in Namibia’s infrastructure?

China is the most visible bilateral partner, funding a N$1 billion-plus freeway linking Windhoek to its international airport. The African Development Bank and World Bank support regional corridor projects. The European Union focuses on water, climate adaptation and sustainable finance, while commercial lenders back energy projects including solar and rail.

World.title: StanChart Kenya Pays 522 Pensioners as Fresh Claims Emerge
World.content:
Africa · Eastern

Key Facts —Payout size. StanChart Kenya is paying roughly KES 7.2 billion (USD 54.2 million) to 629 former employees. —Payments begun. The bank has disbursed KES 1.9 billion to 522 of the 629 retirees so far. —New claimants. Over 500 additional former staff have filed fresh claims demanding similar treatment. —Legal endpoint. Kenya’s Supreme Court dismissed StanChart’s final appeal in September 2025. —Profit hit. The payout equals 86.6 percent of the bank’s half-year net profit to June 2025.

Standard Chartered Bank Kenya has begun paying 522 StanChart Kenya pensioners from a landmark KES 7.2 billion settlement, even as a second wave of over 500 former employees files fresh claims that could extend the bank’s liabilities further.

StanChart pays 522 pensioners amid new claims from former employees (Photo internet reproduction)

A 16-year fight reaches its conclusion

The dispute traces back to January 1999, when StanChart Kenya shifted its staff retirement scheme from a Defined Benefit (DB) plan to a Defined Contribution (DC) plan. Former employees alleged the bank used unlawful actuarial factors and removed housing allowances and cost-of-living adjustments from pension calculations.

A 1997 actuarial valuation had identified a pension fund surplus of KES 1.536 billion. Retirees argued that KES 1.1 billion of this surplus was improperly returned to the bank instead of being used to boost member benefits.

The case, formally known as RBAT Appeal No. 8 of 2021 and led by claimant Abdalla Osman alongside 628 others, wound through Kenya’s legal system for over a decade. The Retirement Benefits Appeals Tribunal (RBAT) ruled in the pensioners’ favour on 28 April 2022, ordering a full recalculation of benefits with arrears dating back to 2009.

Courts reject StanChart’s appeals

The High Court upheld the RBAT decision in 2023, and the Court of Appeal did the same in March 2025. StanChart’s final attempt to overturn the ruling ended on 5 September 2025, when Kenya’s Supreme Court dismissed the appeal for lack of constitutional jurisdiction.

The Supreme Court’s refusal to intervene effectively closed the last avenue of appeal. The ruling affirmed that pension disputes of this nature do not automatically raise constitutional questions, a significant clarification in Kenya’s evolving labour jurisprudence.

Following the Supreme Court defeat, StanChart announced it would begin processing payments from 22 September 2025. Verification of pension details was conducted at Almary Green Business Park in Nairobi, where retirees presented pension statements and identity documents.

The money: what StanChart Kenya pensioners receive

The total payout to the 629 appellants stands at KES 7.2 billion (USD 54.2 million). This is funded by KES 2.0 billion in prior provisions, a KES 4.7 billion top-up to the staff pension fund, and a KES 2.5 billion past-service-cost charge recognised by the bank.

By late reporting, StanChart had disbursed KES 1.9 billion to 522 of the 629 retirees. That averages roughly KES 3.8 million per person in the first tranche.

The financial impact on the bank is substantial. The KES 7 billion payout equals 86.6 percent of StanChart Kenya’s half-year net profit of KES 8.08 billion to June 2025. The bank issued a profit warning for the 2025 financial year, projecting a 25 percent decline in net earnings, and later results showed a 38 percent profit slump with a KES 2.7 billion one-off charge.

Fresh claims from the “Non-629” group

Even as the original 629 StanChart Kenya pensioners receive their payments, a second wave of claimants has emerged. Business Daily Africa reports that over 500 former staff who were not part of the original group have raised fresh claims, while other sources put the figure at more than 600.

A core group of 325 former employees, calling themselves the “Non-629 Former Employees,” has filed formal claims. They argue they were similarly affected by the 1999 pension scheme conversion and demand identical recalculations of their benefits.

StanChart has rejected these new claims outright, stating they “lack any merit in law or fact.” The bank’s legal team argues the Supreme Court judgment applies only to the original parties and cannot be extended to additional claimants who did not participate in the initial case.

Regulators step in as the dispute widens

Kenya’s Retirement Benefits Authority (RBA) has intervened in the new dispute. The regulator has directed trustees of the Standard Chartered Kenya Pension Fund to undertake an independent review of the claims raised by the new group of former employees.

The RBA is examining a 21-point petition submitted by the Non-629 group, which outlines alleged non-compliance with trust deeds and scheme rules. The regulator has acknowledged that over 500 former staff with circumstances similar to the original 629 have made these fresh claims.

The case has also spilled beyond Kenya’s borders. On 2 October 2025, a group of 629 former employees lodged a complaint with the UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), alleging concealment of liabilities by StanChart Kenya and its London-based parent group. If taken up, the complaint could expose Standard Chartered to cross-border regulatory scrutiny over how pension obligations are reported in group financial statements.

What the case means for corporate Kenya and beyond

The StanChart Kenya pensioners case sets a powerful precedent for pension governance across East Africa. The RBAT judgment reinforced the principle that pension surpluses cannot be returned to a corporate sponsor unless the scheme is being wound up, a finding that constrains how employers can redesign schemes and handle surpluses.

For investors, the case serves as a stark reminder of contingent liabilities in emerging markets. Legacy pension obligations can dramatically alter earnings trajectories, and StanChart’s experience suggests that prolonged litigation can backfire when courts and regulators side with workers.

The dispute also fits into a broader recalibration of power between global banks and African regulators, a theme explored in our pillar on Africa: The New Scramble. Kenya’s institutions have demonstrated they can impose significant costs on multinational capital when local rules are breached, and former employees are now extending that push across borders to the UK regulator.

StanChart Kenya has publicly signalled a shift away from litigation toward alternative dispute resolution in future cases. For other foreign banks and corporates in East Africa, the message is clear: aggressive scheme redesigns that erode promised benefits can carry heavy financial and reputational costs.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many StanChart Kenya pensioners have been paid so far?

StanChart Kenya has disbursed KES 1.9 billion to 522 of the 629 retirees covered by the RBAT ruling. The bank began processing payments on 22 September 2025 after Kenya’s Supreme Court dismissed its final appeal. The average payout per person in this first tranche is roughly KES 3.8 million.

What are the new claims against Standard Chartered Kenya?

Over 500 additional former employees, including a core group of 325 calling themselves the “Non-629 Former Employees,” have filed fresh claims. They argue they were similarly affected by the 1999 pension scheme conversion and demand identical recalculations of their benefits. StanChart has rejected these claims, and the Retirement Benefits Authority is now conducting an independent review.

How much has the pension payout cost StanChart Kenya?

The total payout to the 629 appellants is KES 7.2 billion (USD 54.2 million). This equals 86.6 percent of the bank’s half-year net profit to June 2025. StanChart issued a profit warning for the 2025 financial year, and later results showed a 38 percent profit slump with a KES 2.7 billion one-off charge related to the pension settlement.

World.title: São Paulo Nightlife Tonight — July 28, 2026
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

São Paulo · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Tuesdays at Bar Brahma (Centro) if you only have time for ONE place tonight, this is it: a classic, tourist-friendly but authentically Paulistano spot at the corner of Ipiranga and São João, with live MPB and samba on a Tuesday, cold beer, and a historic buzz that welcomes solo newcomers immediately.

Tonight at a Glance —Bar Brahma Iconic MPB and samba in Centro; mixed crowd of locals, tourists and after-work groups; best on music nights like Tuesday —Tokyo Marine Hall / Tokio Marine Hall For a big-production international or national show tonight; Paulista crowd; check the agenda —Vila Madalena boteco crawl Street bar-hopping with a young, bohemian crowd; best from 9pm on any Tuesday —Beco do Batman alleys (no-time-waste drink) A pre-going-out tip: the bars around the graffiti alleys are busy even on weeknights; cheap beer and snapshots —Prainha Paulista (Augusta rooftop) Open-air downtown-ish rooftop with city views and a mixed expat-local scene; a solid Tuesday standby

Tuesday in São Paulo is the city’s stealthy going-out night – Vila Madalena botecos fill with after-work groups, Centro’s classic music houses have reliable live MPB, and the city’s LGBTQ+ anchors warm up for the week. Tonight, Tuesday 28 July 2026, the circuit runs from early-evening chopps to late-night music, with the best energy between 9pm and midnight.

Tonight across Sao Paulo. (Photo internet reproduction)

What’s On Tonight

Live MPB and samba classics — at Bar Brahma, 9pm (music usually starts by 9:30pm). the safest and most iconic Tuesday-night musical introduction to São Paulo, right on the corner of Ipiranga and São João.

Rooftop sunset and after-dark drinks — at Prainha Paulista (Augusta), 6pm–1am. one of the few open-air baixo-centro rooftops that works well on a weekday; order a gin and tonic and watch the light go pink over the Minhocão.

Beco do Batman craft beer and street art — at Hocus Pocus DNA or nearby bar (Vila Madalena), 7pm–late. a no-pressure Tuesday night with the hippest art-covered alleyways, very Instagrammable, and a young crowd sipping craft beer.

Sertanejo and pop remixes, commercial dance floor — at Villa Mix (if open Tuesday, or similar Cambuci-area house), 10pm–3am. for that glittery, Brazilian-country-meets-pop spectacle; best if you want to dance early in the week.

Reliable LGBTQ+ weekday warm-up — at Bar Queen (Consolação), 9pm–2am. kitsch glasses, drag queens behind the bar, and a queue-free Tuesday making it easy to get your first taste of São Paulo’s queer centre.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Early warm-up (6pm–9pm): Empanadas and beer in Baixo Pinheiros or a rooftop in Augusta/Higienópolis – arrive by 7pm to grab outdoor seats.

After-work chopp (7pm–10pm): Vila Madalena corner bars and the Beco do Batman passageways; solo newcomers can pull up a stool at any boteco.

Centro classic (8pm–midnight): Bar Brahma or a nearby live-music spot for MPB/samba; couvert artístico usually R$20–R$40 per person.

After midnight (11pm–3am): Consolação/Augusta LGBTQ+ bars or a commercial club playing sertanejo; metro closes around midnight so plan around Uber.

Late-night eats (1am–4am): Padarias (24-hour bakeries) or a post-club mortadella sandwich at the Municipal Market area (via Uber only).

Weekday reality check: Tuesday is busy but not peak; lines are rare, door policies are relaxed, and this is ideal for a foreigner’s first São Paulo night.

Scenes & Sounds

Samba and MPB — classic Brazilian rhythms, often with a full band and a seated audience sipping ice-cold beer; very welcoming Where: Bar Brahma (Centro), Ó do Borogodó (Pinheiros/Vila Madalena area), Bar Samba (Vila Mariana)

Sertanejo — Brazilian country-pop, big hair, big choruses, a glossy young crowd and two-step dancing Where: Villa Mix (Cambuci), Villa Country (Barra Funda; check Tuesday schedule)

Electronic — deep house and techno in industrial-luxe clubs; a more alternative, fashion-conscious crowd Where: D.Edge (Barra Funda), PISE (Vila Olímpia), Gop Tun parties (check Instagram for tonight location)

Forró — northeastern dance with accordion and triangle; friendly, easy-to-learn partner dancing Where: Casa de Frá yó (Pinheiros) or Canto da Ema (Vila Madalena; verify Tuesday opening)

Hip hop and funk — São Paulo street sound – heavy bass, MCs, a very local and energetic crowd Where: Augusta Street clubs or larger one-off parties in Barra Funda (follow SP Na Rua or similar Instagrams)

Jazz and blues — smoky, intimate rooms with excellent musicians and a date-night feel Where: JazzNosFundos (Vila Madalena), Bourbon Street Music Club (Moema)

Pick Your Night

Solo and safe: Bar Brahma (Centro) – sit at the counter, order a chopp, and the barman will talk to you in a mix of Portuguese and smiles.

Date night: Prainha Paulista rooftop (Augusta) or a jazz club in Vila Madalena; arrive early for sunset.

Dance till sunrise: D.Edge (Barra Funda) for electronic, or a sertanejo house – Tuesdays are less packed so the dance floor feels freer.

Meet locals: Vila Madalena boteco crawl – grab a beer in plastic cups on the street and chat with any group laughing nearby.

Chill and conversation: Craft beer bar in Pinheiros or a candlelit table at a jazz club; aim for 8pm to get a quiet corner before the late set.

Where to Go

Bar Brahma — Centro Established in 1948, this is the most famous corner bar and music house. Great mix of Paulistanos, tourists and a lived-in, welcoming atmosphere. Tonight: Live MPB and samba night. Music normally starts around 9:30pm. Best time: Tuesday through Saturday from 9pm, arriving by 8:45pm to get a good spot before the band. Cost: Couvert artístico typically R$30–R$50 (verify on arrival). Drinks from R$15 (chopp). Card and cash accepted. Address: Avenida São João, 677, Centro Instagram: @barbrahma Website: barbrahma.com.br Getting there: Metro República (Red Line), 5‑min walk. Uber recommended after 11pm. Good to know: For groups of 4+, book by phone at least a day ahead. Smart‑casual, no shorts if you want to avoid standing out.

Prainha Paulista (Rooftop) — Consolação/Augusta Open-air bar with city-skyline views, popular with a stylish but relaxed 25–35 crowd, including expats and digital nomads. Tonight: No specific event listed; reliable Tuesday standby with bar music, drinks and sunset vibe. Best time: Tuesday–Sunday from 6pm; arrive before 7pm for a seat with a view. Cost: No cover. Cocktails R$35–R$45, beer R$12–R$18. Card preferred. Address: Rua Augusta, 2000 (or nearby entrance on co‑working building rooftop; check Instagram for exact door). Instagram: @prainhasaopaulo Getting there: Metro Consolação (Green Line) then 8‑min walk. Uber easy. Good to know: No booking for small groups; first-come, first-served. No tank tops for guys on busier nights.

Hocus Pocus DNA & Beco do Batman bars — Vila Madalena Craft-beer pub right at the Graffiti Alley, with other bars spilling onto the streets. Very young, creative, English-friendly crowd. Tonight: Open Tuesday with tap beer, burgers, and street art photography. Best time: Any warm weekday from 7pm; get there by sunset for alley photos. Cost: No entry fee. Craft beer from R$18 (300ml). Cash and card. Address: Rua Medeiros de Albuquerque, across from Beco do Batman Instagram: @hocuspocus.dna Getting there: Metro Vila Madalena (Green Line), then 12‑min walk or a short Uber. Good to know: No booking. Casual dress, any shoes fine.

Bar Queen (Queer bar) — Consolação LGBTQ+ anchor with a campy interior, drag bartenders and a loud, friendly playlist. Very welcoming for solo newcomers. Tonight: Tuesday is a quieter weeknight; perfect for easy conversation and enjoying the decor. Best time: Wednesday–Saturday for peak drag moments; tonight from 9pm. Cost: No cover. Cocktails R$25–R$35. Card and cash. Address: Rua Dona Veridiana, 547, Santa Cecília / Consolação area Instagram: @barqueensp Getting there: Metro Santa Cecília (Red Line) or Marechal Deodoro (Blue Line). Use Uber to the door late. Good to know: No booking needed tonight. Dress expressive but no strict rule.

D.Edge (Club) — Barra Funda Industrial design, a Funktion-One sound system and the city’s electronic music temple. A cooler, alternative crowd. Tonight: Check D.Edge Instagram for Tuesday line-up; some weeks host live acts, others are quieter. Best time: Friday and Saturday from midnight; on Tuesday arrive by 11pm if a party is on. Cost: Entry R$40–R$80 (varies by night). Beer R$15, cocktails R$35. Comanda system. Address: Avenida Auro Soares de Moura Andrade, 141, Barra Funda Instagram: @dedgeclub Website: dedge.com.br Getting there: Metro Palmeiras-Barra Funda (Red Line). Walk or Uber – pedestrian bridge after Metro. Uber safest at night. Good to know: Advance tickets via website or Instagram bio link for big nights. No strict dress code but people dress up.

Villa Mix — Cambuci Large sertanejo house with a shiny, performance-heavy layout and a crowd that dances and sings along intensely. Tonight: Check Villa Mix Instagram for Tuesday opening; some weeks have a sertanejo live act on Tuesday. Best time: Friday and Saturday, from 10pm; on weekdays confirm schedule. Cost: Entry varies (R$30–R$70). Comanda card. Drinks R$15–R$35. Card mostly. Address: Avenida Lins de Vasconcelos, way 3000, Cambuci Instagram: @villamixsp Website: villamix-sp.com.br Getting there: Metro Santos-Imigrantes (Green Line) then a short Uber. Good to know: Purchase tickets online if there’s a big-name artist. Semi-formal/trendy – jeans, shirts, no flip-flops.

JazzNosFundos — Vila Madalena Hidden basement jazz club under a gallery, fantastic acoustics, a respectful music-audience atmosphere and a bohemian, arty crowd. Tonight: Check Instagram for tonight’s jazz set; Tuesday is a regular music night. Best time: Wednesday–Saturday from 9pm; arrive 30 mins early for good seats in the small room. Cost: Couvert R$25–R$45. Cocktails R$28, beer R$12. Card and cash. Address: Rua Cardeal Arcoverde, 742, Pinheiros Instagram: @jazznosfundos Website: jazznosfundos.com.br Getting there: Metro Faria Lima (Yellow Line) then 10‑min walk or Uber. Good to know: Book through Instagram link to avoid disappointment; intimate seating.

Vila Madalena boteco corner — Vila Madalena Classic São Paulo ritual: buy a beer, stand on the pavement, watch the crowd flow. Spontaneous and easy. Tonight: Busy from 8pm on a Tuesday. Start near Rua Mourato Coelho intersection. Best time: Any evening from 8pm, especially Thursday–Saturday. Tuesday is more after-work and calm. Cost: No cover. Beer R$8–R$12 on the street. Cash or card at each bar. Address: Rua Mourato Coelho, around 400–600s, Vila Madalena Getting there: Metro Vila Madalena (Green Line), then a 10‑min walk downhill. Good to know: No booking. Extremely casual; shorts and sneakers normal.

Bar Samba — Vila Mariana Authentic samba bar with a spirited local crowd, cold beer, and some of the best live samba on a weeknight. Tonight: Check Instagram for Tuesday samba de raiz; typically open with live music. Best time: Weekdays from 9pm with local samba; arrive early to get a table. Cost: Couvert around R$20. Beer R$10. Cash favored. Address: Rua Doutor Eduardo D’Ávila, 17, Vila Mariana Instagram: @barsambaoficial Getting there: Metro Ana Rosa (Blue/Green Line) then a short Uber. Good to know: Call ahead on day to reserve a table. Relaxed dress.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Vila Madalena & Pinheiros: Young, student-bohemian, craft-beer-and-street-art energy; dozens of bars steps apart.

Centro (República/Anhangabaú): Historic, grand-scale and slightly gritty, with classic music houses and a mix of tourists and old-guard Paulistanos.

Augusta & Consolação: A rollercoaster downtown strip mixing LGBTQ+ bars, hipster rooftops, cheap eateries and a fashionista-art-student crowd.

Barra Funda: Clubland: big electronic and sertanejo houses with industrial warehouses and serious sound systems.

Vila Olímpia & Itaim Bibi: Moneyed, polished, with sleek bars, rooftops and electronic clubs; more expensive and English-friendly.

Moema & Vila Mariana: Tree-lined residential sophistication with jazz clubs, refined bars and a slightly older, calmer set.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

Bar Queen (Consolação) — Campy drag bar, ultra-welcoming, cocktails and kitsch; perfect chill Tuesday intro to SP’s queen scene.

Bubu Lounge (República) — upmarket LGBTQ+ club with pop remixes and a lively dance floor; check Tuesday opening on Instagram.

Ursound (sporadic party) — Electronic LGBTQ+ party often held in industrial spaces; find tonight’s location via Instagram @ursound.

Money & How Paying Works The comanda card is your lifeline: you get a plastic or paper tab card at the door; EVERY drink and snack is logged to it; you pay the total at the exit cashier. Losing it can mean a fine of R$100–R$300, so treat it like cash. Couvert artístico is a per-person music charge added to your bill when there’s a live band; it is NOT the tip, nor an entry fee – often R$20–R$50. Cards (Visa/Mastercard contactless) are accepted at almost all formal venues; carry some cash for small botecos, street snacks or splitting a bill. Service is nearly always 10% included on the bill as ‘serviço’; tipping extra is not required but a small extra in cash for a great barman is warmly received.

Getting Home Safe

São Paulo metro closes around midnight. Last trains depart around 00:00 from central stations. If you’re staying out after 11:30pm, plan on using 99 or Uber to get back.

Use 99 or Uber, not street taxis at night. Order from inside the bar, watch the app for the car model and plate, then walk directly to the vehicle when it arrives.

Surge pricing is common on rainy nights and after big events. If surge is heavy, wait 15–20 minutes with a final drink inside and then re-check.

Stick to well-lit, busy streets and follow the ‘movimento’ instinct: if a street feels eerily empty, turn back and take the busier parallel road, even if it means a short Uber.

When waiting for your ride, don’t stand on the kerb scrolling your phone; stay near the venue entrance or a brightly lit shop until the app says the car has arrived.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need to speak Portuguese?

For taxis, menus and door staff, a few firm phrases help massively, but most bars in the expat circuit have some English-speaking staff. Start with ‘Boa noite’ and ‘Eu queria uma cerveja, por favor’.

When should I arrive for a good night?

Warm-up bars fill from 7pm–8:30pm. Live music spots need you seated by 9pm. Clubs are quiet before 11pm. Tuesday is a non‑peak night, so arriving early helps create atmosphere where it’s needed.

How do I pay with the comanda card?

Hand your comanda to the waiter when ordering; they mark each item digitally or on paper. Only pay and return the card when you’re ready to leave. Losing it is expensive.

Sources: metrolinehub.com, rio.com, planrio.com

World.title: Rio de Janeiro Nightlife Tonight — July 28, 2026
World.content:

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Rio de Janeiro · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Rio Scenarium If you only have time for one place tonight, make it this legendary three-storey antique-filled mansion in Lapa. It opens on Tuesdays (unlike most samba houses) and offers the most spectacular introduction to live Brazilian music—samba, choro, MPB—in a setting that feels like a Wes Anderson film. Tourists and cariocas mix beautifully here, and the comanda system means you can roam freely.

Tonight at a Glance —Rio Scenarium The essential Lapa mansion of live samba and MPB; mixed crowd of locals and foreigners; Tuesday is a reliable night. —Carioca da Gema Intimate, spirited samba house under Lapa’s arches; a favourite with serious music lovers; best from 9 pm. —Bar Bukowski Botafogo’s grungy rock temple with cheap drinks and a young, unpretentious crowd; weeknights are buzzing from 10 pm. —Comuna Creative, artsy burger-and-cocktail spot in Botafogo that morphs into a low-key party; great for solo newcomers to meet locals. —Le Boy / La Girl Copacabana’s prime LGBTQ+ twin venue; pop, shows and a lively mixed crowd; weekends are the peak but open on Tuesdays.

Tuesday in Rio is a slow-burn delight: Lapa’s samba houses are open but mercifully uncrowded, Botafogo’s bars hum with students and creatives, and you can still find a late-night dance floor if you know where to look. Tonight is about easing into the city’s rhythm with live music, cold chopp and real conversation before the weekend madness arrives.

Tonight across Rio de Janeiro. (Photo internet reproduction)

What’s On Tonight

Live samba and MPB (rotating resident bands) — at Rio Scenarium, From 8 pm (music starts around 9 pm). Tuesday is one of the house’s reliable opening nights; you get the full antique-splendour experience without the Friday crush.

Samba da Ouvidor (traditional roda de samba) — at Trapiche Gamboa, From 7 pm. A historic, familial roda in a beautiful restored warehouse in Gamboa; mostly locals, very welcoming, and the samba is world-class.

Rock covers and live band nights — at Bar Bukowski, From 10 pm. Botafogo’s go-to for affordable rock; Tuesdays reliably feature live bands or DJs playing classic and indie rock to a student-heavy crowd.

MPB and jazz-influenced Brazilian sounds — at Carioca da Gema, From 9 pm. A smaller, more musician-focused Lapa house; the acoustics are superb and Tuesday line-ups lean towards inventive MPB.

Low-key DJ sets and cultural gatherings — at Comuna, From 8 pm. Comuna’s Tuesday programming often includes art launches or easygoing DJ sets; an excellent place to meet English-speaking cariocas.

Pop, electronic and Brazilian beats — at Le Boy / La Girl, Club from 11 pm. Copacabana’s staple LGBTQ+ spot stays open on Tuesdays; expect a friendly, mixed crowd and themed pop nights.

Choro and instrumental samba — at Café Cultural Sacrilégio, From 8 pm. A laid-back Lapa bar set in a colonial house with a garden; perfect for choro or instrumental samba in a quieter setting.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Warm-up 7–9 pm: Start with sunset caipirinhas at a beach kiosk in Copacabana or Ipanema; the boardwalk kiosks are lively and safe at this hour.

Dinner-and-drinks 8–10 pm: Head to Botafogo’s Rua Nelson Mandela or Cobal do Humaitá for craft beer, burgers and open-air bar-hopping.

Live-music heart 9 pm–midnight: Move to Lapa’s Rua do Lavradio or Rua Riachuelo for samba, MPB and choro at Rio Scenarium, Carioca da Gema or Trapiche Gamboa.

Late shift midnight–2 am: Return to Botafogo for Bukowski’s rock or cross to Copacabana for LGBTQ+ dancing at Le Boy/La Girl.

Weeknight sunrise 2–5 am: For the determined, check Instagram for underground funk or electronic parties in Saúde or a roving ‘baile’—these are word-of-mouth, so ask bartenders.

Recovery: Night buses are not advised; always use Uber or 99 after the metro stops at midnight.

Scenes & Sounds

Samba & Choro — Live Brazilian roots music—joyful samba, elegant choro and bossa nova—in historic Lapa and Gamboa venues. Where: Rio Scenarium, Carioca da Gema, Trapiche Gamboa, Café Sacrilégio in Lapa/Centro.

MPB (Música Popular Brasileira) — Sophisticated Brazilian pop and jazz-inflected sounds; attracts a musically curious crowd. Where: Carioca da Gema, Comuna and special nights at Audio Rebel in Botafogo.

Rock & Indie — Gritty, unpretentious rock bars with live bands and cheap longnecks. Where: Bar Bukowski (Botafogo), Experience Music in Barra, and occasional indie nights in Lapa.

Electronic & Underground — Deep house, techno and bass-heavy parties that start late and run till dawn. Where: Check Instagram for roving parties in Saúde and Centro; permanent clubs like Fosfobox in Copacabana.

Funk Carioca — Rio’s homegrown, heavy-bass party sound; baile funk is a community-rooted experience. Where: Community bailes in favelas (go only with a trusted local guide) and occasional curated club nights in Lapa or Saúde.

Sertanejo & Forró — Brazilian country and northeastern forró dancing; hugely popular with locals. Where: Specialised houses in Barra da Tijuca and occasional forró nights in Lapa’s smaller bars.

Pick Your Night

Date night: Rio Scenarium—the twinkling antiques and live samba create instant romance. Arrive by 8 pm for a table on the mezzanine.

Solo and safe: Comuna in Botafogo—easy counter dining, friendly English-speaking staff, and a relaxed arts crowd. Sit at the bar and you’ll have people to talk to.

Dance till sunrise: Start at Bukowski, then check for a late-night electronic or funk address on Instagram stories; Tuesday demand is low but dedicated parties exist.

Meet locals: Trapiche Gamboa’s Samba da Ouvidor—a genuine neighbourhood roda where you’ll be one of very few foreigners and the welcome is warm.

Chill and conversation: Café Cultural Sacrilégio—an open-air garden in Lapa with gentle choro music; quiet enough to talk and soak in the atmosphere.

Meet other expats: Comuna or Bukowski—both attract international students, digital nomads and English-speaking cariocas, especially on weeknights.

Where to Go

Rio Scenarium — Lapa An astonishing three-floor antiques warehouse turned live-music venue; the city’s most iconic night out, beloved by locals and essential for any visitor. Tonight: Resident samba and MPB bands from around 9 pm; Tuesday is a regular opening night with a more relaxed crowd. Best time: Tuesday–Saturday from 8 pm; arrive by 8 pm to get a table or explore the décor before the music starts. Cost: Couvert artístico typically R$40–R$80; drinks R$20–R$40; comanda card system—pay on exit. Cards accepted. Address: Rua do Lavradio, 20, Lapa Instagram: @rioscenarium Website: rioscenarium.com.br Getting there: Metro to Cinelândia or Carioca, then a short Uber; avoid walking side streets late. Good to know: Not essential on a Tuesday but book a table online to guarantee entry without queuing; smart-casual, no shorts for men in the evening.

Carioca da Gema — Lapa A smaller, wood-panelled samba house with superb acoustics; serious music heads and dancers pack in for live samba, MPB and choro. Tonight: Live samba or MPB from around 9 pm; programming is confirmed weekly on Instagram. Best time: Monday–Saturday from 9 pm; arrive by 9 pm for a good spot near the stage. Cost: Couvert R$30–R$60; drinks R$15–R$30; comanda card, cards accepted. Address: Avenida Mem de Sá, 79, Lapa Instagram: @cariocadagema Getting there: Short walk from Rio Scenarium; use Uber after midnight. Good to know: No booking for small groups; casual dress, just turn up.

Trapiche Gamboa — Gamboa / Saúde A restored port warehouse hosting one of Rio’s most authentic rodas de samba; multi-generational, predominantly local crowd and sublime music. Tonight: Samba da Ouvidor roda from 7 pm; check @trapichegamboa for exact Tuesday confirmation. Best time: Samba da Ouvidor on select weeknights (including some Tuesdays) from 7 pm; arrive early to grab a seat. Cost: Couvert around R$30–R$50; drinks R$15–R$25; comanda card, cards accepted. Address: Rua Sacadura Cabral, 155, Saúde Instagram: @trapichegamboa Getting there: Uber is the best way; metro to Uruguaiana and a ride-share. Good to know: Check Instagram and book via WhatsApp if listed; casual dress.

Bar Bukowski — Botafogo Rio’s long-standing rock bar—loud, dark and gloriously sticky-floored; a student-heavy crowd gathers for cheap drinks and live bands. Tonight: Tuesday rock night—live band or DJ from 10 pm; check @barbukowskioficial for tonight’s act. Best time: Monday–Saturday from 10 pm; Tuesday is reliably busy by midnight. Cost: Entry around R$20–R$50; longneck beers R$10–R$15; comanda card, cash and cards. Address: Rua Paulo Barreto, 15, Botafogo Instagram: @barbukowskioficial Getting there: Metro to Botafogo station, then a 10-minute walk or short Uber. Good to know: No booking; casual rock-and-roll attire—jeans and band tees rule.

Comuna — Botafogo An indie-cultural hub serving creative burgers and cocktails; a magnet for young artists, expats and remote workers, with frequent art shows and DJ sets. Tonight: Cultural programming or low-key DJs from 8 pm; check @comunacultural for tonight’s event. Best time: Tuesday–Saturday from 8 pm; great for a solo dinner that turns into a casual party. Cost: No entry fee normally; burgers R$30–R$45, cocktails R$25–R$40; cards accepted. Address: Rua Sorocaba, 585, Botafogo Instagram: @comunacultural Getting there: Metro to Botafogo, then 15-minute walk or quick Uber. Good to know: No booking needed; very casual.

Le Boy / La Girl — Copacabana Copacabana’s best-known LGBTQ+ twin venue; Le Boy for gay nightlife, La Girl with a mixed, inclusive crowd, pop shows and drag performances. Tonight: Club opens from 11 pm with themed pop nights; check @leboy.rio for tonight’s specifics. Best time: Thursday–Saturday busiest, but Tuesday is open with a smaller, friendly crowd; arrive from 11.30 pm. Cost: Entry R$30–R$60; drinks R$20–R$35; comanda card, cards accepted. Address: Rua Raul Pompeia, 102, Copacabana Instagram: @leboy.rio Getting there: Metro to Cardeal Arcoverde, then a 10-minute walk or Uber to the door. Good to know: No booking for individuals; no shorts or flip-flops for men.

Café Cultural Sacrilégio — Lapa A charming colonial house with a lush garden bar; live choro, samba and MPB in a relaxed, conversation-friendly setting. Tonight: Choro or instrumental samba from 8 pm; a refined Lapa alternative to the big samba halls. Best time: Tuesday–Sunday from 8 pm; arrive for dinner and stay for the music. Cost: Couvert around R$20–R$40; drinks R$15–R$30; cards accepted. Address: Avenida Mem de Sá, 81, Lapa Instagram: @sacrilegiolapa Getting there: Metro to Cinelândia then a short Uber; next door to Carioca da Gema. Good to know: Book a garden table on Instagram; casual-smart.

Baródromo — Lapa A street-level bar under the Arcos da Lapa serving icy chopp and simple petiscos; the perfect first stop to get your bearings in Lapa. Tonight: Open-air drinking and people-watching from early evening until late. Best time: Any night from 7 pm; best for a pre-samba warm-up. Cost: No entry; chopp R$8–R$12; cash preferred for small purchases. Address: Rua Riachuelo, close to the Arcos Getting there: Short walk from Cinelândia metro; stay on the main, lit strip. Good to know: No booking; very casual street-bar vibe.

Fosfobox — Copacabana A subterranean club for late-night electronic, indie and funk parties; small, sweaty and beloved by cariocas who dance till sunrise. Tonight: Check @fosfobox for any special Tuesday programming; otherwise reliably active Thursday–Saturday. Best time: Thursday–Saturday from midnight; Tuesday may have occasional events. Cost: Entry R$30–R$60; drinks R$20–R$35; comanda card, cards accepted. Address: Rua Siqueira Campos, 143, Copacabana Instagram: @fosfobox Getting there: Metro to Cardeal Arcoverde, then a short walk. Good to know: Arrive before 1 am to avoid long queues; no formal dress code but avoid beachwear.

La Cueva — Copacabana A cosy, long-running LGBTQ+ bar and club with a diverse crowd; less flashy than Le Boy, more neighbourly, with strong drinks and a loyal following. Tonight: Open Tuesday from 10 pm; smaller midweek crowd, ideal for a relaxed start. Best time: Thursday–Sunday busiest; Tuesday is quieter and friendlier for newcomers. Cost: No or low entry before midnight; drinks R$15–R$30; comanda card, cards accepted. Address: Rua Miguel Lemos, 51, Copacabana Instagram: @lacuevario Getting there: Metro to Cardeal Arcoverde, then a 5-minute walk. Good to know: No booking; casual, inclusive vibe.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Lapa: The historic nightlife heart; samba spilling onto cobblestones, colonial architecture and a raucous, tourist-meets-local energy under the Arcos.

Botafogo: Student-cool and creative; craft-beer bars, rock dens, and inventive eateries on streets buzzing with young cariocas and expats.

Copacabana: Old-school beach glamour with a strong LGBTQ+ scene; mix of traditional nightclubs and kiosk culture on the boardwalk.

Gamboa / Saúde: Portside renaissance; warehouse parties, authentic samba rodas and a more underground, carioca-rooted night out.

Leblon / Ipanema: Upscale bar-hopping; wine bars and sophisticated dining on Dias Ferreira, with a polished, well-heeled crowd.

Barra da Tijuca: Sprawling and car-dependent; mega-clubs and sertanejo halls for those willing to travel, popular with Zona Oeste locals.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

Le Boy / La Girl — Copacabana’s flagship LGBTQ+ party spot; Le Boy for men, La Girl for a mixed, inclusive dance floor; pop anthems and drag shows; busiest Thursday–Sunday but open Tuesday.

La Cueva — A more low-key, welcoming Copacabana bar-club; diverse crowd, strong cocktails and a neighbourly atmosphere; perfect for a relaxed Tuesday introduction to the scene.

The Week — The mega-club in Saúde attracting national and international LGBTQ+ crowds; huge production, pool parties on weekends; check @theweekrio for Tuesday openings.

Money & How Paying Works The comanda card: At most music venues and clubs, you get a tab card at the door. All drinks are marked on it, and you pay the total at the exit till. If you lose the card, expect a steep fine (often R$150–R$300). Guard it carefully. Couvert artístico: Live-music houses charge an artist cover—this is the ‘entry fee’. It’s added to your comanda or paid at the door. Always confirm the amount before sitting down. Cash vs card: Nearly all the venues in this guide accept credit and debit cards; however, small street bars and botecos may prefer cash, and having R$50–R$100 in reais is wise. Tipping: A 10% service charge (‘serviço’) is normally included on your bill. You don’t need to add more, though rounding up for exceptional service is a kind gesture.

Getting Home Safe

Metro closing: Monday–Saturday the metro runs until midnight exactly; after that, the system shuts. Plan to leave your venue early enough, or accept you’ll need a ride app.

Uber & 99: Both work brilliantly in Rio and are far safer than street taxis at night. Always check the licence plate and driver name, share your trip with a friend, and wait inside your venue until the car is outside.

Surge pricing: Late nights, especially at closing times and weekends, can push fares 1.5× to 2.5× above normal. A short ride within Zona Sul might be R$15–R$25 normally, but R$40–R$60 post-surge. Have the 99 app as a backup.

Stay on main, well-lit streets; in Lapa, stick to the area directly under the Arcos and Rua Riachuelo where police are present. Avoid empty side streets, especially going to or from your Uber.

Do not walk on the beach sand at night—stay on the lit boardwalk. Use your phone only inside a bar, restaurant or the foyer of your accommodation; never wave it around on the pavement while waiting for a ride.

Frequently Asked Questions

What time should I really arrive?

Brazilians go out late. For live music, arrive by 9 pm to get a good spot. For clubs, 11 pm–midnight is normal. If the band starts at 8 pm, that means the first note at 8.40 pm at the earliest.

Will I get by in English?

In tourist-friendly spots like Rio Scenarium and Comuna, staff will have some English. In more local samba houses like Trapiche Gamboa, know a few phrases—‘Uma cerveja, por favor’ goes a long way. Download Google Translate offline.

What should I wear?

Rio is casual but not sloppy. For Lapa samba houses, smart-casual; no shorts or flip-flops for men. In Botafogo bars, jeans and trainers are fine. Gay clubs like Le Boy enforce a no-shorts, no-slippers dress code for men.

Sources: metrolinehub.com, rio.com, planrio.com

World.title: Havana’s Grand Theatres Trace a Turbulent Scenic History
World.content:
Cultural Heritage & Urban Development

Key Facts —Oldest venue. Havana’s first recorded theatre, the Coliseo, opened in 1775, but the tradition of staged performances dates to the 1570s. —Architectural anchor. The Alicia Alonso Grand Theater began as the Teatro Tacón in 1838, once the largest and most luxurious theatre in Latin America. —Cinema explosion. By the late 1950s, Havana operated around 100 movie theatres, up from just 42 in 1919, mirroring the city’s spatial growth. —First film screening. The cinematograph arrived in Havana on 24 January 1897, shown at Paseo del Prado #126, right next to the Tacón Theatre. —Living heritage. The Martí Theatre, opened in 1884, still functions today with first-grade heritage protection and modernised technology.

Havana’s scenic history is etched into its stages and cinema screens, a journey that begins in colonial plazas and stretches to modernist Miramar, revealing how culture, power, and money shaped the city’s built environment.

A street in Old Havana, Cuba.

A Stage Set in the 16th Century

Cubans have gathered for theatrical performances since at least the 1570s. City council minutes from the period record plays tied to Corpus Christi and saints’ day festivals, making performance a civic ritual long before a dedicated venue existed.

The first formal theatre, the Coliseo—later called Teatro Principal—opened in 1775. It marked the beginning of an institutional relationship between Havana’s urban development and its cultural ambitions, a pattern that would accelerate dramatically in the next century.

The Tacón: Latin America’s Grandest Stage

The anchor of Havana’s scenic history is the building now known as the Alicia Alonso Grand Theater. It began as the Teatro Tacón, inaugurated on 15 April 1838 under Captain General Don Miguel Tacón, and was immediately recognised as the largest and most luxurious theatre in Latin America.

The venue occupied a prime block bounded by Paseo del Prado and nearby streets, facing what is now Parque Central. Its stages hosted elite European artists such as Enrico Caruso and Sarah Bernhardt, cementing Havana’s reputation as a major performing-arts capital and a profitable stop on international touring circuits.

In the early 20th century, the Centro Gallego de La Habana acquired the property and demolished the old Tacón structure. The current neo-baroque building, completed between 1914 and 1915 by the firm Purdy & Henderson, rose in its place, adorned with stone and marble allegories of music, theatre, and benevolence.

Alicia Alonso and the Ballet Capital

In 1985, on the initiative of prima ballerina Alicia Alonso, the complex was officially renamed the Gran Teatro de La Habana. Since 2015 it has borne her full name, honouring the dancer who made Cuba a global ballet power.

Today the theatre is home to the National Ballet of Cuba and the main stage of the International Ballet Festival of Havana. The García Lorca auditorium seats about 1,500 spectators and remains one of the most prestigious performance spaces in the Spanish-speaking world, a fact that continues to draw cultural tourists and diplomatic attention to the island.

The Broader Theatrical Landscape of Havana’s Scenic History

A full journey through Havana’s scenic history requires stepping beyond the Gran Teatro. The Martí Theatre, opened as the Teatro Irijoa on 8 June 1884, sits on Calle Zulueta near the Hotel Raquel and holds first-grade heritage protection.

Its neoclassical design and early admission of Black and mixed-race workers made it a progressive force while slavery still existed on the island. The venue became a key home for the Bufo genre, a comic musical theatre form that shaped Cuban popular culture and drew audiences from across the social spectrum.

The Alhambra Theatre, founded on 13 September 1890 at Consulado and Virtudes, was architecturally modest but enormously influential. From 1900 to 1935 it hosted one of the longest continuous theatrical seasons in Cuba, launching new musical genres and elevating comic theatre to what historians describe as invaluable heights.

Cinema Arrives and Reshapes the City

On 24 January 1897, Frenchman Gabriel Veyre brought the cinematograph to Havana and screened the first films at Paseo del Prado #126, right next to the Tacón Theatre. Early shorts with titles like “The Train” and “The Funny Hat” marked the beginning of Cuban film exhibition.

The first purpose-built movie theatre, Actualidades, opened on 18 April 1906 on Monserrate between Neptuno and Ánimas. It is often cited as one of the oldest purpose-built cinemas in Latin America and still stands today, a physical record of the medium’s early commercial promise.

By 1919 Havana had around 42 movie theatres, and Cuba as a whole counted about 300. By the late 1950s, roughly 100 cinemas operated in the capital alone, ranging from small neighbourhood houses to prestige venues like the Yara in Vedado, the Payret on Prado, and the Fausto with its Art Deco remodelling of 1938.

From Pocket Theatres to the Karl Marx

A major shift occurred after 1938, when experimental groups like La Cueva spurred a wave of small “pocket theatres” across Havana. These intimate spaces emphasised modern, experimental work and laid the groundwork for the professionalisation of Cuban theatre.

The post-war period brought a different scale of ambition. The Blanquita theatre, opened in 1949 in Miramar, was originally the largest cinema in Havana with approximately 6,730 seats.

After the 1959 Revolution it was renamed the Karl Marx Theatre and repurposed for live performances and concerts, emblematic of the revolutionary government’s rebranding of cultural spaces.

The expansion of venues from Old Havana into Vedado and Miramar mirrors the city’s spatial growth and changing social geography. For investors and expats, this architectural trail offers a tangible map of where money, power, and audiences moved across a century of urban development.

A Walking Route Through Havana’s Scenic History

Any journey through Havana’s scenic history can begin in Old Havana’s colonial plazas—Plaza de Armas, Plaza de la Catedral, Plaza Vieja—to absorb the city’s 16th-century foundation. From there, a walk along the tree-lined Paseo del Prado passes the Alicia Alonso Grand Theater, the Payret, and the Fausto, facades that speak to late-19th and 20th-century modernity.

The route can extend to Vedado for the Yara cinema, part of the 1945 Warner Radiocentro complex, and onward to Miramar for the Karl Marx. This trajectory traces Havana’s evolution from colonial outpost to cosmopolitan capital, with theatres and cinemas serving as the cultural infrastructure of each era.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the oldest theatre still standing in Havana?

The Martí Theatre, opened in 1884 as the Teatro Irijoa, is among the oldest functioning theatres in Havana. It holds first-grade heritage protection and continues to operate with modernised technology on Calle Zulueta near Old Havana’s colonial core.

When did cinema first arrive in Havana?

The first film screening in Havana took place on 24 January 1897, when Frenchman Gabriel Veyre showed the cinematograph at Paseo del Prado #126, next to the Tacón Theatre. The first purpose-built cinema, Actualidades, opened in 1906 on Monserrate street.

How many theatres and cinemas did Havana have at its peak?

By the late 1950s, Havana operated around 100 movie theatres, up from 42 in 1919. The city also maintained several major live-performance venues, including the Gran Teatro, Martí, Alhambra, and the 6,730-seat Blanquita, later renamed the Karl Marx Theatre.

World.title: Mexico City Horror Fest Macabro 2026 Is Free This August
World.content:
Mexico City · Culture & Entertainment

Key Facts —Dates. Macabro 2026 runs from 12 to 23 August across Mexico City. —Scale. Over 60 short films, multiple feature competitions, and 20 venues are confirmed. —New additions. A dedicated AI day, a gaming showcase, and a true crime night debut this year. —Spotlight premiere. El Heladero, starring Eli Roth, will have its festival premiere with free entry. —Cost. General programming and most special events are free to the public.

Macabro 2026, the Mexico City International Horror Film Festival, returns for its 25th edition from 12 to 23 August with an expanded programme of over 60 short films, competitive feature sections, and new forays into artificial intelligence and gaming across 20 venues.

Macabro, Mexico City’s international horror film festival, marks its 25th edition August 12-23.

What Macabro 2026 Brings to Mexico City

Macabro has grown from a niche gathering into one of Latin America’s most anticipated genre festivals. The 25th edition marks a deliberate expansion beyond cinema into interactive and digital storytelling.

Organisers have confirmed a fully in-person format with complementary online streaming via the platform nuestrocine.mx. Entry to the general programme and most marquee events remains free, a policy that has helped Macabro build a loyal and diverse audience over two and a half decades.

The Competitive Sections and Awards at Macabro 2026

Three feature film competitions anchor the festival: International Horror, Ibero-American Horror, and Dark Fantasy and Sci-Fi. Short film categories cover Mexican horror, international horror, and animated horror.

Winners receive statuettes named after minerals and colours tied to Macabro’s identity. The Macabro Rojo goes to the best international and Ibero-American features, while the Macabro de Jade, Ónix, and Zafiro recognise the best Mexican, international, and animated shorts respectively.

A new Daimon Distribution Award will offer theatrical distribution in Mexico for the winning title. A separate Daimon mention provides distribution consultancy for Mexican productions from the 2025–2026 cycle.

Confirmed Short Films Span 13 Countries

Infobae has published a substantial portion of the short film lineup. The Mexican horror selection includes 17 titles such as MemoNeura, Cuando miras en los ojos de la bestia, Bloody Glamping, and Ofrenda.

The international strand features 23 shorts from 13 countries. Entries come from the United States, Brazil, Argentina, Portugal, Spain, Canada, England, Colombia, Australia, the Netherlands, France, and Venezuela.

The animated horror selection lists 24 titles, nine of which carry backing from Mexico’s FOCINE and PROCINE film funds. The full animated roster will appear in the official programme closer to opening day.

Venues Across the Capital

Macabro 2026 will use 20 venues, blending major institutions with community cultural centres. The Cineteca Nacional México, Cineteca Nacional de las Artes, Casa del Cine, and Cinematógrafo del Chopo are among the confirmed screening sites.

The Biblioteca Vasconcelos, FARO de Oriente, FARO Cosmos, and the Museo Casa de Carranza will host specialised events. The Centro de Cultura Digital takes the AI day, while nuestrocine.mx handles online access for viewers across Mexico.

El Heladero Premiere and Special Programmes

Diamond Films presents the festival premiere of El Heladero, a horror feature starring Ari Millen, Benjamin Byron Davis, and Eli Roth. The story follows a summer town unravelling after an ice cream man distributes treats with terrifying consequences.

Invitations for the free screening will be distributed through Macabro’s social media channels. The film is expected to be one of the highest-profile events of the 25th edition.

True Crime Night Debuts at Museo Casa de Carranza

For the first time, Macabro will host a True Crime Night on 18 August. The programme explores documentary cinema about real criminal cases and their hold on audiences.

The flagship film is Altona, created by the award-winning Affolter brothers. It combines animation with live testimonies to examine the aftermath of a lethal attack on a community and the survivor confronting his own demons.

AI Day and Gaming Expand the Festival’s Reach

Macabro 2026 dedicates 20 August to artificial intelligence in cinema at the Centro de Cultura Digital. Spanish filmmaker José Texeira will lead a masterclass on AI-driven horror storytelling.

Screenings include Memoria Lacerada, the second AI-made film by Mexican director Lex Ortega, and the short Margoth et Kassandra by León Landazuri. Both entries signal growing Latin American experimentation with generative tools in genre filmmaking.

The festival also enters the gaming space for the first time. In partnership with the Feria Geek, Macabro will present eight independent horror video game projects, reaching audiences beyond traditional cinema.

What Macabro 2026 Means for Mexico City’s Cultural Economy

Free-admission festivals like Macabro generate foot traffic across multiple neighbourhoods and cultural venues. The 20-venue spread pushes visitors into spaces such as FARO de Oriente and FARO Cosmos, which sit outside the city’s central tourist corridor.

For investors and expats tracking Mexico’s creative industries, Macabro’s expansion into AI and gaming reflects broader convergence trends in Latin American media. The involvement of FOCINE and PROCINE in funding animated shorts also signals continued public-sector support for genre filmmaking.

The Daimon Distribution Award adds a commercial layer. By offering theatrical distribution to the winning title, the festival bridges the gap between festival exposure and box-office viability, a persistent challenge for independent horror in Latin America.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where does Macabro 2026 take place?

Macabro 2026 runs from 12 to 23 August across 20 venues in Mexico City. Key locations include the Cineteca Nacional México, Casa del Cine, Cinematógrafo del Chopo, Biblioteca Vasconcelos, and the Centro de Cultura Digital.

Online streaming is available via nuestrocine.mx for viewers in Mexico.

Is entry to Macabro 2026 free?

Yes, the general programme and most special events are free to the public. Some screenings, such as the El Heladero premiere, require invitations distributed through Macabro’s official social media channels.

Specific activities may also require prior registration.

What is new at Macabro 2026 compared to previous editions?

The 25th edition introduces a dedicated AI day with a masterclass and screenings, a True Crime Night featuring the documentary Altona, and Macabro’s first gaming showcase with eight independent horror video game projects. A new Daimon Distribution Award also offers theatrical distribution to the winning feature.

World.title: Environmental Statistics Advisory Committee and partners discuss Belize Environmental Geoportal
World.content:
Environmental Statistics Advisory Committee and partners discuss Belize Environmental Geoportal

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Environmental Statistics Advisory Committee (ESAC) convened its third meeting, bringing together representatives from key government agencies and partner organizations to advance the production, management, and dissemination of environmental statistics in Belize.

Discussions included updating the Belize Environmental Geoportal.

Participants joined an interactive session with consultant Yvette Alonzo, who is leading the validation and updating of the Belize Environmental Geoportal.

Committee members reviewed existing datasets, identified priority data gaps, and provided recommendations to further enhance the Geoportal as a centralized platform for environmental information.

The Department of the Environment explained that the Belize Environmental Geoportal plays a vital role in supporting evidence-based decision-making, national and international environmental reporting, and public access to reliable environmental data. Through continued collaboration, ESAC remains committed to strengthening Belize’s environmental information systems and ensuring that accurate, up-to-date environmental data is available to support sustainable development and informed policymaking.

World.title: Belize Police Department hosts 27th Annual Cadet Corps Summer Program
World.content:
Belize Police Department hosts 27th Annual Cadet Corps Summer Program

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Police Department (BPD) is hosting the 27th Annual Cadet Corps Summer Program.

The program features a vibrant fusion of education, culture, and spirited competition, as 279 cadets from across Belize gathered at Ecumenical High School.

Sessions include personal and community development, featuring rotational lectures delivered by Community Policing Officers on essential topics including Anger Management, Knowing Your Community, and Effective Communication. Building on this foundation of knowledge, the cadets then engaged with interactive educational booth displays presented by the National Drug Abuse Control Council (NDACC), the Ministry of Rural Transformation, and the Department of Youth Services.

In addition, cadets enjoyed a lively practical dance session led by the Hanigi Cultural Dance Group, allowing the young participants to celebrate Belize’s rich heritage through movement.

“The spirit of camaraderie carried into the afternoon as the cadets transitioned to the auditorium for a high-energy volleyball competition.

Displaying exceptional athleticism and teamwork, the Eastern Region emerged victorious, clinching the title after winning two of three sets, with the Northern Region securing a strong second place, followed by the South in third, and the West rounding out the top four,” the BPD said.

The cadets also participated in cultural presentations from the various precincts, showcasing the diverse talents within the corps and solidifying another successful day of growth and unity at the annual summer program.

World.title: Belize Bank invests in Belize’s future, awards scholarships to 16 Students!
World.content:
Belize Bank invests in Belize’s future, awards scholarships to 16 Students!

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Bank Limited has awarded scholarships to 16 students from across the country as part of its 14th Annual Scholarship Award Ceremony.

The scholarships are awarded based on academic excellence and financial need and are aimed at supporting students in pursuing their educational goals.

The Belize Bank said that since the scholarship program began, it has invested in the education of 230 Belizean youths, including 140 high school students and 90 sixth form scholars. The 2026 recipients join the program’s growing network of young Belizeans receiving financial support and mentorship.

The ceremony featured the participation of Minister of State in the Ministry of Education, Culture, Science and Technology, Ramon Cervantes, who delivered the keynote address and highlighted the importance of accessible education.

Belize Bank Chairman and CEO Filippo Alario also addressed the students, emphasizing the importance of family support and the bank’s mentorship program, which connects scholars with bank managers for professional guidance.

The scholarship program provides full tuition and school fees, school supplies and mentorship.

High school recipients receive four years of support, including an annual $300 book grant, while 6th form scholars receive two years of support valued at $3,000 annually for tuition and school fees, along with professional mentorship and career guidance.

The 2026 scholarship recipients include 6th form scholars Aaron Bradley, Itzany Montes, Markell Pott, Aliza Doniz, Jaylen Hendy and Ezequiel Blanco. High school scholars are Zion Santos, Zairen Carrillo, Kryselle Arjona, Nimrod Fitzgibbon, Juliana Belisle, Khaleesi Neal, Yendi Flowers, Franklin Diaz, Jorge Mancia and Shaquana Ciego.

World.title: Grandson’s phone call catches banana thief in the act
World.content:
Grandson’s phone call catches banana thief in the act

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A quick trip to buy dinner turned into a police matter for an Independence Village man, after his young grandson called to report that a relative had walked onto the family veranda and made off with a box of green bananas.

According to the Belize Police Department, a 50-year-old manager of Independence Village reported that on Saturday, July 25, 2026, at about 8:30 p.m., he left his home to purchase food at a restaurant in the New Site area of the village.

While at the restaurant, he received a phone call from his 12-year-old grandson, who informed him that a man, a relative of the complainant’s wife whom he has known for approximately twenty years, had entered his veranda and stolen a box of green bananas valued at $15.

The man told police he did not give anyone permission to remove the box of bananas, and he requested court action.

A 25-year-old unemployed man of Independence Village was detained in connection with the report. As he has not been formally charged, his identity is being withheld.

The matter remains under investigation.

World.title: Man charged with threatening to kill villager he calls family
World.content:
Man charged with threatening to kill villager he calls family

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A quiet Saturday evening in a hammock ended with a death threat at the window for a San Roman Village man, and the person he says delivered it, a man he has known for twenty-five years and considers family, has been formally charged.

According to the Belize Police Department, a 45-year-old construction worker of the Stann Creek District village reported that on Saturday, July 25, 2026, at approximately 8:05 p.m., he was at his residence relaxing in his hammock when he heard a knock at his front door and a male voice calling him out with a vulgar taunt.

When he got up and looked through his window, he observed a man he has known for approximately twenty-five years, pointing a sharp-pointed object about two feet in length at him. According to the report, the man then uttered the words, “Bwai I wa kill you,” causing the complainant to fear for his life. He requested court action.

Police moved quickly. On Sunday, July 26, an officer swore an information and complaint, obtained a warrant in the first instance, and formally arrested and charged 25-year-old Anthony Sabal, a construction worker of San Roman Village, with the crime of threat of death. Cautioned after the charge, he chose to remain silent.

World.title: Father and daughter, 5, run off road twice by suspected drunk driver
World.content:
Father and daughter, 5, run off road twice by suspected drunk driver

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A Bella Vista Village father riding his bicycle with his five-year-old daughter seated on the crossbar escaped injury twice in a matter of seconds, after a pickup truck swerved in front of him and then reversed to within inches of his front wheel, and the driver, who police say showed signs of intoxication, has been detained.

According to the Belize Police Department, a 30-year-old project supervisor of the Toledo District village reported that on Sunday, July 26, 2026, at approximately 7:00 p.m., he was riding his beach cruiser bicycle along a village street with his five-year-old daughter seated on the crossbar in front of him when he observed a green pickup truck parked on the right-hand side.

As he attempted to pass the vehicle on the left, he reported, the driver suddenly drove off and swerved in front of him, forcing him off the street. The truck then stopped about ten feet ahead and abruptly reversed, coming to within about five inches of his bicycle’s front wheel and almost striking him a second time, causing him to fear for his life and placing his daughter’s life in danger.

The father approached the driver, observed that he appeared to be intoxicated, and went directly to the Bella Vista Police Station to make a formal report, requesting court action.

Police located the driver, a 29-year-old construction worker of the village, in his vehicle and detained him. According to police, he appeared to be under the influence of alcohol, emitting a strong odour of alcohol from his breath, speaking with slurred speech, and staggering while walking. He was informed of the offence of driving a motor vehicle with an alcohol concentration above the prescribed limit.

Checks on the truck added to his troubles. The vehicle’s insurance policy was found to have expired on June 25, 2026, and its licence expired on November 30, 2025. He was additionally informed of the offences of driving a motor vehicle not covered by third-party risk insurance and driving an unlicensed motor vehicle.

As the man has not yet been formally charged, his identity is being withheld. The matter remains under investigation.

World.title: World Hepatitis Day 2026 calls for action to break barriers to testing and treatment
World.content:
World Hepatitis Day 2026 calls for action to break barriers to testing and treatment

By Zoila Palma: World Hepatitis Day is observed each year on July 28 to raise awareness of viral hepatitis, an inflammation of the liver that can lead to severe liver disease and liver cancer.

The 2026 campaign, themed “Hepatitis: Let’s break it down,” calls for greater efforts to remove the barriers preventing people from accessing prevention, testing, treatment and care.

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), viral hepatitis remains a major cause of preventable illness and death worldwide, despite the availability of effective vaccines, accurate diagnostic tools, curative treatments for hepatitis C and lifelong therapies for hepatitis B. Millions of people remain undiagnosed or untreated because of stigma, limited awareness, gaps in health systems and persistent inequalities.

WHO says expanding access to testing and treatment is among the most important steps needed to achieve global hepatitis elimination goals by 2030.

The 2026 campaign urges governments to strengthen political commitment and investment, place affected people and communities at the center of hepatitis programmes, and ensure that services reach underserved and vulnerable populations.

World.title: Security officer David Lucas dies in early-morning motorcycle crash in front of KHMH
World.content:
Security officer David Lucas dies in early-morning motorcycle crash in front of KHMH

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 31-year-old Belize City security officer was killed in a motorcycle accident early Tuesday morning on Princess Margaret Drive.

Police say David Enenero Lucas, a resident of Fabers Road, was travelling toward the Philip Goldson Highway on a black Lifan motorcycle when he apparently lost control at the roundabout near the intersection with Coney Drive.

The motorcycle collided with a metal lamp post in the median opposite the Belize Council for the Visually Impaired Eye Clinic. Lucas was flung from the motorcycle and landed near the clinic’s entrance, suffering severe head injuries. A portion of his helmet was reportedly broken during the impact.

Personnel from the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital transported Lucas to the emergency room, where he was pronounced dead at 5:09 a.m.

Police processed the scene and transported the damaged motorcycle to the Queen Street Police Station for inspection. Investigators are also seeking surveillance footage from the area as their inquiry continues.
