World.title: Abkhazia to buy Russian electricity ‘just in case’ from August to November
World.content:
The state-owned energy company Chernomorenergo plans to import electricity from Russia into Abkhazia between August and November to preserve water levels in the Jvar reservoir, which supplies the Ingur hydropower plant.

Until now, electricity imports took place only during the winter months, when water levels at the plant dropped. However, as electricity prices are significantly higher during that period, the Abkhaz authorities have decided to stock up on electricity while it is cheaper.

The 40% share of electricity generated by the Inguri hydropower plant allocated to Abkhazia under an informal agreement reached after the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war has, over the past decade, proved insufficient to meet the republic’s electricity needs.

According to Chernomorenergo Director General Timur Dzhindzholia, the annual shortfall amounts to around 500–650 million kWh. While Abkhazia’s budget now includes funding for electricity imports, it is not enough to fully cover the deficit. As a result, the government has opted to purchase Russian electricity during the months when prices are at their lowest.

As recently as two years ago, largely because of uncontrolled cryptocurrency mining, electricity consumption in Abkhazia reached 3 billion kWh a year. During the autumn and winter months, the republic experienced rolling blackouts.

A series of measures to optimise electricity consumption has significantly reduced the deficit. In 2025, around 320 million kWh was covered by humanitarian electricity supplies from Russia, while the remaining shortfall had to be met through commercial imports.

Timur Dzhindzholia said that eliminating the deficit entirely would require the construction of new power generation facilities.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Electricity imports from Russia to Abkhazia

World.title: Study finds women in Armenia work more hours than men because of unpaid household work
World.content:
Women in Armenia work more than men, study finds

Women in Armenia work roughly four to five times more than men on unpaid household and care responsibilities, according to a study conducted by Ameria for the Armenian office of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA). The study found that women spend an average of 15.3 hours a week on household chores, including cooking, cleaning and laundry. They also devote another 8.6 hours to childcare, caring for elderly family members and other family responsibilities.

According to economist Tigran Jrbashyan, head of management consulting at Ameria, women aged 30 to 35 carry the heaviest workload. They spend between 44 and 49 hours a week on these responsibilities.

“This is unpaid labour. No one pays for it. Yet by doing this work, women create value. That is extremely important and deserves recognition,” Jrbashyan said.

By comparison, men spend an average of less than four hours (3.6) a week on household chores. They devote just over two hours (2.2) to caring for family members. Men aged 30 to 40 record the highest figures, spending between eight and 11 hours a week.

Women receive no pay for 78% of the work they do

The researchers found that women in Armenia spend more time on various activities than men. Much of that time goes to household responsibilities, placing a heavier physical burden on them. Yet no one pays them for caring for their families.

According to Tigran Jrbashyan, women receive no pay for 78% of the work they do, as household responsibilities account for that share of their overall workload.

“In effect, women receive pay for only 22% of the work they do. For men, unpaid work accounts for around 11%, while paid work makes up the remaining 89%.”

‘It is important to make workplaces more family-friendly’

Lusine Sargsyan, head of the Yerevan office of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), says that spending 44 to 49 hours a week on unpaid household work often forces women to make a choice: whether to enter the workforce, whether to prioritise their careers or focus on starting a family and having children.

“We need to create conditions where women no longer have to choose one or the other. They should be able to have both. It is important that women can pursue formal employment while also having time for their families. Otherwise, the country will face demographic challenges,” she said.

When Sargsyan talks about creating better conditions for working women, she refers in particular to expanding access to nurseries and kindergartens, as well as developing childcare centres for young children.

Remote work is already available in Armenia, and working mothers can take advantage of it with their employer’s consent. The government has also recently introduced a “parental hour” policy. Under the new rules, working parents with children under the age of 12 can either arrive at work later or leave earlier. Parents with one or two children can reduce their working day by 30 minutes. Those with three or more children can shorten it by one hour. However, experts say these measures do not go far enough to create a truly family-friendly working environment.

Lusine Sargsyan stresses that spending 44 to 49 hours a week on household responsibilities means some women effectively work two full-time jobs. In addition to unpaid domestic work, they spend another 40 hours a week working for an employer.

She argues that this is problematic both economically and from a human rights perspective because women are left with little or no time for themselves. She also says excessive workloads reduce productivity at work and affect the quality of care they can provide for their children at home.

Sargsyan emphasises that workplaces need to become more family-friendly. That would allow women to fulfil their potential while also spending meaningful time with their families.

“Employers need to recognise that their employees have families. It is extremely important that women do not live with a constant sense of guilt. They should not feel guilty about spending too little time with their families. Nor should they worry at home about work they did not finish,” she explained.

Both Sargsyan and Jrbashyan stressed that many women are highly productive and, in many cases, better educated than men.

They argue that the country needs to create better conditions for women to work. Otherwise, the economy risks missing out on the higher value they could generate.

At the same time, both experts stressed that they are not arguing every woman should have formal employment or receive pay for household work. Instead, they say women should have the freedom to decide how they want to organise their lives. They believe giving women that choice would benefit the country’s economy, improve business performance and create a healthier family environment.

Women in Armenia work more than men, study finds

World.title: GYLA: ‘Georgia has effectively created an informal ‘morality police’, which could become a new form of violence’
World.content:
GYLA warns violence could escalate in Georgia

The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) has responded to reports about the creation of a movement to protect traditional values, warning that alongside existing legal restrictions on freedom of expression, assembly and civic participation, the initiative could introduce new mechanisms of violence in the country.

The movement was announced on 26 July by MMA fighter Giorgi Kartvelishvili and several supporters. At a press briefing, he said the organisation would “respond immediately” to issues involving the country’s ancestors, religion, history and other subjects that the group considers offensive. Kartvelishvili said the movement would be “highly active, respectable and constructive”, adding that any “patriotic Georgian” would be welcome to join. Members of the group also said they were prepared to take responsibility for their actions, including serving prison sentences if necessary.

GYLA described the initiative as the creation of an informal “morality police”, warning that it poses a threat to freedom of expression in Georgia.

According to the organisation, “everything suggests that the group’s aim may be to informally monitor, intimidate or pressure people who are critical of the authorities.”

GYLA’s lawyers added that “attempts to establish vigilante groups in the country are particularly alarming” given the rise in violence and intimidation targeting government critics in recent years.

GYLA said members of the new group are using defamatory and disinformation-laden language that closely mirrors narratives promoted by the authorities and pro-government media.

In particular, the group says it is launching a campaign “against people and organisations funded from abroad, enslaved to foreign interests and driven by a perverse ideology.”

According to GYLA, the group’s statements contain signs of incitement to violence. The lawyers pointed in particular to its declaration that “if circumstances leave no alternative, members of the group will not be afraid of going to prison.”

GYLA said the group has already demanded an apology from stand-up comedian Onise Okriashvili, who was recently severely beaten in the street after making a joke referring to Georgian literary classic Nodar Dumbadze.

The group has also asked prosecutors not to seek a prison sentence for the person accused of attacking Okriashvili. Otherwise, its representatives warned, there could be reprisals, according to GYLA.

“We will hold people accountable for every action and comment that insults the dignity of the Georgian people,” the group said in a statement cited by GYLA.

GYLA said such statements echo remarks made by senior officials from the ruling Georgian Dream party which, in the organisation’s view, call for greater control over freedom of expression.

The organisation also noted that attacks by third parties targeting people critical of the government were widely documented during the 2024 protests and in the months that followed.

According to GYLA, such incidents were often accompanied by statements from state officials appearing to support the attackers or by an inadequate response from law enforcement.

“Against this background, it is clear that the creation of a vigilante group and its declared intention to police citizens’ freedom of expression are closely linked to the state’s ongoing normalisation of violence,” GYLA said.

The organisation noted that Georgian criminal law prohibits the creation, leadership or membership of illegal armed or violent groups. It also bans the establishment of associations, or participation in them, if their activities involve violence against individuals.

GYLA said law enforcement authorities must take all measures provided for by law to prevent violence or intimidation against people exercising their fundamental rights.

According to the organisation, “pro-government media are actively contributing to the demonisation and targeting of individuals, which may amount to incitement to violence and complicity in it. The inaction or delayed response of state institutions creates an environment that enables violence to spread.”

GYLA warns violence could escalate in Georgia

World.title: Georgian banks to continue servicing local subsidiaries of sanctioned Russian energy giant Inter RAO
World.content:
Georgian banks to continue servicing Telasi

The National Bank of Georgia has announced that the country’s commercial banks will continue providing services in the national currency to Telasi, despite the company being owned by Russian energy giant Inter RAO, which was included in the European Union’s latest, 21st package of sanctions against Russia. The central bank confirmed the decision to BM.GE.

At the end of July, the European Union imposed sanctions on the Russian state-controlled energy company Inter RAO. Through its subsidiaries, the company is the indirect owner of Georgia’s electricity distribution companies Telasi and Telmiko, as well as the Khramhesi-1 and Khramhesi-2 hydropower plants.

The National Bank said that Telasi itself is not included on any sanctions list and that its uninterrupted operation is essential for the country’s population and economy. According to the central bank, while compliance with international sanctions is important, it is equally crucial to ensure the uninterrupted provision of essential services to the public.

The National Bank said that each sanctions-related case would be assessed on its individual merits. As a result, banks will continue providing services to Telasi “in compliance with the applicable sanctions regime, as well as in accordance with their own internal policies and risk assessment procedures.”

Georgian banks to continue servicing Telasi

World.title: Azerbaijan’s Toplum TV case: Nine defendants sentenced to combined 121 years in prison
World.content:
Azerbaijan’s Toplum TV case

On 27 July, the Baku Serious Crimes Court, chaired by Judge Azer Tagiyev, delivered its verdict in the Toplum TV case.

Nine people linked to Toplum TV and the Institute for Democratic Initiatives (IDI), including journalists, media law experts, project coordinators and members of the Third Republic Platform, were sentenced to between 12 and 15 years in prison. They were also banned from holding certain positions for two years and six months. The court additionally granted a civil claim, including the confiscation of the defendants’ property.

Following the verdict, Elmir Abbasov, one of the outlet’s employees, was taken into custody in the courtroom.

Defence lawyers said the trial had been unfair, arguing that defence motions had been routinely rejected and that the case was politically motivated. They said they would appeal the verdict.

International organisations described the sentences as “excessively harsh and politically motivated” and called for the immediate release of those convicted.

Arrested in the Toplum TV case. Top row (left to right): Elmir Abbasov, Ali Zeynal, Farid Ismayilov, Ramil Babayev and Ilkin Amrakhov; bottom row (left to right): Alasgar Mammadli, Akif Gurbanov, Mushfig Jabbar and Ruslan Izzatli. | Illustration: Toplum TV

Case and charges

On 6 March 2024, Azerbaijan’s Interior Ministry searched the offices of Toplum TV and the Institute for Democratic Initiatives (IDI), as well as several other locations. The defendants were initially charged under Article 206.3.2 of Azerbaijan’s Criminal Code with smuggling foreign currency as part of a group acting by prior conspiracy.

The charges were later expanded to include illegal entrepreneurship, money laundering on an especially large scale, tax evasion, document forgery, and the alleged unlawful receipt and use of funds from Western donors to finance Toplum TV, the Institute for Democratic Initiatives, the Fakt Yoxla fact-checking platform and the Third Republic Platform as part of an organised criminal group.

Prosecutors described the defendants as members of an “organised criminal group” and sought prison terms of between 13 and 16 years. All of the defendants rejected the charges, saying the evidence had either been fabricated or was unfounded, and that the arrests were intended to suppress independent media and democratic initiatives.

During the trial, defence lawyers repeatedly raised concerns over the health of several defendants, including Alasgar Mammadli, the court’s refusal to grant requests for house arrest, allegations that witnesses had been pressured into giving testimony, and other alleged procedural violations.

Toplum TV was an independent online television platform and news outlet established in 2016. It covered political and social issues, corruption and human rights. The Institute for Democratic Initiatives focused on promoting democratic initiatives, youth education and media training.

Defendants’ final statements

In their final statements, the defendants rejected all charges against them, describing the case as politically motivated.

Speaking on 20 July, Akif Gurbanov said democratic ideals could not be destroyed. He accused the authorities of acting in the spirit of the Soviet regime by refusing to acknowledge their own mistakes, and criticised the concentration of economic resources in the hands of those in power, as well as the lack of independent media and an independent judiciary:

“Even if they try for centuries, they will not be able to destroy the ideals of the republic… They do not want independent media or an independent judiciary. We do not intend to submit to this system,” he said.

He said Toplum TV and Fakt Yoxla had been established to promote professional journalism and counter disinformation.

Instead of delivering a final statement, Ruslan Izzatli read a letter addressed to his son.

Other defendants also argued that the prosecution had failed to present sufficient evidence. They said, in particular, that the allegation they had smuggled 837,000 manats (about $492,500) in cash was inconsistent with the way international donor organisations operate.

They also criticised what they described as the one-sided nature of the trial and politically motivated prosecution. Journalist Farid Ismayilov and several other defendants reported health problems and said they had received threats while in detention.

Below are brief profiles of each defendant, including their background, role in the organisations, the charges brought against them and the sentence imposed.

Akif Gurbanov – 15 years in prison

Akif Gurbanov

Akif Gurbanov was born on 3 August 1981 in Georgia. He graduated from Azerbaijan Medical University in 2004, the Council of Europe’s School of Political Studies in Strasbourg in 2008, and the Faculty of Law at Kharkiv National University in 2016. He is married and has three children.

Gurbanov began his political career in 2002 with the Umid (Hope) party, where he served as deputy chair for youth affairs and head of its election campaign headquarters. Between 2006 and 2016, he was a member of Azerbaijan’s Central Election Commission.

He is the founder and director of the Institute for Democratic Initiatives (IDI), a co-founder of Fakt Yoxla and Toplum TV, and one of the founders of the Third Republic Platform. Since 2024, he has served as the platform’s spokesperson. He was arrested on 6 March 2024.

Charges: smuggling, illegal entrepreneurship, money laundering and other offences allegedly committed as part of an organised criminal group.

Sentence: 15 years in prison and a two-and-a-half-year ban on holding certain positions.

Ruslan Izzatli – 15 years in prison

Ruslan Izzatli

Ruslan Izzatli was born on 18 April 1989 in Aghdam. Following the occupation of Aghdam, he lived in Barda. He graduated from the Azerbaijan State University of Culture and Arts with a degree in art history in 2012, later completing a master’s degree in Global Politics and International Relations at Bahçeşehir University. He also studied at the Council of Europe’s School of Political Studies. He is married and has one child.

Between 2009 and 2012, he headed the Whole Azerbaijan youth organisation. He served as deputy chair of the Umid (Hope) party from 2012 to 2013 and led the D18 movement between 2013 and 2021. He ran for parliament in 2015 and 2020.

He took part in the Second Karabakh War and was awarded the For the Liberation of Fuzuli medal and the Participant in the Patriotic War medal. He is one of the founders of the Third Republic Platform. He was arrested in March 2024.

Charges: participation in an organised criminal group and financial offences.

Sentence: 15 years in prison and a ban on holding certain positions.

Alasgar Mammadli – 14 years in prison

Alasgar Mammadli

Alasgar Mammadli was born on 24 May 1968 in the settlement of Guzanly in Aghdam District to a family of teachers. He graduated from the Faculty of Law at Istanbul University in 1996 and obtained a master’s degree from the Public Administration Institute for Turkey and the Middle East (TODAİE) in Ankara in 2001. He is married and has two children.

A media law expert, Mammadli worked as a lawyer and manager for Internews and IREX between 2002 and 2014. He is one of the founders of the Media Law Institute and has delivered hundreds of professional training courses. Since 2016, he has been the legal founder of Toplum TV. He was arrested in March 2024.

Charges: participation in an organised criminal group and financial offences.

During the trial, concerns over Mammadli’s health were repeatedly raised, particularly regarding a tumour in his throat and the need for surgery. The court rejected repeated requests to transfer him to house arrest. Mammadli maintained that his income had been lawfully earned, that all taxes had been paid, and that he was a political hostage.

Sentence: 14 years in prison and a ban on holding certain positions.

Ali Zeynal – 14 years in prison

Ali Zeynal

Ali Zeynal was born on 24 February 1996. An independent multimedia journalist, he has worked as a reporter, presenter, fact-checker and trainer since 2016. At the Institute for Democratic Initiatives (IDI), he coordinated a programme for young journalists and served as their mentor.

He was arrested on 6 March 2024. According to the prosecution, searches of his home uncovered €10,150 and $9,060 in cash.

Charges: smuggling, as well as additional financial offence charges brought later in the investigation.

According to available information, Zeynal was subjected to pressure while in detention, placed in solitary confinement as a disciplinary measure, and faced harassment over his reporting.

Sentence: 14 years in prison and a ban on holding certain positions.

Mushfig Jabbar – 13 years in prison

Mushfig Jabbar

Mushfig Jabbar worked as a video editor for Toplum TV. He was arrested on 6 March 2024.

Charges: smuggling and other financial offences.

During the trial, Jabbar criticised the quality of the investigation. He said investigators had attempted to link the smuggling charge to the question: “Can you run?” He also said the court had rejected requests to transfer him to house arrest.

Sentence: 13 years in prison and a ban on holding certain positions.

Ramil Babayev – 13 years in prison

Ramil Babayev

Ramil Babayev worked as a project coordinator at the Institute for Democratic Initiatives (IDI). He was arrested in March 2024. He is considered the first prisoner in Azerbaijan to openly state that he is a vegan.

Charges: participation in an organised criminal group and financial offences.

According to available information, Babayev was subjected to pressure while in pre-trial detention, went on hunger strikes and complained about conditions in the detention centre.

Sentence: 13 years in prison and a ban on holding certain positions.

Ilkin Amrakhov – 13 years in prison

Ilkin Amrakhov

Ilkin Amrakhov was born on 4 December 2001. He graduated from the Faculty of International Relations at the Academy of Public Administration under the President of Azerbaijan. He completed the Institute for Democratic Initiatives’ (IDI) Young Project Leaders programme, later interned at the organisation and subsequently worked there as a team coordinator.

He was arrested on 6 March 2024.

Charges: the same as those brought against the other defendants in the case.

During the trial, Amrakhov described what he alleged were unlawful actions carried out during the search of the organisation’s office.

Sentence: 13 years in prison and a ban on holding certain positions.

Farid Ismayilov – 12 years in prison

Farid Ismayilov

Farid Ismayilov was born on 4 September 1998 in Khirdalan. He graduated from the Azerbaijan State Oil and Industry University before completing a master’s degree at Baku Engineering University. He served in the military between 2021 and 2022.

He has worked as a journalist since 2019. He previously worked for Kanal 13 and joined Toplum TV as a reporter in 2022. In 2023, he underwent lung surgery. Initially released under police supervision following his detention in March 2024, he was re-arrested on 17 January 2025.

Charges: smuggling, as well as additional financial offence charges brought later in the investigation.

While in detention, Ismayilov complained of threats against him and health problems.

Sentence: 12 years in prison and a ban on holding certain positions.

Elmir Abbasov – 12 years in prison

Elmir Abbasov

Elmir Abbasov worked as Toplum TV’s social media manager. He was initially released under police supervision and was later transferred to house arrest. Unlike the other defendants, he remained at liberty until the verdict was delivered.

During the investigation into the Toplum TV case, Abbasov’s mother—his only close relative—died.

Charges: participation in an organised criminal group and financial offences.

Following the verdict, Abbasov was taken into custody in the courtroom.

Sentence: 12 years in prison and a ban on holding certain positions.

World.title: Opinion: ‘Georgia government’s anti-European rhetoric enters new phase’
World.content:
Sociologist Iago Kachkachishvili says the Georgian government’s anti-European messaging has undergone a significant shift. In his view, Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili’s recent suggestion that Georgia could even benefit from remaining outside the European Union indicates that the authorities are no longer merely criticising what they describe as the EU’s current course. Instead, they are beginning to challenge the very idea of Georgia joining the bloc.

Earlier, Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili said that European Union membership should not be an end in itself, while criticising proposals that, he said, would weaken the principle of consensus in the bloc’s decision-making process. He argued that if such changes were introduced, remaining outside the EU could become more advantageous for some smaller states, as they would have greater freedom to make independent decisions

Iago Kachkachishvili: “Shalva Papuashvili has openly written that it could even be beneficial for Georgia not to join the European Union, ‘because, at the very least, it would retain the freedom to make independent decisions.’

Openly discussing the benefits of staying out of the EU marks a significant shift in the anti-European propaganda of the ruling Georgian Dream party. Until now, it sought to convince the public—primarily its own supporters—that the problem lay with the EU in its current, liberal form. According to its narrative, liberal forces in the bloc would gradually be replaced by conservatives, right-wing parties would come to power across the EU, and they would then throw open the doors to Georgia, allowing it to join the European family ‘with dignity’. This has largely been the core message of Georgian Dream’s propaganda.

Why, until now, was Georgian Dream unable to abandon the goal of EU membership? First, Article 78 of Georgia’s Constitution obliges the authorities to ensure that ‘the constitutional bodies shall take all measures within the scope of their competences to ensure the full integration of Georgia into the European Union and the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.’ In addition, every public opinion survey showed that even among Georgian Dream supporters, a majority—around 60%—favoured joining the EU.

The role of Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán should also be taken into account. He was Georgian Dream’s main ally and one of the leading advocates of right-wing forces within the European Union. Nor should we forget that, following Donald Trump’s election as US president, Georgian Dream expected liberal forces around the world to suffer a major setback. The party also anticipated that Russia—seen as the European Union’s principal adversary—would prevail in its war against Ukraine.

What is the situation now?

Georgian Dream appears to have concluded that its narrative about a future right-wing European Union has largely failed. Orbán has suffered setbacks, while the Trump administration has shown little sign of actively promoting the global rise of the radical right. Meanwhile, even commentators loyal to Vladimir Putin have begun acknowledging Russia’s inability to win the war. At the same time, the latest EU-funded survey, conducted in 2026, found that 71% of Georgians support joining the European Union, 17% are neutral, and 10% oppose membership. Clearly, the government’s aggressive anti-Western messaging has had some effect, with support falling from around 80–85%—most likely due to declining enthusiasm among Georgian Dream supporters.

Although EU membership is still backed by a clear majority of the population (71%), Georgian Dream now appears to be going all in. Until recently, the authorities argued that Georgia’s path towards Europe had merely been temporarily delayed. Now, however, they are attempting to fundamentally redefine the value of the European choice itself. Their apparent goal is to reduce support for EU membership, at least among their own supporters. At the same time, they seek to eliminate the opposition as a political force, secure a constitutional majority in the 2028 elections, and amend Article 78 of the Constitution, which commits the country to European integration. The authorities’ daily suppression of public protest serves the same objective. All of this is taking place under increasingly authoritarian domestic rule, without any guaranteed backing from right-wing allies abroad.

The coming months will show whether this new phase of anti-Western politics delivers the results Georgian Dream hopes for. For those resisting the government’s course, however, the guiding principle remains unchanged: protest at home, sanctions from abroad.

Georgian government’s anti-European rhetoric

World.title: Marathon 24-hour Qantas flight tracked by 3.6 million internet users
World.content:
A Qantas aircraft set to be used for direct flights between Australia and Europe has been tracked by millions of internet users as it completed a marathon 24-hour test flight from Melbourne to France.

The specially adapted Airbus A350-1000ULR is one of 12 aircraft set to be delivered to Qantas as part of Project Sunrise, which is due to deliver non-stop Sydney to London flights from next year.

When launched, the route will become the world's longest commercial passenger service.

The aircraft's test flight was watched by more than 3.6 million people on FlightRadar24. (Supplied: FlightRadar24)

Airbus said the aircraft, which boasts a specially designed extra fuel tank, remained in the air for 24 hours and 24 minutes, covering 23,075 km without stopping, before landing at the aircraft manufacturer's factory in Toulouse, France.

Flight-tracking provider Flightradar24 said the trip was the second-most-tracked flight ever on its channels — behind a 2024 flight carrying Queen Elizabeth II's coffin — with more than 3.6 million people following its progress northwards via Canada.

Sydney-to-London unveiled as first route for Qantas's Project Sunrise The flights, set to begin take off from next year, will mark the first time flights from the east coast will complete the Kangaroo Route without a stop over.

In 2005, a Boeing 777-200LR Worldliner flew 21,601.7 kilometres from Hong Kong to London in 22 hours and 42 minutes.

Qantas has ordered 12 modified A350-1000ULR aircraft, designed to connect Australia's east coast with London and New York in about 20 hours.

The services aim to turn what was once a five-day journey on the "Kangaroo Route" to London into a single flight lasting 19 to 21 hours, depending on routing and winds.

The first aircraft, which carries 20,000 litres of fuel and can seat 238 passengers, is due for delivery in April 2027.

Qantas expects to operate daily nonstop flights between Sydney and London from October 2027.

World.title: Home loan borrowers missing out on millions in offset savings
World.content:
Millions of Australians use mortgage offset accounts to reduce interest costs on their home loans, but the corporate regulator says some banks are not delivering the savings as promised.

Australian banks have paid more than $55 million in compensation in just two years, after failures with offset accounts left customers paying more interest than they should have, a review by ASIC found.

The watchdog examined eight banks representing more than 70 per cent of Australia's home loan market and found weaknesses across all of them in how offset accounts were set up, monitored and managed.

Offset accounts are linked to home loans, often for a package fee charged by the bank. (ABC News: Tony Ibrahim)

ASIC chair Sarah Court said the problems could be particularly difficult for borrowers to detect because mortgage repayments may stay the same, masking the fact they are paying more interest than they should.

"When offset accounts don't operate correctly, the harm can be hidden," Ms Court said.

" Loan repayments stay the same, while customers unknowingly pay more interest and take longer to repay their loan. "

Ms Court said, in some cases, the failures went undetected by the banks until ASIC started asking questions.

"That should concern every bank offering offset accounts."

Sarah Court says the harm of offset account failures can be hidden from customers. (AAP: Diego Fedele)

Reports made to ASIC between September 1, 2023 and August 31, 2025 show AMP, ANZ, CBA, Credit Union Australia, HSBC, ING, Macquarie and Westpac collectively paid more than $55 million in compensation for offset-account failures.

What is a mortgage offset account?

An offset account is a separate transaction or savings account linked to an eligible home loan.

The money remains available for the customer to spend, just like a normal transaction account, but the balance reduces the amount of the mortgage on which the bank calculates interest.

For example, someone with a $500,000 mortgage and $50,000 in a 100 per cent offset account should generally be charged interest on $450,000, rather than the full loan balance.

That can produce substantial savings over the life of a mortgage, provided the account is correctly linked and operating as intended.

Many lenders charge a premium for an offset through additional fees and, in some cases, higher interest rates.

Offset accounts are increasingly popular as Australians face higher interest rates. (Adobe Stock)

Brooke thought her savings were reducing her mortgage interest

Brisbane-based home owner Brooke, who asked for her surname to be withheld for privacy reasons, and her husband thought they were doing exactly what borrowers are encouraged to do — putting their savings into an offset account to reduce the interest on their first home loan.

They had taken out the mortgage with one of Australia's big four banks and, for about two years, deposited their savings into what they believed was an account offsetting their mortgage.

It was only when they decided to refinance with another bank and went into a branch to close their accounts that they discovered the savings had not been reducing their interest as expected.

Brooke's bank offered compensation but she had no way to check the calculations. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

Their mortgage broker, Cara Haines, said there had been two problems.

The mortgage had been split into two loan accounts, allowing part of the loan to be fixed after settlement.

Ms Haines said the offset was initially linked to the wrong loan account, and the link then fell off when part of the loan was fixed, with the bank not providing any prior notice or information to the customer.

The discovery came just before Christmas, while Brooke and her husband were in the middle of settling their new loan.

"I had a cold chill through my heart," Brooke said.

" We had no idea how much money we were actually out of pocket. "

After an investigation, the bank offered the couple more than $5,000 in compensation.

But Brooke said it was difficult to independently determine whether that figure fully reflected their loss.

"Why would I trust the bank at that point?" she said.

"For us, though, it was such a stressful time that we did just take the money and we needed to move on."

The experience prompted Ms Haines to review other customers she had with the same bank.

Cara Haines discovered errors with several clients' mortgage offsets. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

She said the review found another customer in a similar position, who was ultimately compensated more than $10,000.

Banks struggle to find their own failures

ASIC's review identified four broad weaknesses, and provided stark examples of failures — which, in some cases, had gone unnoticed until the regulator started asking questions.

Should I use an offset account, credit card combo? Using a credit card linked to your offset account can save on your mortgage but you need to be aware of the pitfalls to decide whether it will work for you.

First, the regulator said many banks struggled to establish whether customers had requested an offset account in the first place.

Seven of the eight banks relied on manual processing for some requests to set up or re-link offsets, particularly when borrowers refinanced or changed their loan.

At one bank, a key form recording customers' requests was not digitised. The bank estimated that establishing when offsets had been requested across its customers would have required more than 20 employees working for four weeks.

Second, ASIC found banks were not reliably detecting when things went wrong.

Banks had failed to identify 77 per cent of the reported offset-account failures before ASIC requested the data, although the regulator noted one bank accounted for most of those cases.

Human error was the dominant cause, with manual staff errors accounting for 86 per cent of the failures reported by banks.

In one striking example, a bank discovered in September 2025 that a report designed to flag potential offset-linking failures had not been reviewed for almost five years.

ASIC found many banks struggle to establish whether borrowers have requested an offset account. (ABC News: Daniel Irvine)

ASIC said even when banks knew there was a potential problem, customers were not always compensated or problems quickly fixed.

ASIC also found one bank had identified a process flaw that could delay an offset being linked by up to 21 days, but did not fully fix the process for about two years.

Fourth, the regulator found customers were not always clearly told that changes to their mortgage could stop their offset from working.

For example, some banks did not adequately explain that a loan change could de-link an offset, or that customers might need to make a separate request to have it linked again.

Complaint records showed many borrowers did not realise they needed to take that additional step.

ASIC said it was not enough for banks to rely on information buried in terms and conditions, particularly when customers could continue paying extra interest without knowing anything was wrong.

Employed people in distress amid rate rises Almost 14,000 Australians rang the National Debt Helpline last month, with most callers saying they are struggling to pay their home loans and are facing mortgage stress, according to new data.

The CEO of the Consumer Action Law Centre, Stephanie Tonkin, said the mortgage offset account issue went to the heart of why customers had less trust in the financial services sector.

"They need to invest far more in their systems and be more transparent — especially important where banking products are complex like offset accounts and consumers have limited visibility over whether they’re set up correctly."

The Australian Banking Association's CEO, Simon Birmingham, said customers should "take confidence" that the vast majority of mortgage offset accounts were working as intended.

"The good news is that offset accounts are working for well over 99 per cent of Australians, saving them thousands of dollars on their mortgages," he said.

Mr Birmingham said banks were "resolving those issues, compensating customers, and improving systems" where problems had been identified.

While acknowledging there had been "manual failures" and isolated mistakes, he said the report showed banks were identifying issues and working with ASIC to improve their systems.

"Banks aspire for every system to work perfectly 100 per cent of the time," Mr Birmingham said.

The ABC understands the $55 million in remediation was paid to hundreds of thousands of borrowers.

Offset accounts are increasingly popular

The potential impact of these failures is growing as offset accounts become an increasingly common feature of Australian mortgages.

Reserve Bank data shows 55 per cent of housing loan facilities now have an offset account as of March 2026.

Canstar data insights director Sally Tindall said higher interest rates had given borrowers an even greater incentive to make their savings work against their mortgage.

"People that have spare dollars are funnelling it into their offset accounts in order to reduce the amount of interest that they pay to the bank," she said.

Mortgages burdening households at record levels Who had it tougher on housing? These stats may put the generational debate to bed.

It's not a new problem — ASIC has dealt with similar offset-account failures before, with banks previously forced to refund customers who were overcharged interest.

In 2017, Bankwest refunded about 10,800 customers more than $4.9 million after it failed to properly link some offset accounts to home loans.

That same year, NAB refunded $1.7 million to 966 home-loan customers after it found some offset accounts had not been properly linked to broker-originated loans.

And in 2022, the Federal Court ordered ANZ to pay a $25 million penalty after the bank failed to provide some customers with promised benefits attached to offset transaction accounts and its former Breakfree package, including fee waivers and interest-rate discounts.

In response to ASIC's latest review, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said Australians were already under financial pressure and should not be paying more interest than they had been promised.

"Every dollar matters, and so the last thing Australians need is to pay more interest than was promised," he said.

ASIC said a number of banks have already begun remediation following its review and compensation payments are continuing.

The regulator said it will provide individual feedback to the banks, monitor how the deficiencies are addressed and consider further regulatory action where appropriate.

World.title: Australia supplants China as Pacific's biggest lender
World.content:
Australia has supplanted China as the dominant lender and infrastructure investor across the Pacific as the government ploughs billions of dollars into the region through both foreign aid and loans.

The latest version of the Lowy Institute's Pacific Aid Map also shows that Australia has also maintained its position as by far the largest aid donor in the region, with the federal government providing around 37 per cent of all development spending across the Pacific in 2024.

That puts Australia well ahead of the other countries, with New Zealand sitting at 11 per cent, the US at 8 per cent, China at 6 per cent and Japan at 3 per cent.

The map's lead author, Riley Duke, said the latest data showed a "striking" shift, with China's lending to the region continuing to fall away.

"Historically this has been an area very much dominated by China. Beijing has built a lot of relationships and influence through these big loan finance infrastructure deals," he said.

"So, it's significant that Australia seems to have crowded out China in this space."

China's lending to the Pacific has continued to decline. (Supplied: SPTO)

The shift means that Australia will face growing pressure to show it can deliver major infrastructure effectively without saddling Pacific nations with unsustainable debt.

A small number of Pacific countries, particularly Tonga, have struggled with the financial implications of Chinese loans, and the issue has generated political controversy over several years.

Mr Duke said it was far too early to judge the success of Australia's push into the infrastructure space, because it was still a newcomer.

"Australia has inked a lot of these deals but there's still a lot in the pipeline that hasn't yet been delivered," he said.

"How successfully Australia is able to deliver these projects will determine the legacy of this push into the infrastructure and lending space."

Much of Australia's new infrastructure funding has been funnelled through the Australian Infrastructure Financing Facility for the Pacific (AIFFP), which has already committed more than a billion dollars in loans as well as more than $850 million in grants since being established in 2019.

The Lowy Institute estimates the government has signed new loan agreements worth $US2.4 billion ($3.44 billion) since 2021.

Mr Duke said the key would be delivering projects on time and on budget, and ensuring they funded projects which boosted economic activity in Pacific nations.

"Everything hinges on the quality," he told the ABC.

"If a project is well-built and it contributes to economic growth, then it pays itself off."

Sources of debt financing in the Pacific, disbursed loans in constant 2024 US dollars. (Source: Lowy Institute Aid Map)

Australia's emergence as the key lender in the region has not completely sidelined Beijing across the Pacific.

The Asian Development Bank and the World Bank are still major lenders in the region, contributing 11 per cent and 10 per cent of total overall development spending respectively: ahead of all countries other than Australia and New Zealand.

And the Lowy Institute's Riley Duke said Chinese construction firms still "dominated" many contests for major World Bank and ADB projects, despite Australian government attempts to shift their operating model.

"This year we have data showing over the last decade over half the infrastructure contracts awarded by volume [by the ABD and World Bank] have been won by Chinese state-owned firms," he said.

" So this means that China, while its infrastructure lending has gone down, is still playing a major role in the infrastructure space, and a very visible one, on the ground. "

He said China was also increasing the amount of money it was handing to the Pacific through grants, with the money often being poured into smaller but equally visible projects like health clinics, roads and schools.

The Aid Map also found that while Donald Trump's aid cuts had fuelled uncertainty in the Pacific, the US administration's move to renew the US Compacts of Free Association with the Federated States of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands and Palau — worth more than $7 billion over two decades from 2024 — meant that its overall commitment to the region remained relatively steady.

World.title: Reports of multiple deaths after earthquake strikes Japan – as it happened
World.content:
Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has confirmed the earthquake rescue effort across the country's southwest will continue through the night.

"Human casualties, building collapses, road damage, fires... have been confirmed so far," she wrote on X. "I extend my heartfelt sympathies to everyone affected by this disaster."

She said there was concern about heatstroke in the region, with power and water supplies affected.

Japan has been sweltering through a heatwave as the country endures one of its hottest summers on record.

Essential supplies, including food and water, portable cooling units and mobile power, would be delivered to the area, Takaichi said.

World.title: Multiple people feared dead in collapsed shopping mall following Japan quake
World.content:
Japan's south-western Kyushu island has been struck by two strong earthquakes within an hour,, with multiple people presumed dead after an explosion at a shopping centre.

As it happened: Read back on how Tuesday's quake unfolded

An initial magnitude-7.1 quake hit the Kumamoto south-western prefecture at 4:35pm local time (5:35pm AEST) on Tuesday.

The prefecture was then struck by 26 additional aftershocks ranging in magnitude between 3.3 and 4.5, before a magnitude-6.1 tremor was recorded at 5:12pm (6:12pm AEST).

Loading...

The quakes hit just south of the town of Uki, near the prefecture's capital city, local authorities reported.

"Human casualties, building collapses, road damage, fires... have been confirmed so far," Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said.

"I extend my heartfelt sympathies to everyone affected by this disaster."

A major rescue operation is underway at the Aeon Mall shopping centre where "many people" have been trapped after the complex's second floor collapsed.

Police said "quite a few" were presumed dead in the incident, broadcaster TBS reported.

An Aeon spokesperson said customers and employees were evacuated right after the initial quake and that the exact cause of the ensuing explosion was unclear.

Between 20 and 30 workers trapped at the mall could not be reached, according to broadcaster NHK.

Emergency services say "many people" were trapped inside a shopping centre after an explosion occurred following the earthquake. (Kyodo via Reuters)

The shopping centre, which had about 200 shops and businesses inside, had only recently reopened after it was badly damaged in the magnitude 7.3 Kumamoto earthquake in April 2016.

Kazuya Tsurunaga told TBS he heard the explosion while cleaning up dishes broken by the earthquake inside a pub about 300 metres from the Aeon mall.

"It was a huge impact," he said.

"A large cloud of smoke billowed up, and because the wind happened to be blowing and the wind direction was towards the shop, the area around us was in a state like volcanic ash was falling."

A chimney collapsed at Nippon Paper Industries' Yatsushiro Mill. (Reuters: Kyodo)

Multiple people were also unaccounted for after a chimney collapsed at a Nippon Paper Industries factory, NHK reported.

Seismology authorities from Geoscience Australia and the United States Geological Survey reported the initial quake struck at a depth of 10 kilometres below the sea's surface.

A tsunami warning for a wave measuring 1 metre was issued after the earthquake, the JMA said.

The warning was lifted about two hours later.

Japan’s Meteorological Agency (JMA) has recorded at least 75 additional quakes in the Kumamoto Prefecture, which could remain a concern for about a week after the initial earthquake.

The crowded Hakata JR station in Fukuoka, southern Japan, after Kyushu Shinkansen operations were suspended. (Reuters: Kyodo)

Urgent response

The Japanese government also issued emergency earthquake warnings for Kumamoto, Nagasaki, Kagoshima, Fukuoka, Saga, Oita, and Miyazaki prefectures, all on Japan's southern Kyushu island.

The tremor caused power outages for at least 48,000 households in the Kumamoto prefecture and fires broke out in several locations, broadcaster NHK reported.

Ms Takaichi also confirmed a meeting of the country's Emergency Assembly Team was called in the Countermeasures Room to assess the quake.

She said local fire stations were responding to the incidents and urged all people to stay away from the coast.

"The investigation team was dispatched from the government cabinet office and human and physical casualties have been investigated," Ms Takaichi told the media.

"There are places where power outages are taking place. I urge people to take shelter and evacuate to safe places."

The extent of damage to the area is being assessed. (Supplied: Nippon Hoso Kyokai )

NHK reported that police are seeking the whereabouts of nine people and that a train was derailed during the earthquake.

Ms Takaichi released a statement on X that urged local government ministries and emergency response agencies to immediately assess damage and to prioritise any necessary rescue of residents.

Japan's south-western Kumamoto prefecture has been hit by a magnitude-7.1 earthquake, followed by a magnitude-6.1 tremor less than an hour later. (Reuters)

Kyushu Electric Power said there were no ‌reports of irregularities at ⁠its Sendai and Genkai nuclear power stations after the earthquake.

Japan's Nuclear Regulation Authority said no abnormalities were found at three nearby nuclear power plants.

The UN nuclear watchdog said on Tuesday that Japan's nuclear regulation authority has informed it that there is no damage or safety issues at the Sendai nuclear power plant after a 7.1-magnitude earthquake hit Japan's southern Kumamoto prefecture.

"The IAEA will continue to monitor the situation," said the watchdog in a post on X.

Train operator JR Kyushu said it had suspended ⁠services, including its high-speed Shinkansen trains following the quake.

Kumamoto airport has also shut its runway, as airlines diverted and cancelled flights with the airport planning "to resume normal operations" on Wednesday.

Earthquake prone area

Japan is one of the world's most earthquake-prone countries, with a tremor occurring at least every five minutes.

Located along the "Ring of Fire" of volcanoes and oceanic trenches partly encircling ⁠the Pacific Basin, ‌Japan accounts for about 20 per cent ‌of the world's earthquakes of magnitude-6 or more.

Kumamoto was hit with a deadly quake in 2016 that left more than 50 people dead, 1,800 injured and tens of thousands of homes damaged or destroyed.

AP/Reuters

World.title: With a forceful declaration, Ben Carroll halted Jacinta Allan's agenda
World.content:
With a forceful declaration, Ben Carroll brought the Allan government's agenda to a skidding halt.

"Let me make one thing very clear: I am not Daniel Andrews, I am not Jacinta Allan," the new Victorian premier said.

This was a clear distinction offered up by the new premier in his maiden speech to journalists and the public. It was deliberate.

With this statement he's given himself less than four months to convince Victorians that their lives and the state will be different under his leadership.

It's a big ask.

Allan's critics often complained she had failed to differentiate herself from Andrews's dominant reign.

Already, Carroll has put integrity front and centre of his new regime, committing to a royal commission into the construction sector and a special prosecutor to probe corruption.

This is designed to cauterise the allegations of criminality on government building sites that dogged Allan and ultimately triggered the first knifing of a Victorian Labor premier this century.

While he was all smiles after he won the ballot, Carroll needs to show Victorians he is serious about poor behaviour.

Ben Carroll was smiling as he left the chaotic meeting where he was eventually elected as leader. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Allan's refusal to act has meant some voters now believe the government has something to hide.

It may mean difficult hearings for Labor supporters with the record of Jacinta Allan and her predecessors potentially coming under the microscope.

But this is all part of Carroll's message.

"It is clear that Victorians want change," he said.

" That change starts today. "

Labor desperate for clear air

Carroll is also pledging to be more pro-business and tougher on crime.

It sounds a bit like a Coalition pitch, but one he'll try to steer to middle and working class Victorians: the communities that polls show have deserted Labor.

It's also a pitch to return Labor to the type of centrist, Labor right faction-leaning government championed by past premiers Steve Bracks and John Brumby from 1999–2010.

Carroll, like Bracks, is from Labor's right faction, while Allan and Andrews were from the left.

Bracks says Carroll's immediate commitments on integrity will give him "clear air" to promote his own agenda.

"Essentially he's really saying, 'I am my own man, judge me on what I will do,'" Bracks told ABC's Afternoon Briefing.

"He didn't say he's not Steve Bracks," he quipped.

The other spectre that looms is the $34.5 billion Suburban Rail Loop — Allan's signature project.

Will Carroll pause the project that is eating up billions of dollars? At his first press conference he said he had no announcements to make.

That's not a no.

Ben Carroll appears at his first press conference as Victorian premier, alongside Gabrielle Williams, who will serve as his deputy. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Carroll is biting off a lot in just four months. And there's only three more sitting weeks before Victorians head to the polls in November.

But Labor is desperate. That's why they've acted.

To use Carroll's own words: "Circumstances have changed."

Carroll's ScoMo moment

Ben Carroll will also have to convince Victorians he can be trusted.

There's a transactional cost of a coup, especially when he famously looked his former boss in the eye at a June press conference and said he supported her because he wanted his daughter to be proud he backed her.

It was his ScoMo moment.

Scott Morrison famously hugged then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull, saying he was "ambitious" for his leader before replacing him a few days later.

He went on to win the 2019 election.

Carroll will also have to rebuild trust with a caucus who have been battered and bruised by their first hostile leadership takeover since 1999.

Jacinta Allan walks into Labor caucus meeting flanked by her loyal minister Sonya Kilkenny, who went on to make a chaotic, failed bid for leadership. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

As Victorians waited to hear the outcome of the Labor leadership ballot, those of us waiting outside could actually hear the yelling from inside the caucus room.

I've stood outside that party room many times before and I've never heard yelling like that.

The messages coming out from MPs were this room is a mess. This is chaos. This is diabolical.

From here, Labor and Carroll have just four months to keep it together.

Ben Carroll pictured after he was unanimously elected as state Labor leader following the resignation of premier Jacinta Allan. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

This isn't necessarily about winning the election.

It's about stopping the bleeding and ensuring the party doesn't get decimated on election day. It's a possibility many feared.

Allan's appalling personal approval ratings were a drag on the vote, and it meant voters weren't even willing to consider Labor.

Carroll is trying to change that by at least being part of the conversation.

The public has shown at the last two elections that it's sceptical on the Liberal Party's credentials to govern.

This change may let Labor re-enter the discussion, especially with One Nation's resurgence.

One Nation's influence complicates the electoral calculus, with Labor figures believing the Coalition will not be able to win a majority but will instead have to rely on One Nation.

So if Labor can save some of the furniture and be a strong opposition it could find itself back in power in four years.

Ben Carroll is setting himself up to do much more. The clock is ticking.

World.title: Hanson reveals who paid for Italy trip with Gina Rinehart
World.content:
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has confirmed mining magnate Gina Rinehart paid for her flights from London to Sicily, via Rome, and for her to attend a high-end fashion parade on the luxurious Italian island.

Senator Hanson updated her parliamentary register of interests on Tuesday and also confirmed she personally paid for her accommodation, meals and other daily expenses during the trip from July 11 to 16.

The trip made headlines when the pair were spotted seaside in Sicily, but until now she had not revealed how the travel was funded, other than to insist taxpayers did not pay "one cent".

Ms Hanson has previously declared a series of gifts from Mrs Rinehart and Hancock Prospecting in her register, including interstate flights, hospitality and a "bloody big orange bulldozer" that was gifted by the billionaire on stage at a regional summit while she made bulldozer sounds.

The disclosure log reveals Pauline Hanson, right, attended two Dolce & Gabbana fashion shows in Italy earlier this month. (Instagram: @beatyesterday_art)

The updated disclosure does not include reference to how her flights from Australia to London were funded, although if she personally footed the bill, she would not have to declare that.

The ABC has asked Ms Hanson's office how these flights were paid for.

Senator Hanson last week posted an apparent pitch from producers for Seven's Spotlight, which filmed part of her London visit, suggesting the program might cover some of her UK travel costs.

In the document, a senior producer said Spotlight wanted Senator Hanson to meet UK Reform leader Nigel Farage in Britain, but this fell through after he resigned from parliament around the time the pair were due to meet.

Instead, Senator Hanson took part in a podcast interview hosted by UK far-right activist Tommy Robinson, who has an extensive criminal record and has served prison sentences for offences including assault, fraud and contempt of court.

Hanson defends Europe trip, anti-immigration comments In her first appearance since returning to Australia, Pauline Hanson fields questions about her trip to Europe with billionaire Gina Rinehart.

She also participated in a street walk with Mr Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, in his hometown of Luton.

A Seven spokesperson later said the program only paid for "incidentals" related to the interactions with Mr Robinson, "including a vehicle used in the production process and a hotel room used for filming purposes as well as security to protect Seven staff while recording on UK streets".

Mrs Rinehart and Senator Hanson have appeared to grow increasingly close over recent months, as the senator's popularity in published opinion polls has soared.

In April, the Queensland senator also accepted a new $1 million Cirrus G7 plane from Mrs Rinehart, which she described as "sexy" and "fast".

World.title: Commonwealth Games LIVE: Australia’s gymnastics gold rush; Peter Bol to risk all in chasing 800m glory
World.content:
A devastated Kiana Elliott has spoken with us in the mixed media area. The Aussie weightlifter looked set to clinch a medal in the women’s 63kg category, her maiden Commonwealth Games victory. But she dropped the bar on her final attempt and was knocked out of contention.

“I have no idea what happened on that third attempt,” she said. “All I wanted to do today was put absolutely everything into what I did out there on the platform and I think that’s what I did.

Kiana Elliott falls on her third attempt in the clean and jerk portion of the competition. Getty Images

“I’m gutted for fourth, I was fourth four years go [in Birmingham] but I came in to put up a fight and I think I did that ... I didn’t pick the easy option.

World.title: Deaths confirmed after powerful earthquake, shopping mall blast in Japan
World.content:
Updated WorldAsiaEarthquakes Deaths confirmed after powerful earthquake, shopping mall blast in Japan Anton Bridge and Mariko Katsumura Updated July 29, 2026 — 2:21am ,first published 10:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A powerful 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck Japan’s southwestern island of Kyushu on Tuesday, killing at least three people, injuring dozens and damaging buildings including a shopping mall where many people were feared trapped after an explosion. The tremor was centred around Kumamoto prefecture, about 900 kilometres from central Tokyo, and hit at an extremely shallow depth of 10km, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA). Aerial image showing the damaged Aeon Mall after an earthquake in Kashima, Kumamoto prefecture, southern Japan. AP Rescue workers at the shopping centre after the earthquake. undefined/Kyodo News via AP The blast occurred at an Aeon mall in the Kumamoto prefecture town of Kashima, according to a spokesperson. Around 20 to 30 workers at the prefecture’s largest shopping centre were unaccounted for, broadcaster NHK said. Fire services earlier said multiple people were trapped inside.



Two people were also presumed dead at a Nippon Paper Industries plant in Yatsushiro, where a chimney collapsed, with nine people still missing, according to NHK. A smokestack at Nippon Paper Industries’ Yatsushiro Mill collapsed in the earthquake. undefined/Kyodo News via AP Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told media she had received initial reports of injuries, while NHK reported that at least 80 people had been hurt. Kyodo News reported that one person had been killed in a collapsed home. Several passengers aboard high-speed trains at the time of the quake were also injured, operators said.



Speaking to reporters at her office in Tokyo, Takaichi said authorities were still assessing the full extent of the damage in the area, which was devastated by a deadly quake a decade ago. “We have already been informed that people have been injured. Power outages and fires have occurred in some areas, and there has also been damage to roads and bridges and the collapse of buildings,” she said. “I ask everyone to take action to protect themselves, including evacuating to a safe location.” Around 300,000 people have been instructed to go to evacuation centres, the disaster management agency said, while Takaichi said 3600 soldiers would be deployed to help with the disaster recovery as aftershocks continued to rumble. The quake’s maximum seismic intensity was estimated at 7 on a Japanese scale of 7. Shaking of that intensity makes it impossible to stand, according to the JMA. An initial quake just before 4.30pm Japan time was followed by a series of aftershocks in the same region.



An Aeon spokesperson said customers and employees were evacuated right after the initial quake and that the exact cause of the ensuing explosion was unclear. Kazuya Tsurunaga told TBS he heard the explosion while cleaning up dishes broken by the earthquake inside a pub about 300 metres from the Aeon mall. “It was a huge impact,” he said. “A large cloud of smoke billowed up, and because the wind happened to be blowing and the wind direction was towards the shop, the area around us was in a state like volcanic ash was falling.” The Aeon mall had just reopened last month as a new and improved shopping and entertainment complex to commemorate its recovery from a deadly tremor a decade ago.



The mall was so badly damaged in the 7.3-magnitude Kumamoto earthquake in April 2016 that it had to close for months and rebuild over even longer periods. As it went through a 2017 redevelopment and expansion, the mall highlighted its seismically reinforced ceilings and overall improvements to safety and resilience. A store sign of a restaurant is seen fallen on the ground after an earthquake in Kumamoto in the Kyushu island, southern Japan, undefined/Kyodo News via AP Rail operator JR Kyushu stopped all its services, while Kumamoto airport’s runway was closed for safety checks, with no time set for reopening. Power outages were reported at some 7-Eleven stores in Kumamoto, while NTT Docomo experienced disruptions to mobile services. No irregularities were reported at nuclear power facilities, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing said it evacuated staff at its Japan Advanced Semiconductor Manufacturing facility. TSMC, the go-to chipmaker for Nvidia and Apple operates a factory in Kumamoto prefecture, with a second facility under construction.



Sony Group produces image sensors in Kyushu that are used in smartphones, while Tokyo Electron makes chip tools and advanced packaging equipment in the region. An aerial image shows part of a bridge that collapsed after the earthquake in Yatsushiro, Kumamoto prefecture, southern Japan. undefined/Kyodo News via AP Chip making in particular is highly sensitive to physical shocks or disruptions in power and processes, and minor hiccups can sometimes destroy whole batches of valuable product. Japan is one of the world’s most earthquake-prone countries, with a tremor occurring at least every five minutes. Located along the “Ring of Fire” of volcanoes and oceanic trenches partly encircling the Pacific Basin, Japan accounts for about 20 per cent of the world’s earthquakes of magnitude 6.0 or more. A tsunami warning was issued immediately after Tuesday’s quake, but was later lifted.



An earthquake in 2016 caused substantial damage to Kumamoto. Yusuke Ogata Kyushu Electric Power said 48,000 homes had lost power as a result of the latest quake. A massive earthquake in Kumamoto 10 years ago killed 275 people and injured a further 2739, according to an official count, and damaged thousands of buildings including the city’s castle, a top tourist site. Some portions of the stone walls at the castle also collapsed as a result of Tuesday’s quake, an official at the castle’s office said. Reuters/Bloomberg Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: The multibillion-dollar cost of students who can’t – or won’t – engage with school
World.content:
NationalVictoriaEducation The multibillion-dollar cost of students who can’t – or won’t – engage with school Jackson Graham July 29, 2026 — 12:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The 26,457 Victorian year 8 students who are disengaged from school this year will cost the state economy $33 billion over the course of their lives, research has estimated. One in three students are not engaged in their schooling during years 7 to 9, which costs the state 5 per cent of GDP and each household more than $13,000, according to a report by the Institute for Educational Reform released on Wednesday. Institute for Educational Reform chair David Loader with students. Simon Schluter The figure includes students who are absent from school and those who are present but falling behind in class because of disengagement, as well as those who are gifted but disengaged. It estimates the potential lost personal income, productivity and taxes, as well as the social costs including through the health and justice systems, over the 45-year working life of those students. It also accounts for students who regain focus in later life.



“The cost is $33 billion because once these kids become adults and enter the workforce, about a quarter never enter the workforce in a formal way,” said former NSW Treasury chief economist Stephen Walters, who calculated the figure. “And of the rest who do work over their lives, a lot of it is intermittent. Related Article Education Schools of last resort grow fast as classroom disengagement booms “So what that leaves over the 45 years or so of their working lives is a big forgone income because they could have been working at a higher level.” Walters has estimated this cost for the first time at a state level, finding the biggest losses come from low wages and missed productivity rather than the excess burden on the Victorian taxpayer or forgone taxes. “The social costs outweigh the direct fiscal costs by a factor of five to one,” he said.



“There’s a massive social benefit [to students being engaged] because it generates income in the economy – that generates investment, it generates more jobs.” Australian students are estimated to miss about four weeks of schooling a year on average, adding up to a year between the first day of school and the end of year 10. Related Article Exclusive

Education Off-the-books school suspensions fuelling Melbourne’s youth crime crisis In Victoria, attendance rates for years 7 to 10 dropped from 92.4 per cent in 2016 to 86.9 per cent in 2025. The scale of disengagement also appears in the state government’s Attitudes to School Survey, released in March, which showed 50.2 per cent of students in years 7 to 9 had a sense of belonging in their school, and only 52.8 per cent said their teachers made them interested in learning.



Institute for Educational Reform chair David Loader, a former principal of 32 years, said the cost was a wake-up call that leaving behind students in their middle years was a missed opportunity. “If they were more involved, our community would benefit enormously,” he said. Giving principals more autonomy to speak up about fixes in schools and ensuring teachers had the time and resources to focus on individual students were part of the solution, Loader said. However, he acknowledged there wasn’t a silver bullet. As a principal, Loader introduced residential education programs including at MLC, where year 9 students live together in Marshmead in East Gippsland for eight weeks, and at Wesley College, where students go to Clunes, north of Ballarat. He said these programs helped students gain personal growth outside academic learning in years when they were at risk of disengagement at school. “A school that’s helping young people to grow as opposed to a school that’s focused on a number at year 12 is a very different thing,” he said. “That’s the cultural change we’re looking for – we no longer look at students as a number, but we look for personal growth.” A Victorian government spokesperson did not directly respond to questions about student disengagement in the classroom but acknowledged that regular attendance was critical to success.



Related Article Education Trouble getting your kids to school? So do many Australians Since 2023, Victoria’s year 12 completion rates have grown to 97 per cent, up 5 percentage points, and the year 10 to 12 retention rate of 85 per cent is the highest in eight years. The vocational major is also reshaping the pathways students take to the workforce. “We’ve made a record investment in student mental health, putting mental health workers in every public school,” the government spokesperson said. “Victoria’s school attendance rates continue to improve, thanks to the exceptional efforts of teachers and school leaders who work hard to ensure every student is engaged in their learning and feels like they belong at their school.” Opposition education spokesperson Brad Rowswell blamed Education Minister and now Premier Ben Carroll for “declining school attendance, falling student engagement, collapsing teacher morale, and serious safety concerns in early childhood services”.
