World.title: This value predicts future quality of life. In Australia, it’s tanking
World.content:
Analysis NationalScience This value predicts future quality of life. In Australia, it’s tanking Angus Dalton July 29, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Most Australians believe they live in a scientific powerhouse. They’d be wrong. Hundreds of scientists are sounding the alarm over our woefully unambitious level of investment in research and development, which has eroded over 15 years to the point that our quality of life is under threat. Australian science funding has crashed to historic lows. Aresna Villanueva Since a peak in 2009, overall investment into R&D has crashed to 1.69 per cent of GDP, a historic low that runs way below the OECD average of 2.7 per cent and could see Australia ranked last in the OECD within five years. As that value has edged downward, the facilities of Australia’s premier science organisation, CSIRO, have also quietly fallen into disrepair. The agency’s chief executive, Professor Doug Hilton, will tell the National Press Club on Wednesday that 80 per cent of CSIRO’s 800 buildings are at their technical end of life or not fit for purpose.



Maintenance costs are why the axe has had to swing on 350 jobs despite an additional $387.4 million funding injection from the latest budget, according to a draft version of Hilton’s speech. Amid feeble funding and slashed research jobs, most with a stake in science agree we are at a crossroads between choosing a vigorous reversal of scientific decline or accepting descent into becoming The Dumb Country. That’s why the Australian Academy of Science, comprising about 650 distinguished researchers, has marshalled its biggest campaign in 70 years. Science funding tied to quality of life Australia is good at waving the flag for science. In 2024, the late Professor Richard Scolyer and colleague Professor Georgina Long were named dual Australians of the Year for their work on melanoma. This year it’s space engineer Katherine Bennell-Pegg.



A survey by the academy showed 86 per cent of Australians assumed our investment in science is on par with other countries. The reality shocked them. Australian scientists may be world-class, but every stroke of their brilliance – synthetic DNA, new heart-rescuing drugs crafted from funnel-web venom, and ultra-efficient solar panels – has been made despite chronic underfunding, a Byzantine grants system and ailing facilities. “We haven’t really seen science being an election issue for a very long time, and it’s probably just complacency because the public believes that everything’s doing great,” says Dr Hayley Teasdale, a neuroscience researcher and head of science with the academy. “But scientists are now telling their kids not to follow in their footsteps, and that is heartbreaking.”



Teasdale knows the feeling of dashed scientific dreams. There was no local work in her field when she completed her PhD in Canberra. Dr Hayley Teasdale, head of science policy and advice at the Australian Academy of Science. Alex Ellinghausen But her expertise was keenly desired elsewhere: a neurotech company in San Francisco hired Teasdale as their lead scientist, to work on non-invasive brain stimulation treating the symptoms of Parkinson’s disease and depression. She returned to Australia during COVID. “There were no jobs here for me to continue my research in Australia,” she says. “I’ve lived the story.” Teasdale is now a torchbearer for the academy’s Restore Science campaign, which has rallied almost 18,000 people to write to their MPs calling for the return of research investment to an internationally competitive level.



The campaign follows the release of the Ambitious Australia report, a road map to a bolder, stronger science sector, commissioned by the government and delivered in March. The report calls for the reversal of declining research grants; lifting spending to the OECD average would require a boost of 43 per cent, or $2 billion. Science improves our lives through cheaper energy, more nutritious food, better medicine, new materials to use and sell, and more biodiverse cities. Without strong science and the urgent diversification of our economy beyond what we dig from the ground, the report warned, our lives in future decades will be worse. “The imperative for change is clear,” wrote the report’s leader, Tesla chair Robyn Denholm. “Future generations of Australians face a substantial reduction in their standard of living unless there are bold, nation-changing reforms.”



Some reform has followed. Last week, the government overhauled the Australian Research Council’s National Competitive Grants Program – one of the major sources of government science funding – from 15 schemes to seven, and simplified the process to reduce time burnt by researchers applying for grants (which can take up as much as half of a senior scientist’s workload). But that refresh, and the recent measures in the budget, did not deliver more cash. It just rearranged lab stools on the Titanic. If there’s one thing the report stressed, it’s that incremental change is no longer enough to save science. CSIRO cuts over, but 10-year upgrades needed With its axed researchers and ageing facilities, CSIRO has served as a metaphorical microcosm for the broader state of Australian science. But the exit of 800 support staff and 350 researchers – including from the health and biosecurity unit and climate modelling teams – has put the organisation back on steady ground, Hilton says. Some senior CSIRO staff have said mismanagement of COVID-era funds put the organisation in the red. Hilton says the job cuts were required after previous executives prioritised science jobs over building upgrades.



“I can understand why in the past people have preferenced keeping scientists on board and keeping our research portfolio broad, at the expense of repairs and maintenance,” he says. “But there’s a point where it does become unsustainable.” CSIRO chief executive Doug Hilton. Martin Ollman Addressing the maintenance and facility upgrade backlog will be a 10-year job, he warns. But he doesn’t foresee any more broad job losses in the pipeline: “The scale of those major cuts are behind us now.” Speaking broadly about the state of research funding, Hilton says science has to prove its worth against all the other pillars of a nation the government has to answer to: defence, the NDIS, an ageing population, the environment. “If science wants to contest for [funding], then we genuinely have to ask ourselves as organisational leaders, as team leaders in science, and as individual scientists, whether we’re doing absolutely everything to create the case that we are delivering the best value for money,” he says.



“I think that’s part of being a good steward of public money, and it’s part of the trust people have in science and scientists.” Related Article Exclusive

Science Australians made a pill to protect us from nuclear attack. We could lose it to the US He, too, sees us at a momentous junction between regression, inaction and forging a new path ahead. “I’m really sympathetic to the campaign the Academy of Sciences is running,” Hilton says. “But for me, it’s not about restoring science back to something that it was in the 1970s or 1980s. It’s how do we chart a new course for science where people widely across a big continent – in rural and regional areas, in outer suburban areas, in inner metro areas – they can all see the absolutely crucial nature of science in their future?” The Examine newsletter explains and analyses science with a rigorous focus on the evidence. World.title: Hanson reveals Rinehart paid for London, Rome and Sicily flights
World.content:
PoliticsFederalOne Nation Hanson reveals Rinehart paid for London, Rome and Sicily flights Rob Harris Updated July 28, 2026 — 10:30pm ,first published 4:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Pauline Hanson says One Nation will begin unveiling its Victorian election candidates within days, claiming the party has almost completed a statewide slate as it attempts to turn a surge in support into seats at November’s election. Appearing in a one-hour special hosted by Paul Murray on News24, the rebranded Sky News Australia, Hanson said the party would start with upper house candidates as early as Friday before announcing its lower house contenders and releasing its Victorian policy platform. Pauline Hanson said her party will begin to name their candidates for the Victorian election. Luca Marino She said One Nation had secured candidates for about 74 of Victoria’s 88 electorates and expected to be represented in every seat across the state. She declined to name who would lead the party at a state level, telling Murray: “No, Paul. That’s not part of the deal.” Seeking to reassure voters that One Nation has learned from years of candidate controversies, Hanson said the party had introduced a tougher screening process ahead of the Victorian and next federal elections.



Hanson said there had been strong interest from prospective candidates, with about 1200 expressions of interest received in Victoria and 1500 nationally to contest the federal election. The party’s sole Victorian representative, Shepparton-based upper-house MP Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell, was re-endorsed on Tuesday. “It hasn’t been easy for the party over a period of time because the last election we got about six-and-a-half per cent,” she said. “So people are thinking they want to support us and give it a go and stand as a candidate ... but this time around there’s a real chance that we can actually win seats in the lower house and the Senate.” Gina Rinehart (left) and Hanson at a resort in Sicily earlier this month. The television appearance came hours after Hanson updated her parliamentary register of interests to disclose that mining billionaire Gina Rinehart paid for flights to London, Rome and Sicily, as well as inviting her to attend a Dolce & Gabbana fashion parade during her recent European trip.



Hanson declared she personally paid for her accommodation, meals and daily expenses. The disclosure followed scrutiny of the One Nation leader’s close relationship with Rinehart after photographs emerged of the pair together at the luxury Grand Hotel San Pietro in Taormina, Sicily, where the billionaire attended a Dolce & Gabbana event. Related Article One Nation Hanson blasted for White Australia comments after attending lavish Italian fashion show The push into Victoria comes as One Nation records its strongest polling in years. The latest Resolve Political Monitor for this masthead put the party on 22 per cent in the state, behind Labor and the Coalition, which were tied on 27 per cent. Hanson said Victoria had become a “basket case” following Tuesday’s leadership change that saw Ben Carroll replace Jacinta Allan as premier, arguing voters were increasingly looking beyond the major parties.



The claims of campaign readiness follow questions about the party’s preparations in Victoria. The Herald Sun reported earlier this month that One Nation’s Victorian leadership had moved to reassure frustrated prospective candidates that its election campaign was progressing, after some applicants complained about delays, secrecy around the campaign structure and uncertainty over candidate selection. The party told candidates that recruitment, policy development and organisational planning were under way, while regional committees were being established to help build a Victorian campaign operation. Loading Some candidates raised concerns about confidentiality agreements and fees of up to $5500 associated with running, with one applicant questioning whether the party had invested enough in the infrastructure needed to compete in a major state election.



One Nation has defended the secrecy around its preparations, arguing campaign strategy needed to be protected from leaks. Hanson said the party had introduced a far more extensive vetting process using advanced artificial intelligence technology to weed out rogue applications. She said the tougher screening process was designed to ensure candidates were prepared for the responsibility of representing One Nation as the party seeks to convert voter dissatisfaction into electoral gains. The system, developed by One Nation general manager Kelvin Morton and Hanson’s chief of staff, James Ashby, examines prospective candidates’ criminal records, financial history, civil litigation and social media activity. “So if you’ve got something that you’ve done somewhere else in the world, it’ll find you,” Hanson said.



Related Article Updated

Courts Pauline Hanson loses bid to overturn racial vilification ruling “It’ll tell us if you’ve got a criminal offence internationally. It’ll tell us if you’ve been a bankrupt, if you’re owing money to the taxation office. It’ll tell us if you’ve made any comment or put on Facebook some stupid comment.” The overhaul follows a history of damaging controversies involving One Nation candidates and elected members, including former senators Brian Burston, Fraser Anning and Rod Culleton. Other candidates have been forced to withdraw after offensive antisemitic or homophobic material posted online resurfaced, or after falling out with the party leadership. World.title: Australia vastly outspends China on Pacific aid. But there’s a catch
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPacific diplomacy Australia vastly outspends China on Pacific aid. But there’s a catch Matthew Knott July 28, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The perception China is pumping vast sums of development assistance into the Pacific compared with other nations is not borne out by the evidence, with Australia spending significantly more on aid, infrastructure funding and loans in the region than any other nation. However, Beijing has focused on maximising the pay-off of its spending by funding smaller but highly visible projects such as school upgrades, sports stadiums and medical clinics. The Aiwo Port Terminal in Nauru, which was recently upgraded with the help of a Chinese state-owned company. Facebook Chinese state-owned enterprises are also the dominant construction contractors for Pacific infrastructure, leaving Australian companies lagging far behind. Australia spent a total of $2.15 billion on aid to the Pacific in 2024, the most recent year with full data available, according to the Lowy Institute’s latest Pacific Aid Map, a detailed report on overseas development assistance in the region.



Australia accounted for 37 per cent of all development finance to the region, three times more than the next biggest aid contributor – New Zealand – and far ahead of China on 6 per cent. The release of the new database came as Chinese ambassador Xiao Qian bid farewell to associates at a ceremony in Canberra on Tuesday following an eventful 4½-year posting in the country. China’s ambassador to Australia, Xiao Qian, is departing after more than four years in the role. Alex Ellinghausen He will be replaced by Liu Jinsong, a seasoned diplomat who currently serves as the head of the Chinese foreign ministry’s department for Asian affairs. Xiao’s tenure was marked by friendlier relations, especially on trade, after China put Australia in the diplomatic deep freezer, but there were still moments of acrimony during his posting.



This included a fiery recent opinion piece Xiao wrote for this masthead accusing ASIO and other Western intelligence agencies of overhyping spying claims against China. Xiao told an audience at the Chinese embassy – including Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade deputy secretary Elly Lawson and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s top international adviser Rod Hilton – that the China-Australia relationship had “emerged from a low point and regained stability”, achieving a “comprehensive turnaround” from the days of outright hostility. The Lowy report shows the web of diplomatic arrangements the Albanese government has struck since it came to office is translating into dollars, with Papua New Guinea a particularly notable recipient of recent Australian funds. Australia struck a new military alliance and sweeping economic agreement with Fiji earlier this month, following similar previous deals with PNG, Vanuatu, Nauru and Tuvalu.



China test-fired a missile from a nuclear-powered submarine into the Pacific, landing near the Solomon Islands, on the same day Australia struck the Fiji agreements, drawing complaints from many Pacific nations. Related Article Exclusive

China relations China ambassador attacks ASIO, rejects foreign interference accusations Australia has also signed $3.4 billion in new loan agreements since 2021, making it the region’s largest source of new lending over that period. This is a major change from much of the 2010s when China was the dominant lender to the Pacific, drawing claims of being involved in “debt trap diplomacy”. “As other donors retreat and repeated economic shocks hit the region, Australia’s large and sustained support has been a stabilising factor for Pacific economies,” the report’s lead author, Riley Duke, said.



“Australia’s push into infrastructure, particularly strategic infrastructure, is reshaping the regional aid picture.” From 2010 to 2019, China signed about $5.2 billion in loans to Pacific countries, more than one-third of all lending deals in the region. Since 2020, China has committed just $558 million in new loan deals, falling well behind Australia. Despite this, the most recent Lowy Poll has found that 39 per cent of Australians believe China is the most influential country in the Pacific, ahead of Australia on 33 per cent. The United States spends little on aid in the region outside its three “compact of association” states – the Federated States of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands, and Palau – and US President Donald Trump has gutted foreign aid spending since returning to office.



As for Chinese aid in the Pacific, Duke said it “is highly reactive to diplomatic developments, functioning as a strategic lever Beijing can pull”. “When a country switches diplomatic recognition from Taipei to Beijing, or opens strategic negotiations with Australia, Chinese aid flows react,” he said. Related Article Pacific diplomacy Australia to spend $1b on defence alliance with Fiji in blow to China For example, since Nauru switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China in 2024, Beijing has funded its national sports stadium, as well as solar streetlights, schoolbag and computer donations, a medical clinic and a press conference room for the Ministry of Media. In Vanuatu, China has provided police with motorcycles, drones, riot equipment and training programs, as well as ongoing medical equipment donations and scholarship and training programs.



About 40 per cent of Pacific infrastructure projects involve a Chinese state-owned enterprise, even as China’s direct investment has declined. “As a result, they play a dominant and highly visible role in infrastructure across the region, one that extends well beyond China’s own bilateral financing,” the report finds. World.title: $90 million boost revealed in bid to address major world rugby disparity
World.content:
Exclusive SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby $90 million boost revealed in bid to address major world rugby disparity Nick Wright July 28, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A $90 million injection into grassroots rugby will create new women’s leagues and expand existing competitions to help the sport compete with cross code rivals ahead of the 2029 World Cup on home soil. While the federal government funding will not specifically target the top-flight Super Rugby Women’s, a beefed-up grassroots product shapes as a crucial building block towards growing the competition in the future. The Super Rugby Women’s season of just four rounds with a two-week finals system pales in comparison to countries such as England, where the Premiership Women’s Rugby is played over 20 weeks with nine teams. This has helped England feature in nine of 10 World Cup finals. The Wallaroos have not made it past the World Cup quarter-finals since 2010. Getty Images Rugby Australia has increased the Test program to at least 10 fixtures a year from 2026, but it has still grappled with player defections to the ever-growing NRLW, including Rugby 7s star Teagan Levi (Gold Coast Titans) and former Test squad member Caitlin Urwin (Brisbane Broncos).



The early program rollouts of the Australian Legacy funding into rugby have already generated an 8 per cent increase in female participation. Minister for Sport Anika Wells said a long-term legacy beyond the World Cup will be created from the initiative. Related Article Wallabies ‘Is this the end?’: Contract call twists fate for plagued Wallaby “The Albanese government’s $90 million investment will get more women, girls and grassroots players into rugby, growing the sport in Australia and the Pacific and leaving a lasting legacy from these major competitions,” Wells said. “The benefits of these tournaments will be felt well beyond the final whistle, encouraging Australians – especially women and girls – to pick up a ball and get involved.” The funding will also go towards women’s facility upgrades and the creation of courses to help more women and girls become coaches, referees and officials.



According to an AusPlay survey funded and led by the Australian Sports Commission, 39 per cent of Australians aged 15 and over who participated as a sports official in 2025 were women. However, that figure is not represented across the higher levels. Of the 44 clubs in the four women’s football codes – Super Rugby Women’s, NRLW, AFLW and A-League Women’s – only five head coaches are female: Karyn Murphy (Titans), Tamara Hyett (Western Bulldogs), Lisa Webb (Fremantle Dockers), Daisy Pearce (West Coast Eagles), and Natalie Wood (Essendon Bombers). Loading The federal government said the funding would also help deliver both Rugby World Cups – with the men’s 2027 showcase in Australia expected to generate more than $2 billion – while continuing to aid the Pacific Legacy program, which now operates in Fiji, Samoa and Tonga. “This is another way we are working with our Pacific neighbours to grow and strengthen our ties through sport,” Wells said. World.title: Deaths confirmed after powerful earthquake, shopping mall blast in Japan
World.content:
Updated WorldAsiaEarthquakes Deaths confirmed after powerful earthquake, shopping mall blast in Japan Anton Bridge and Mariko Katsumura Updated July 29, 2026 — 2:21am ,first published 10:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A powerful 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck Japan’s southwestern island of Kyushu on Tuesday, killing at least three people, injuring dozens and damaging buildings including a shopping mall where many people were feared trapped after an explosion. The tremor was centred around Kumamoto prefecture, about 900 kilometres from central Tokyo, and hit at an extremely shallow depth of 10km, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA). Aerial image showing the damaged Aeon Mall after an earthquake in Kashima, Kumamoto prefecture, southern Japan. AP Rescue workers at the shopping centre after the earthquake. undefined/Kyodo News via AP The blast occurred at an Aeon mall in the Kumamoto prefecture town of Kashima, according to a spokesperson. Around 20 to 30 workers at the prefecture’s largest shopping centre were unaccounted for, broadcaster NHK said. Fire services earlier said multiple people were trapped inside.



Two people were also presumed dead at a Nippon Paper Industries plant in Yatsushiro, where a chimney collapsed, with nine people still missing, according to NHK. A smokestack at Nippon Paper Industries’ Yatsushiro Mill collapsed in the earthquake. undefined/Kyodo News via AP Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told media she had received initial reports of injuries, while NHK reported that at least 80 people had been hurt. Kyodo News reported that one person had been killed in a collapsed home. Several passengers aboard high-speed trains at the time of the quake were also injured, operators said.



Speaking to reporters at her office in Tokyo, Takaichi said authorities were still assessing the full extent of the damage in the area, which was devastated by a deadly quake a decade ago. “We have already been informed that people have been injured. Power outages and fires have occurred in some areas, and there has also been damage to roads and bridges and the collapse of buildings,” she said. “I ask everyone to take action to protect themselves, including evacuating to a safe location.” Around 300,000 people have been instructed to go to evacuation centres, the disaster management agency said, while Takaichi said 3600 soldiers would be deployed to help with the disaster recovery as aftershocks continued to rumble. The quake’s maximum seismic intensity was estimated at 7 on a Japanese scale of 7. Shaking of that intensity makes it impossible to stand, according to the JMA. An initial quake just before 4.30pm Japan time was followed by a series of aftershocks in the same region.



An Aeon spokesperson said customers and employees were evacuated right after the initial quake and that the exact cause of the ensuing explosion was unclear. Kazuya Tsurunaga told TBS he heard the explosion while cleaning up dishes broken by the earthquake inside a pub about 300 metres from the Aeon mall. “It was a huge impact,” he said. “A large cloud of smoke billowed up, and because the wind happened to be blowing and the wind direction was towards the shop, the area around us was in a state like volcanic ash was falling.” The Aeon mall had just reopened last month as a new and improved shopping and entertainment complex to commemorate its recovery from a deadly tremor a decade ago.



The mall was so badly damaged in the 7.3-magnitude Kumamoto earthquake in April 2016 that it had to close for months and rebuild over even longer periods. As it went through a 2017 redevelopment and expansion, the mall highlighted its seismically reinforced ceilings and overall improvements to safety and resilience. A store sign of a restaurant is seen fallen on the ground after an earthquake in Kumamoto in the Kyushu island, southern Japan, undefined/Kyodo News via AP Rail operator JR Kyushu stopped all its services, while Kumamoto airport’s runway was closed for safety checks, with no time set for reopening. Power outages were reported at some 7-Eleven stores in Kumamoto, while NTT Docomo experienced disruptions to mobile services. No irregularities were reported at nuclear power facilities, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing said it evacuated staff at its Japan Advanced Semiconductor Manufacturing facility. TSMC, the go-to chipmaker for Nvidia and Apple operates a factory in Kumamoto prefecture, with a second facility under construction.



Sony Group produces image sensors in Kyushu that are used in smartphones, while Tokyo Electron makes chip tools and advanced packaging equipment in the region. An aerial image shows part of a bridge that collapsed after the earthquake in Yatsushiro, Kumamoto prefecture, southern Japan. undefined/Kyodo News via AP Chip making in particular is highly sensitive to physical shocks or disruptions in power and processes, and minor hiccups can sometimes destroy whole batches of valuable product. Japan is one of the world’s most earthquake-prone countries, with a tremor occurring at least every five minutes. Located along the “Ring of Fire” of volcanoes and oceanic trenches partly encircling the Pacific Basin, Japan accounts for about 20 per cent of the world’s earthquakes of magnitude 6.0 or more. A tsunami warning was issued immediately after Tuesday’s quake, but was later lifted.



A 6.5 magnitude earthquake in 2016 caused substantial damage to Kumamoto. Yusuke Ogata Kyushu Electric Power said 48,000 homes had lost power as a result of the latest quake. A massive earthquake in Kumamoto 10 years ago killed 275 people and injured a further 2739, according to an official count, and damaged thousands of buildings including the city’s castle, a top tourist site. Some portions of the stone walls at the castle also collapsed as a result of Tuesday’s quake, an official at the castle’s office said. Reuters/Bloomberg Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: The multibillion-dollar cost of students who can’t – or won’t – engage with school
World.content:
NationalVictoriaEducation The multibillion-dollar cost of students who can’t – or won’t – engage with school Jackson Graham July 29, 2026 — 12:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The 26,457 Victorian year 8 students who are disengaged from school this year will cost the state economy $33 billion over the course of their lives, research has estimated. One in three students are not engaged in their schooling during years 7 to 9, which costs the state 5 per cent of GDP and each household more than $13,000, according to a report by the Institute for Educational Reform released on Wednesday. Institute for Educational Reform chair David Loader with students. Simon Schluter The figure includes students who are absent from school and those who are present but falling behind in class because of disengagement, as well as those who are gifted but disengaged. It estimates the potential lost personal income, productivity and taxes, as well as the social costs including through the health and justice systems, over the 45-year working life of those students. It also accounts for students who regain focus in later life.



“The cost is $33 billion because once these kids become adults and enter the workforce, about a quarter never enter the workforce in a formal way,” said former NSW Treasury chief economist Stephen Walters, who calculated the figure. “And of the rest who do work over their lives, a lot of it is intermittent. Related Article Education Schools of last resort grow fast as classroom disengagement booms “So what that leaves over the 45 years or so of their working lives is a big forgone income because they could have been working at a higher level.” Walters has estimated this cost for the first time at a state level, finding the biggest losses come from low wages and missed productivity rather than the excess burden on the Victorian taxpayer or forgone taxes. “The social costs outweigh the direct fiscal costs by a factor of five to one,” he said.



“There’s a massive social benefit [to students being engaged] because it generates income in the economy – that generates investment, it generates more jobs.” Australian students are estimated to miss about four weeks of schooling a year on average, adding up to a year between the first day of school and the end of year 10. Related Article Exclusive

Education Off-the-books school suspensions fuelling Melbourne’s youth crime crisis In Victoria, attendance rates for years 7 to 10 dropped from 92.4 per cent in 2016 to 86.9 per cent in 2025. The scale of disengagement also appears in the state government’s Attitudes to School Survey, released in March, which showed 50.2 per cent of students in years 7 to 9 had a sense of belonging in their school, and only 52.8 per cent said their teachers made them interested in learning.



Institute for Educational Reform chair David Loader, a former principal of 32 years, said the cost was a wake-up call that leaving behind students in their middle years was a missed opportunity. “If they were more involved, our community would benefit enormously,” he said. Giving principals more autonomy to speak up about fixes in schools and ensuring teachers had the time and resources to focus on individual students were part of the solution, Loader said. However, he acknowledged there wasn’t a silver bullet. As a principal, Loader introduced residential education programs including at MLC, where year 9 students live together in Marshmead in East Gippsland for eight weeks, and at Wesley College, where students go to Clunes, north of Ballarat. He said these programs helped students gain personal growth outside academic learning in years when they were at risk of disengagement at school. “A school that’s helping young people to grow as opposed to a school that’s focused on a number at year 12 is a very different thing,” he said. “That’s the cultural change we’re looking for – we no longer look at students as a number, but we look for personal growth.” A Victorian government spokesperson did not directly respond to questions about student disengagement in the classroom but acknowledged that regular attendance was critical to success.



Related Article Education Trouble getting your kids to school? So do many Australians Since 2023, Victoria’s year 12 completion rates have grown to 97 per cent, up 5 percentage points, and the year 10 to 12 retention rate of 85 per cent is the highest in eight years. The vocational major is also reshaping the pathways students take to the workforce. “We’ve made a record investment in student mental health, putting mental health workers in every public school,” the government spokesperson said. “Victoria’s school attendance rates continue to improve, thanks to the exceptional efforts of teachers and school leaders who work hard to ensure every student is engaged in their learning and feels like they belong at their school.” Opposition education spokesperson Brad Rowswell blamed Education Minister and now Premier Ben Carroll for “declining school attendance, falling student engagement, collapsing teacher morale, and serious safety concerns in early childhood services”. World.title: This value predicts future quality of life. In Australia, it’s tanking
World.content:
Analysis NationalScience This value predicts future quality of life. In Australia, it’s tanking Angus Dalton July 29, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Most Australians believe they live in a scientific powerhouse. They’d be wrong. Hundreds of scientists are sounding the alarm over our woefully unambitious level of investment in research and development, which has eroded over 15 years to the point that our quality of life is under threat. Australian science funding has crashed to historic lows. Aresna Villanueva Since a peak in 2009, overall investment into R&D has crashed to 1.69 per cent of GDP, a historic low that runs way below the OECD average of 2.7 per cent and could see Australia ranked last in the OECD within five years. As that value has edged downward, the facilities of Australia’s premier science organisation, CSIRO, have also quietly fallen into disrepair. The agency’s chief executive, Professor Doug Hilton, will tell the National Press Club on Wednesday that 80 per cent of CSIRO’s 800 buildings are at their technical end of life or not fit for purpose.



Maintenance costs are why the axe has had to swing on 350 jobs despite an additional $387.4 million funding injection from the latest budget, according to a draft version of Hilton’s speech. Amid feeble funding and slashed research jobs, most with a stake in science agree we are at a crossroads between choosing a vigorous reversal of scientific decline or accepting descent into becoming The Dumb Country. That’s why the Australian Academy of Science, comprising about 650 distinguished researchers, has marshalled its biggest campaign in 70 years. Science funding tied to quality of life Australia is good at waving the flag for science. In 2024, the late Professor Richard Scolyer and colleague Professor Georgina Long were named dual Australians of the Year for their work on melanoma. This year it’s space engineer Katherine Bennell-Pegg.



A survey by the academy showed 86 per cent of Australians assumed our investment in science is on par with other countries. The reality shocked them. Australian scientists may be world-class, but every stroke of their brilliance – synthetic DNA, new heart-rescuing drugs crafted from funnel-web venom, and ultra-efficient solar panels – has been made despite chronic underfunding, a Byzantine grants system and ailing facilities. “We haven’t really seen science being an election issue for a very long time, and it’s probably just complacency because the public believes that everything’s doing great,” says Dr Hayley Teasdale, a neuroscience researcher and head of science with the academy. “But scientists are now telling their kids not to follow in their footsteps, and that is heartbreaking.”



Teasdale knows the feeling of dashed scientific dreams. There was no local work in her field when she completed her PhD in Canberra. Dr Hayley Teasdale, head of science policy and advice at the Australian Academy of Science. Alex Ellinghausen But her expertise was keenly desired elsewhere: a neurotech company in San Francisco hired Teasdale as their lead scientist, to work on non-invasive brain stimulation treating the symptoms of Parkinson’s disease and depression. She returned to Australia during COVID. “There were no jobs here for me to continue my research in Australia,” she says. “I’ve lived the story.” Teasdale is now a torchbearer for the academy’s Restore Science campaign, which has rallied almost 18,000 people to write to their MPs calling for the return of research investment to an internationally competitive level.



The campaign follows the release of the Ambitious Australia report, a road map to a bolder, stronger science sector, commissioned by the government and delivered in March. The report calls for the reversal of declining research grants; lifting spending to the OECD average would require a boost of 43 per cent, or $2 billion. Science improves our lives through cheaper energy, more nutritious food, better medicine, new materials to use and sell, and more biodiverse cities. Without strong science and the urgent diversification of our economy beyond what we dig from the ground, the report warned, our lives in future decades will be worse. “The imperative for change is clear,” wrote the report’s leader, Tesla chair Robyn Denholm. “Future generations of Australians face a substantial reduction in their standard of living unless there are bold, nation-changing reforms.”



Some reform has followed. Last week, the government overhauled the Australian Research Council’s National Competitive Grants Program – one of the major sources of government science funding – from 15 schemes to seven, and simplified the process to reduce time burnt by researchers applying for grants (which can take up as much as half of a senior scientist’s workload). But that refresh, and the recent measures in the budget, did not deliver more cash. It just rearranged lab stools on the Titanic. If there’s one thing the report stressed, it’s that incremental change is no longer enough to save science. CSIRO cuts over, but 10-year upgrades needed With its axed researchers and ageing facilities, CSIRO has served as a metaphorical microcosm for the broader state of Australian science. But the exit of 800 support staff and 350 researchers – including from the health and biosecurity unit and climate modelling teams – has put the organisation back on steady ground, Hilton says. Some senior CSIRO staff have said mismanagement of COVID-era funds put the organisation in the red. Hilton says the job cuts were required after previous executives prioritised science jobs over building upgrades.



“I can understand why in the past people have preferenced keeping scientists on board and keeping our research portfolio broad, at the expense of repairs and maintenance,” he says. “But there’s a point where it does become unsustainable.” CSIRO chief executive Doug Hilton. Martin Ollman Addressing the maintenance and facility upgrade backlog will be a 10-year job, he warns. But he doesn’t foresee any more broad job losses in the pipeline: “The scale of those major cuts are behind us now.” Speaking broadly about the state of research funding, Hilton says science has to prove its worth against all the other pillars of a nation the government has to answer to: defence, the NDIS, an ageing population, the environment. “If science wants to contest for [funding], then we genuinely have to ask ourselves as organisational leaders, as team leaders in science, and as individual scientists, whether we’re doing absolutely everything to create the case that we are delivering the best value for money,” he says.



“I think that’s part of being a good steward of public money, and it’s part of the trust people have in science and scientists.” Related Article Exclusive

Science Australians made a pill to protect us from nuclear attack. We could lose it to the US He, too, sees us at a momentous junction between regression, inaction and forging a new path ahead. “I’m really sympathetic to the campaign the Academy of Sciences is running,” Hilton says. “But for me, it’s not about restoring science back to something that it was in the 1970s or 1980s. It’s how do we chart a new course for science where people widely across a big continent – in rural and regional areas, in outer suburban areas, in inner metro areas – they can all see the absolutely crucial nature of science in their future?” The Examine newsletter explains and analyses science with a rigorous focus on the evidence. Sign up to get it each week.

World.title: Hanson reveals Rinehart paid for London, Rome and Sicily flights
World.content:
PoliticsFederalOne Nation Hanson reveals Rinehart paid for London, Rome and Sicily flights Rob Harris Updated July 28, 2026 — 10:30pm ,first published 4:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Pauline Hanson says One Nation will begin unveiling its Victorian election candidates within days, claiming the party has almost completed a statewide slate as it attempts to turn a surge in support into seats at November’s election. Appearing in a one-hour special hosted by Paul Murray on News24, the rebranded Sky News Australia, Hanson said the party would start with upper house candidates as early as Friday before announcing its lower house contenders and releasing its Victorian policy platform. Pauline Hanson said her party will begin to name their candidates for the Victorian election. Luca Marino She said One Nation had secured candidates for about 74 of Victoria’s 88 electorates and expected to be represented in every seat across the state. She declined to name who would lead the party at a state level, telling Murray: “No, Paul. That’s not part of the deal.” Seeking to reassure voters that One Nation has learned from years of candidate controversies, Hanson said the party had introduced a tougher screening process ahead of the Victorian and next federal elections.



Hanson said there had been strong interest from prospective candidates, with about 1200 expressions of interest received in Victoria and 1500 nationally to contest the federal election. The party’s sole Victorian representative, Shepparton-based upper-house MP Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell, was re-endorsed on Tuesday. “It hasn’t been easy for the party over a period of time because the last election we got about six-and-a-half per cent,” she said. “So people are thinking they want to support us and give it a go and stand as a candidate ... but this time around there’s a real chance that we can actually win seats in the lower house and the Senate.” Gina Rinehart (left) and Hanson at a resort in Sicily earlier this month. The television appearance came hours after Hanson updated her parliamentary register of interests to disclose that mining billionaire Gina Rinehart paid for flights to London, Rome and Sicily, as well as inviting her to attend a Dolce & Gabbana fashion parade during her recent European trip.



Hanson declared she personally paid for her accommodation, meals and daily expenses. The disclosure followed scrutiny of the One Nation leader’s close relationship with Rinehart after photographs emerged of the pair together at the luxury Grand Hotel San Pietro in Taormina, Sicily, where the billionaire attended a Dolce & Gabbana event. Related Article One Nation Hanson blasted for White Australia comments after attending lavish Italian fashion show The push into Victoria comes as One Nation records its strongest polling in years. The latest Resolve Political Monitor for this masthead put the party on 22 per cent in the state, behind Labor and the Coalition, which were tied on 27 per cent. Hanson said Victoria had become a “basket case” following Tuesday’s leadership change that saw Ben Carroll replace Jacinta Allan as premier, arguing voters were increasingly looking beyond the major parties.



The claims of campaign readiness follow questions about the party’s preparations in Victoria. The Herald Sun reported earlier this month that One Nation’s Victorian leadership had moved to reassure frustrated prospective candidates that its election campaign was progressing, after some applicants complained about delays, secrecy around the campaign structure and uncertainty over candidate selection. The party told candidates that recruitment, policy development and organisational planning were under way, while regional committees were being established to help build a Victorian campaign operation. Loading Some candidates raised concerns about confidentiality agreements and fees of up to $5500 associated with running, with one applicant questioning whether the party had invested enough in the infrastructure needed to compete in a major state election.



One Nation has defended the secrecy around its preparations, arguing campaign strategy needed to be protected from leaks. Hanson said the party had introduced a far more extensive vetting process using advanced artificial intelligence technology to weed out rogue applications. She said the tougher screening process was designed to ensure candidates were prepared for the responsibility of representing One Nation as the party seeks to convert voter dissatisfaction into electoral gains. The system, developed by One Nation general manager Kelvin Morton and Hanson’s chief of staff, James Ashby, examines prospective candidates’ criminal records, financial history, civil litigation and social media activity. “So if you’ve got something that you’ve done somewhere else in the world, it’ll find you,” Hanson said.



Related Article Updated

Courts Pauline Hanson loses bid to overturn racial vilification ruling “It’ll tell us if you’ve got a criminal offence internationally. It’ll tell us if you’ve been a bankrupt, if you’re owing money to the taxation office. It’ll tell us if you’ve made any comment or put on Facebook some stupid comment.” The overhaul follows a history of damaging controversies involving One Nation candidates and elected members, including former senators Brian Burston, Fraser Anning and Rod Culleton. Other candidates have been forced to withdraw after offensive antisemitic or homophobic material posted online resurfaced, or after falling out with the party leadership. World.title: Australia vastly outspends China on Pacific aid. But there’s a catch
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPacific diplomacy Australia vastly outspends China on Pacific aid. But there’s a catch Matthew Knott July 28, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The perception China is pumping vast sums of development assistance into the Pacific compared with other nations is not borne out by the evidence, with Australia spending significantly more on aid, infrastructure funding and loans in the region than any other nation. However, Beijing has focused on maximising the pay-off of its spending by funding smaller but highly visible projects such as school upgrades, sports stadiums and medical clinics. The Aiwo Port Terminal in Nauru, which was recently upgraded with the help of a Chinese state-owned company. Facebook Chinese state-owned enterprises are also the dominant construction contractors for Pacific infrastructure, leaving Australian companies lagging far behind. Australia spent a total of $2.15 billion on aid to the Pacific in 2024, the most recent year with full data available, according to the Lowy Institute’s latest Pacific Aid Map, a detailed report on overseas development assistance in the region.



Australia accounted for 37 per cent of all development finance to the region, three times more than the next biggest aid contributor – New Zealand – and far ahead of China on 6 per cent. The release of the new database came as Chinese ambassador Xiao Qian bid farewell to associates at a ceremony in Canberra on Tuesday following an eventful 4½-year posting in the country. China’s ambassador to Australia, Xiao Qian, is departing after more than four years in the role. Alex Ellinghausen He will be replaced by Liu Jinsong, a seasoned diplomat who currently serves as the head of the Chinese foreign ministry’s department for Asian affairs. Xiao’s tenure was marked by friendlier relations, especially on trade, after China put Australia in the diplomatic deep freezer, but there were still moments of acrimony during his posting.



This included a fiery recent opinion piece Xiao wrote for this masthead accusing ASIO and other Western intelligence agencies of overhyping spying claims against China. Xiao told an audience at the Chinese embassy – including Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade deputy secretary Elly Lawson and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s top international adviser Rod Hilton – that the China-Australia relationship had “emerged from a low point and regained stability”, achieving a “comprehensive turnaround” from the days of outright hostility. The Lowy report shows the web of diplomatic arrangements the Albanese government has struck since it came to office is translating into dollars, with Papua New Guinea a particularly notable recipient of recent Australian funds. Australia struck a new military alliance and sweeping economic agreement with Fiji earlier this month, following similar previous deals with PNG, Vanuatu, Nauru and Tuvalu.



China test-fired a missile from a nuclear-powered submarine into the Pacific, landing near the Solomon Islands, on the same day Australia struck the Fiji agreements, drawing complaints from many Pacific nations. Related Article Exclusive

China relations China ambassador attacks ASIO, rejects foreign interference accusations Australia has also signed $3.4 billion in new loan agreements since 2021, making it the region’s largest source of new lending over that period. This is a major change from much of the 2010s when China was the dominant lender to the Pacific, drawing claims of being involved in “debt trap diplomacy”. “As other donors retreat and repeated economic shocks hit the region, Australia’s large and sustained support has been a stabilising factor for Pacific economies,” the report’s lead author, Riley Duke, said.



“Australia’s push into infrastructure, particularly strategic infrastructure, is reshaping the regional aid picture.” From 2010 to 2019, China signed about $5.2 billion in loans to Pacific countries, more than one-third of all lending deals in the region. Since 2020, China has committed just $558 million in new loan deals, falling well behind Australia. Despite this, the most recent Lowy Poll has found that 39 per cent of Australians believe China is the most influential country in the Pacific, ahead of Australia on 33 per cent. The United States spends little on aid in the region outside its three “compact of association” states – the Federated States of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands, and Palau – and US President Donald Trump has gutted foreign aid spending since returning to office.



As for Chinese aid in the Pacific, Duke said it “is highly reactive to diplomatic developments, functioning as a strategic lever Beijing can pull”. “When a country switches diplomatic recognition from Taipei to Beijing, or opens strategic negotiations with Australia, Chinese aid flows react,” he said. Related Article Pacific diplomacy Australia to spend $1b on defence alliance with Fiji in blow to China For example, since Nauru switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China in 2024, Beijing has funded its national sports stadium, as well as solar streetlights, schoolbag and computer donations, a medical clinic and a press conference room for the Ministry of Media. In Vanuatu, China has provided police with motorcycles, drones, riot equipment and training programs, as well as ongoing medical equipment donations and scholarship and training programs.



About 40 per cent of Pacific infrastructure projects involve a Chinese state-owned enterprise, even as China’s direct investment has declined. “As a result, they play a dominant and highly visible role in infrastructure across the region, one that extends well beyond China’s own bilateral financing,” the report finds. World.title: $90 million boost revealed in bid to address major world rugby disparity
World.content:
Exclusive SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby $90 million boost revealed in bid to address major world rugby disparity Nick Wright July 28, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A $90 million injection into grassroots rugby will create new women’s leagues and expand existing competitions to help the sport compete with cross code rivals ahead of the 2029 World Cup on home soil. While the federal government funding will not specifically target the top-flight Super Rugby Women’s, a beefed-up grassroots product shapes as a crucial building block towards growing the competition in the future. The Super Rugby Women’s season of just four rounds with a two-week finals system pales in comparison to countries such as England, where the Premiership Women’s Rugby is played over 20 weeks with nine teams. This has helped England feature in nine of 10 World Cup finals. The Wallaroos have not made it past the World Cup quarter-finals since 2010. Getty Images Rugby Australia has increased the Test program to at least 10 fixtures a year from 2026, but it has still grappled with player defections to the ever-growing NRLW, including Rugby 7s star Teagan Levi (Gold Coast Titans) and former Test squad member Caitlin Urwin (Brisbane Broncos).



The early program rollouts of the Australian Legacy funding into rugby have already generated an 8 per cent increase in female participation. Minister for Sport Anika Wells said a long-term legacy beyond the World Cup will be created from the initiative. Related Article Wallabies ‘Is this the end?’: Contract call twists fate for plagued Wallaby “The Albanese government’s $90 million investment will get more women, girls and grassroots players into rugby, growing the sport in Australia and the Pacific and leaving a lasting legacy from these major competitions,” Wells said. “The benefits of these tournaments will be felt well beyond the final whistle, encouraging Australians – especially women and girls – to pick up a ball and get involved.” The funding will also go towards women’s facility upgrades and the creation of courses to help more women and girls become coaches, referees and officials.



According to an AusPlay survey funded and led by the Australian Sports Commission, 39 per cent of Australians aged 15 and over who participated as a sports official in 2025 were women. However, that figure is not represented across the higher levels. Of the 44 clubs in the four women’s football codes – Super Rugby Women’s, NRLW, AFLW and A-League Women’s – only five head coaches are female: Karyn Murphy (Titans), Tamara Hyett (Western Bulldogs), Lisa Webb (Fremantle Dockers), Daisy Pearce (West Coast Eagles), and Natalie Wood (Essendon Bombers). Loading The federal government said the funding would also help deliver both Rugby World Cups – with the men’s 2027 showcase in Australia expected to generate more than $2 billion – while continuing to aid the Pacific Legacy program, which now operates in Fiji, Samoa and Tonga. “This is another way we are working with our Pacific neighbours to grow and strengthen our ties through sport,” Wells said. World.title: Upper Hutt mayor wants Trentham race course turned into high-density housing
World.content:
The mayor of Upper Hutt is already eyeing the marked-for-closure Trentham race course for high density housing.

Trentham is one of seven tracks proposed to be shut down as part of a masterplan to keep the horse racing industry afloat, announced on Tuesday.

Mayor Peri Zee said it could be an opportunity for the growing city.

"It's up to the racing bodies what they do with their sites, but it does create some potential opportunities for Upper Hutt if they do go ahead and close it," she said.

"As a large piece of land, there's always other things that could be done on that site if there was no racing to be done, something like a high density residential development with retail, which we all know we need more housing in the region, so that could potentially be beneficial."

Upper Hutt Mayor Peri Zee. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

She said the racecourse was once a major destination for Upper Hutt.

"It's obviously going to be sad for the people who have been involved in the racing industry and have fond memories there, but times do change," she said.

"When I was a teenager it was the place to go, we all used to get dressed up and go in big groups, walk down to the race track. It was more about, I think, getting dressed up and being all together than necessarily watching the horses, but it was the place to be.

"[Since then] it does seem there has been declining attendance and less buzz around big events."

She said demand for housing in Upper Hutt was massive.

"I'd be really happy to have additional housing capacity in Upper Hutt, we've had the highest number of first home buyers and part of that is because we have higher density housing coming here and we expect that to continue," Zee said.

"If that's their decision we'll look forward to working with them on what the future of that site could be."

Racing expert and former commentator Sheldon Murtha said track closures had been a long time coming.

"Anyone else who's in this game has said it's overdue," he said.

"It has to happen, there's been a race track in every corner of New Zealand since back in the day when racing was massive. It's not so massive [anymore].

"It's still a viable industry, it's still a sport people want to go and see in the holidays, people still want to participate in it whether they're fans or bettors... It's just not as big as it used to be."

He expected most in the industry would accept it as inevitable, but it wouldn't necessarily be popular.

World.title: Christchurch City Mission raises alarm as rough sleepers battle below freezing temperatures
World.content:
Christchurch City Mission says its team members are worried about finding dead rough sleepers as temperatures drop below freezing.

In a social media post, the charity said the past week had been tough for the unhoused.

Temperatures fell to minus four degrees celsius over the weekend.

The Mission's outreach team said it had been checking on the unhoused community - including those sleeping in cars - during the cold snap.

It was offering emergency shelter, warm clothing and sleeping gear.

"Our guys are genuinely worried they are going to find someone who has not made it through the night," the post read.

It said it was especially concerned as more elderly people were out on the streets.

World.title: Australian surgeon pledges Kiwi patients' fees towards new vascular compressions research
World.content:
The new RNZ investigative series All in Her Head has prompted an Australian surgeon to put his Kiwi patients' fees towards new research into a controversial and unfunded condition.

Canberra vascular surgeon Gert Frahm-Jensen has treated nine New Zealanders with multiple abdominal vascular compression syndromes - a rare and controversial condition in which blood vessels are squeezed, causing pain, nausea and, in severe cases, an inability to eat. He said he has consulted on about 20 New Zealand patients seeking treatment.

There are four main types of abdominal vascular compression syndrome, plus one in the pelvis. Having a single compression syndrome is - according to medical literature - extremely rare. But people with the connective tissue disorders hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS) and hypermobility spectrum disorder (HSD) are increasingly being diagnosed with up to all five at once, a trend that is dividing doctors.

The controversy is laid out in detail in All In Her Head, an RNZ podcast and multimedia investigation that examines the debate from all sides.

There is no scientific consensus on the link between hEDS/HSD and multiple abdominal vascular compression syndromes, whether patients can genuinely have more than one, or whether surgery is the answer.

While Health New Zealand will fund surgery to treat a single compression syndrome if needed, surgery to fix multiple compressions at once is not offered publicly or privately. Its official guidance goes further, warning against paying for surgery overseas, describing the operations as "experimental", with results "mostly of no benefit or significant harm".

Vascular Society of Aotearoa chair Kes Wicks said he had seen this in his own patients who had sought surgery overseas. The evidence simply "doesn't exist" to justify treating multiple compressions in hEDS and HSD patients, he said.

AIHH Episode One - The Girl Who Couldn't Eat All In Her Head Download MP3 46m

Those views, aired in the first episode of All In Her Head, have now prompted Frahm-Jensen, who had already been weighing up a research study, to act.

"We want to do more research on compression disorders... but I guess your podcast has just given us some impetus to really put the gears into motion, so to speak," he told RNZ.

He was "disappointed" in Health NZ's position.

"So I thought, well, why don't I put the fees that New Zealand patients pay me to come here and have surgery? I'll gladly donate that towards this research project until we get some data that can inform practice one way or another."

* New episodes of All In Her Head are out every Wednesday on RNZ, Apple, Spotify iHeart and wherever you get podcasts.

The study will track outcomes for patients having multiple abdominal vascular compression surgery - not only his own patients, but hopefully those of other doctors too.

"We're hopeful that we can develop a model where we can actually determine in what domains people benefit after surgery," he said.

"If we find that the majority of people do not actually have any benefit after surgery, or they report poor outcomes, then really that is a positive finding in a way, because that stops patients from having potentially major operations with very little improvement.

"And vice versa, if we can show that people actually do have a positive result ... that can really help to drive perhaps some reform, or maybe even some funding for the same research to be done in New Zealand on New Zealand patients," Frahm-Jensen said.

The study still needed to get ethics approval, but he hoped it would be up and running within three to six months.

"If the information turns out to to support treatment of multiple vascular compressions, then maybe that will be enough to shine the spotlight on it in New Zealand, so that these patients don't have to travel internationally to get surgery because it is a luxury for people who can afford it," he said.

'Alarm bells' over surgeries

Frahm-Jensen said he operates on up to three compression syndromes at a time, and will do these in the public health system for Australian patients where warranted.

His willingness to operate puts him at odds with New Zealand's vascular establishment.

Wicks, who has practised for three decades, said he has personally never confirmed a case meeting the threshold for surgery in a hypermobile patient, despite assessing several.

He described patients returning from overseas surgery with unresolved or worsened symptoms, in one case seeking a reversal that isn't medically possible. "That raises alarm bells," he said.

Frahm-Jensen said surgeons like Wicks may be subject to "observership bias" - seeing only the patients whose surgery didn't work, because those with good outcomes don't return to the public system.

His own patients had "mostly positive to moderately positive" results from the surgery, he said, though some had no change in symptoms at all.

Frahm-Jensen has only been offering this surgery for the past 18 months, and will only operate on patients older than 17.

Rachel Weatherly, from Whakatane, had surgery with Frahm-Jensen in September 2025 on two compression syndromes. Her journey is documented in All In Her Head. She now lives pain-free.

Many New Zealand patients instead travel to Germany for similar surgery with Professor Wilhelm Sandmann, who will operate on younger patients and uses slightly different surgical techniques. Health NZ withdrew public funding for his surgery in 2023 after a review found his methods experimental and risky.

Chris Holdaway. Supplied

Hamilton vascular surgeon Chris Holdaway has travelled to Germany to observe operations performed by Sandmann, with a view to performing similar surgeries in New Zealand but has been unable to get approval from the New Zealand health system to do so.

NZ 'not currently considering' its own research

Dr Frahm-Jensen said New Zealand's health system may actually be well placed to answer some of the unresolved questions around these surgeries. He pointed to New Zealand's reputation for supporting clinical research, including early trials of new medical devices in vascular surgery, as New Zealand had a more streamlined pathway than Australia for trialing new devices.

"I would have thought perhaps New Zealand would actually be ripe for doing this kind of research," he said.

Health NZ did not respond to RNZ's specific questions about the surgery now being offered in Canberra.

In a statement, national chief medical officer Dame Helen Stokes-Lampard said clinicians "always strive to provide effective treatments based on the best available evidence and that are in our patients' best interests, and appropriate for their individual needs". The health service avoided "inappropriate clinical interventions that risk causing unnecessary harm", she said.

Dame Helen Stokes-Lampard. supplied

Clinicians "regularly consider new and updated scientific evidence" on the benefits and wellbeing of patients within the public health system, in line with Medical Council principles.

The Vascular Society has also called for more research, suggesting Health New Zealand could fund a clinical registry of hEDS/HSD patients to track their condition and treatment outcomes over time.

Health NZ said it was currently doing a stocktake of all its clinical registries.

World.title: Wider review of former police officer's cases to be decided after historical case investigation - Police
World.content:
WARNING: This story contains content that may be distressing to some readers.

Police will decide whether a wider review of a former police officer's cases is needed once an investigation into a historical sexual assault case has concluded.

The case has been re-opened following a damning review, which has prompted calls for police to review other cases investigated by the former police officer.

RNZ earlier revealed an internal police review found the sexual assault investigation by former Detective Senior Sergeant Darren Folau was "poor", that the complainant was "not listened to and not believed" and that the young man's sporting career was "prioritised over [the complainant and any offending against her"].

The police said that, based on the review of the original investigation, the sportsman did not have a defence and was culpable of sexual conduct with a person under 16-years-old.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

The sportsman has been granted an injunction after he was approached by RNZ. The injunction means RNZ is not able to report his identity.

Territorial superintendent Ross McKay earlier confirmed in a statement to RNZ that police had reopened an investigation into historical claims of sexual assault dating back to 2010, after an initial review last year found "concerning management of the original file".

"An independent investigation team from another district is now leading the reinvestigation and review into the handling of the original inquiry."

On Tuesday, McKay told RNZ that once the current investigations had concluded "a decision can be made about whether other cases need to be assessed".

He also confirmed that assistant commissioner Corrie Parnell was the detective senior sergeant responsible for the Canterbury District Child Protection at the time.

"His role was to receive all case files and assign them to specific child protection investigators. It would not be appropriate to comment further while that case remains under investigation."

Calls for 'robust review of other cases'

HELP Auckland executive director Kathryn McPhillips earlier told RNZ the organisation would welcome any decision to further investigate sexual violence cases handled by Folau.

"The case already identified as requiring review raises legitimate questions about whether other cases he was involved in should also be reconsidered.

"Transparency and a willingness to critically examine whether cases were handled professionally, impartially and with the interests of survivors at the centre are essential to maintaining trust in the justice system.

"The findings in this case are deeply concerning and highlight the lasting harm that occurs when this does not happen," McPhillips said.

She said the organisation's thoughts were with the complainant.

"We welcome New Zealand Police's continued efforts to review and reopen cases where reports of sexual violence have not been handled appropriately. It is important that survivors know concerns can be revisited when failures are identified, and we hope this commitment to reviewing past cases continues."

Wellington Rape Crisis general manager Kyla Rayner said they also wanted to see a "robust review of other cases".

"A young woman disclosed. The investigation found she was not listened to, not believed, and that the sportsman's career was explicitly weighed in the balance. She then spent years - her words - feeling like what happened to her wasn't bad enough. That is what a failed investigation costs a person. The reinvestigation is the right step. But survivors are watching what comes next.

"For many survivors, the greatest harm is not only the violence they experience but the experience of not being believed, not being taken seriously, or feeling that other interests are prioritised over their safety and dignity. Trust in the justice system depends on survivors knowing they will be treated with fairness, respect and impartiality."

Rayner said reopening a file was not the same as restoring trust.

"Trust depends on what happens inside that reinvestigation - whether the survivor is supported, whether prosecutions follow where the evidence warrants, and whether the officer accountability process is genuinely independent."

The complainant told RNZ she believed it was important that police reviewed other cases Folau was involved in.

"His attitudes towards my reporting show he did not follow correct processes or work in a victim-centric way.

"It's possible that there are other children and young people who were also not believed, not listened to and not centred in their investigations."

She said police had told her that the culture had changed in police.

"To ensure police culture truly changes, they must do everything they can to rebuild trust. Genuinely owning their mistakes and reviewing historic cases is a first step."

RNZ approached Folau for comment on Wednesday. He said he was "not in a position to make any decisions or commentary".

In response to further questions, Folau said because of the little information he had, he did not think he could make any comments.

"The context I have is that I understand a review of an historical case is underway.

"I am comfortable that any recommendations I may have had input into will have been evidence based."

The sportsman said in a brief statement to RNZ he understood police were re-investigating the matter.

"So, it would be improper of me to make any comments at this stage. I have complete trust in the police."
